News.title: Yobs vandalise 4,000-year-old Bronze Age burial mound after removing rocks from protected historical site
News.content:
Next

A 4,000-year-old Bronze Age burial mound has been vandalised by yobs after removing rocks from the protected historical site.

The damage to Fire Beacon Cairn, near Crowcombe on the Quantock Hills National Landscape in Somerset, was spotted by a landowner on two occasions.



The shocking incidents were reported to local rangers and Historic England and marks the second time the monument has been vandalised in recent years.

Iain Porter, head ranger on the Quantock Hills, said he wanted visitors to grasp the historical importance of the ancient monuments.



He said: “It’s not a pile of stones – it’s a very important historic site… showing the ceremonial nature of that landscape historically.”

Fire Beacon Cairn is just one of around 50 scheduled monuments across the hills and it is a criminal offence to move the rocks or dig into the ground.

The cairn is a man-made mound, formed from a stack of stones marking a burial site – it is intended to measure around 4.9ft high and 82ft in diameter.

“Archaeologists and heritage officers are very concerned because if there are any finds or if there is any archaeological evidence of use and dating material, that’s where it’s going to be,” Mr Porter said.



He added that repairing the damage inflicted on the monument by vandals would likely come at a financial cost.

Dr Richard Brunning, senior historic environment officer at the South West Heritage Trust, said it was “especially worrying” when ancient monuments were damaged.

He said: “They’ve survived this long, it’d be terrible just to be destroyed on someone’s whim.”

Dr Brunning described the cairn as an “important relic of this very distant past”.

He added: “Archaeologically, they’re very important when they’re excavated because as they hold human remains that gives us a very good evidence for what past people were like.



“We can do all sorts of wonderful bits of science that you could never do in the past, such as looking at DNA from people buried that long ago.”

A Historic England spokesperson said the cairn had only recently been repaired after being vandalised two years ago.

They added: “We ask that the public remain vigilant and report any further vandalism to Historic England and the Quantock Hills National Landscape team.”

Quantock Hills National Landscape said the latest damage occurred “last week, and again over the weekend”.

A spokesperson added: “Information and evidence has been sent to Historic England.



“The pre-historic landscape is a key feature of the Quantock Hills with over 50 Scheduled Monuments and damage to a Scheduled Monument is a criminal offence.

“At these sites it is illegal to move rocks, stones or soil, to dig into or to cause any damage. It is also illegal to use metal detectors.”

Mr Porter, manager of the Quantock Hills National Landscape Team, said: “It is upsetting to see the level of damage caused to this Scheduled Monument.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“These sites (there are over fifty Scheduled Monuments on the Quantock Hills), form a vast network allowing us to understand the ceremonial importance of the hills from the Neolithic, through the Bronze-Age and into the Iron Age.

“We are working with the landowner and partners from Historic England and the South West Heritage Trust to assess the damage and to repair the site.”

News.title: Andy Burnham doubles down on trying to reach Net Zero by 2050 despite soaring energy bills
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has doubled down on trying to reach Net Zero by 2050.

The PM rejected demands to pull back on the eco dash to try to keep down energy bills.



He wrote in the Guardian: “The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility.

“In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy.



“I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh confirmed that Labour would not grant new North Sea oil and gas licences.



But she is expected to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields.

Those fields already had licences but need her final sign-off.

She also dismissed rumours that a decision would not come before the Holborn and St Pancras by-election where the Greens are a threat.

But Reform’s Richard Tice said: “Burnham babbles on with Labour’s Net Stupid Zero zealotry whilst our bills soar.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s ‘acting like Santa’ and must make tough cuts to get Britain back on track, blasts Iceland boss
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has been told to stop acting like Santa and make the tough cuts Britain needs to get back on track.

Iceland boss Lord Walker, the Government’s former cost-of-living tsar, blasted the Prime Minister for piling promises on taxpayers while ducking unpopular decisions.



Since taking office, Mr Burnham has pledged to axe VAT on household electricity, keep the £2 bus fare cap, end rough sleeping and slash business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues.

But Lord Walker warned Britain can no longer borrow its way out of trouble – and said firms must not be treated like a “piggy bank”.



He told LBC: “Andy Burnham has been Father Christmas so far, and it would be great if he’d start to get a bit more unpopular.

“For the last 50 years, Chancellors on the Left or the Right haven’t been too dramatic on raising taxes or reducing spending because they’ve been able to borrow a little bit more.



“Borrowing, increasing borrowing, is now off the table as an option. The bond markets are teaching us that lesson. Therefore, tough choices are now needed.”

His broadside came as Mr Burnham warned that his first Budget next month would be “challenging”, with the war in Iran pushing up oil and gas prices.

Lord Walker said Britain must “stop focusing on the cost-of-living crisis and start focusing on the cost of getting Britain back to work”.

He added: “We cannot, for the sake of us all, keep taxing business and viewing it as a piggy bank that can constantly be raided, because only business creates growth.



“We must therefore start reducing spending – or at least slow the rate at which it is increasing.”

Former Bank of England economist Andy Haldane has also accused the Government of failing to rein in public spending.

But ministers insisted their priority remained helping squeezed families and making everyday life more affordable across the country.

News.title: Labour under pressure to save Freeview after millions of England fans hit by World Cup streaming chaos
News.content:
Next

LABOUR is under mounting pressure to protect Freeview TV after millions of England fans saw their World Cup streams buffer, freeze or stop altogether over the summer.

Almost one in two footie fans who streamed a Three Lions match experienced the game cutting out, new polling suggests.



It comes as Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was concerned about plans to stop free-to-air TV for good.

The Prime Minister told the Commons he was concerned about the proposals and wanted to have a “proper look” at them.



The Sun has launched a Save Our Sets campaign to protect free TV and has seen the MPs’ letter.

More than 40 per cent of footie fans had streaming problems with the World Cup final.

One in five Brits have had regular difficulties while trying to watch a big live event.

Meanwhile 34 per cent of people had problems during the FA Cup final and Eurovision.

Rotherham MP Sarah Champion said: “This polling shows the extent that free TV is still relied on including by many of my constituents in Rotherham and by over ten million homes across the UK, for some of those, the television connects them to the outside world.”

A Broadcast 2040+ spokesman added that nobody had voted to “have their telly switched off” and urged ministers to listen to people’s concerns.



They added: “Terrestrial TV is the one platform that never lets the nation down. It reaches almost every home, it’s free, and it doesn’t crash when 20 million people tune in at once.

Strand Partners surveyed 1000 members of the public in September.

Almost 70 per cent of punters have previously said they believe the PM will have broken his word if he goes ahead with the switch off.

News.title: Third person dies from malaria linked to Frankfurt Airport after ‘mosquito gets trapped on plane’ in rare outbreak
News.content:
FLYING FEVER Third person dies from malaria linked to Frankfurt Airport after ‘mosquito gets trapped on plane’ in rare outbreak







Next

A THIRD person has died of malaria after a single mosquito was reportedly trapped on a plane to Germany.

Several people were rushed to hospital following the rare outbreak of the tropical disease aboard a flight to Frankfurt.



Traps were set up around Germany‘s busiest transport hub in July as officials desperately tried to contain the outbreak.

But in August, one airport worker tragically died of the disease.



Now, an infected resident of Schwanheim, north of the airport, has passed away in hospital, city officials revealed on Thursday.

Shockingly, the victim was not an airport employee nor had they travelled to a malaria-riddled region.

Another resident of the area has also been struck down with malaria.

A statement from city officials confirmed: “Both individuals had become infected with the malaria-causing parasite, even though they had not travelled to a malaria-endemic region and had not worked at the airport”.

The terrifying phenomenon is known as “airport malaria” – and can strike anyone who comes into contact with the infected insect.

Parasites can be stowed away on flights from malaria regions – and then escape to bite people on the other side.



Malaria can only be contracted from the bite of an infected mosquito and cannot be spread human to human.

The disease can cause fever, chills and debilitating headaches.

Infections can even become life-threatening if they remain untreated, according to the World Health Organisation.

But public health officials said: “For the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low.

Four employees were previously reported to have fallen ill with malaria between July 4 and 6.



News of the first infections was reported on July 16, with officials saying the employees were likely bitten earlier in the week.

An airport spokesperson said the victims worked in the airport’s baggage handling section.

It is unclear from where the plane had been flying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Between 1969 and 2024, 145 cases were reported – including nine in Germany.

The last known case of malaria at Frankfurt Airport happened in 2023.

News.title: Mystery death of Ukrainian Putin critic in Portugal being probed amid fears it was a Kremlin hit
News.content:
Next

THE death of a Vladimir Putin critic is being investigated amid fears it was a Kremlin hit.

Pavlo Sadokha, 56, was found dead at Quarteira, Algarve, on Sunday.



The Ukrainian had a history of heart disease and, at first, police cited natural causes.

But family said his health was “perfectly under control” — leading Portuguese prosecutors to investigate.



The family also want toxicology checks.

In June 2025 Sadokha claimed the Kremlin was using youth games to militarise children of Russian expats in Spain.

He lived in Portugal for two decades.

Putin’s FSB assassins are known to be hunting prominent Ukrainians across Europe.

Suspects are still at large over the 2024 gun murder of Russian defector Maxim Kuzminov near Benidorm.

The 28-year-old airman, who flew his Russian Mi-8 helicopter to Ukraine, was executed by six shots in a car park after starting a new life in Spain.



His killers – who fled in a car later found torched – have never been found.

News.title: Fury as ‘staggeringly naive’ Archbishop of Canterbury gives award to Bin Laden apologist on 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Next

THE Archbishop of Canterbury has been blasted as “staggeringly naive” for giving an Osama Bin Laden apologist an award — on last week’s 25th anniversary of September 11.

Dame Sarah Mullally presented the “reconciliation and interfaith co-operation” honour to Tahir Ashrafi, chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council.



In 2007, Ashrafi sparked fury when he condemned the award of a knighthood to Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie. The bearded Muslim leader hit back further by announcing he would award Bin Laden the title of Saifullah, or “Sword of God” honour.

Ashrafi said at the time: “If a blasphemer can be given the title ‘Sir’ by the West then a mujahid who has been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British must be given the lofty title of Islam, Saifullah.



“We are pleased to award the title of Saifullah after the British Government’s decision to bestow the title of ‘Sir’ on blasphemer Rushdie. This is the highest title for a Muslim warrior.”

Left-leaning Dame Sarah beamed as she set aside Ashrafi’s views to salute him at Lambeth Palace.



Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy MP said: “The naivety of the Archbishop in presenting an award to someone who openly praised Bin Laden is staggering — and on the anniversary of 9/11, too.

“Our leaders must face up to the reality not all cultures are based on the same foundations as ours, and not all share our desire for co-operation and freedom.



“Western political and religious leaders should stand up vigorously for our own values and achievements, rather than apologising for our history or celebrating those who seek to do us harm.”

Victim support campaigner Travis Frain OBE, a survivor of the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack, called the Archbishop’s move “a grave misjudgment by the Church”.

Tim Dieppe, at Christian Concern, added: “The absurdity of this beggars belief. Mullally is clearly uninformed about both Ashrafi and about Islam. There is no justification for giving him an award.”

However, last night a Church spokesman said: “Previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light . . . and we can now confirm the award has been withdrawn.”

News.title: Tributes to ‘beautiful and loving’ mum, 34, who died after being knocked down while waiting for bus – as man arrested
News.content:
BUS TRAGEDY Tributes to ‘beautiful and loving’ mum, 34, who died after being knocked down while waiting for bus – as man arrested







Next

TRIBUTES have been paid to a “beautiful and loving” mum who died after she was knocked down while waiting for a bus.

Danielle Sharpe, 34, was pronounced dead at the scene following the horror crash in Corby, Northamptonshire, on September 11.



Northamptonshire Police said a black Vauxhall Insignia smashed into a bus stop at around 7.30am.

The force said a 55-year-old man from Corby was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving a vehicle while unfit through drugs.



He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Now, Danielle’s family has released a heartbreaking tribute, describing her as a “loving mother, daughter, granddaughter, sister and aunty”.



It read: “Danielle was such a beautiful and loving mother, daughter, granddaughter, sister and aunty and was loved by so many.

“We are just beyond heartbroken and cannot believe that she has gone.

“In her short life she left a remarkable stamp on this world, and we cannot put into words just how much we are going to miss her.

“We are so thankful for everybody’s love and support during this difficult time, but while we try to come to terms with the loss of Danielle, we would appreciate some time and space to grieve in private.



“We would also ask that people do not speculate about what happened on social media and please allow the police to investigate the collision.”

Cops say the black Vauxhall was travelling along Willow Brook Road and “appeared to be turning left into Fotheringhay Road, when the vehicle left its intended path and collided with a bus stop”.

A teenage boy was also left with minor injuries following the incident.

A police spokesperson said: “Detectives from the Serious Collision Investigation Unit would still like to hear from anyone who may have dash-cam footage which captured any part of the collision.”

News.title: Vladimir Putin eyes another election win as Russia votes for first time since Ukraine war
News.content:
Vladimir Putin eyes another election win as Russia votes for first time since Ukraine war

The next three days will primarily settle how seats are divided across the Duma, Russia's principal legislative body, as Putin eyes another election win

View 3 Images Russia votes, and Putin remains a surefire win (Image: (Image: Getty))

Russians are heading to the polls in the first election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine commenced in 2022.

‌



The three-day vote will determine the seat distribution in Russia's lower house, known as the Duma. For the first time, the polls will also encompass four illegally annexed Ukrainian regions.

‌



With 111 million Russian voters casting their ballots between now and Sunday, most political analysts are in agreement that the result is already a foregone conclusion: President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party is virtually certain to triumph.

‌



The next three days will primarily settle how seats are divided across the Duma, Russia's principal legislative body.

United Russia - Putin's own party - currently holds more than two-thirds of the Duma's seats.

As for the opposition, there are 18 other parties in total. Of those 18, only 10 appear on the ballot and have been cherry-picked by the Kremlin.

‌



View 3 Images A man at a polling station during voting in the State Duma of the Russian Federation in St. Petersburg in 2021 (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

These 10 parties will neither challenge the government with opposing legislation nor voice open criticism.

The majority are also unlikely to secure enough support to earn a place in Parliament.

‌



Nevertheless, Russia analyst Mark Galeotti suggests the Kremlin will ensure it "is still absolutely dominant within the Duma", though United Russia may be "allowed to slip a little" for the sake of credibility.

The previous Russian election, held in 2021, was condemned for irregularities by leading independent election monitor Golos. As Russian citizens headed to the polls this weekend, anxiety in Poland continued to mount amid growing fears that the Kremlin is plotting to extend its aggression beyond Ukraine to the wider European continent.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk cautioned on Thursday that Russia is scheming to launch hybrid attacks using drones or missiles against European nations backing Ukraine, including Poland.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (Image: ROLAND SCHLAGER, APA/AFP via Getty Images)

Russia would claim the strikes were "accidental" in order to "paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries" to come to the aid of any member state falling under attack, Mr Tusk warned in an address to the Polish parliament.

"There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction," he cautioned. "The official narration will be that it's an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response."

News.title: Royal Family live: Prince Harry says it's 'good to be back' on first public outing since UK return
News.content:
Prince Harry said "it's good to be back on British soil" as he made his first public appearance since moving back to the UK.

The Duke of Sussex appeared in an exuberant mood as he arrived for the inaugural Spirit of Invictus awards at the Old Naval College in London.

Asked how things were going before be went into the venue, he said: "Good! It’s good to be back on British soil.” In a speech tonight Harry told the audience of armed forces veterans "your service matters".

The duke spoke about his journey setting up the global Invictus Games and how competitors have gone on to achieve the impossible and join "the best community in the world".

He said: "Tonight you will hear extraordinary stories, but I hope we don’t simply applaud them. I hope we recognise what they ask of us.

"Because Invictus was never created so that the rest of us could sit back and admire resilience. It was created so that people who have served know that when their lives change, we don’t disappear.

"They served us. We must continue to show up for them, and I guarantee you, we all benefit when we do.

"And to the veterans here tonight, and those wherever you are around the world, I want to say this as one soldier to another: your service matters. What you gave in uniform matters. And people far beyond the military community who see in your example what courage, resilience and leadership actually look like.

"People are watching. The teammate who is struggling. The young soldier wondering what life after uniform might look like. The family trying to find its way forward.

"At a time when societies around the world are being tested, the Invictus spirit has something to teach all of us. This community doesn’t just demonstrate resilience. It helps build it. Never underestimate what your example gives to the world."

News.title: Australia airport outage: Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane all hit by delays after 'technical issue'
News.content:
Australia airport outage: Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane all hit by delays after 'technical issue'

Travellers have been thanked for their patience after the outage which affected passengers at Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane airports on Friday morning, September 18

View 2 Images Queues at Sydney Airport [file image] (Image: AAP/PA Images)

A technical outage in Australia has caused major delays across three international airports, with Border Force officials launching an investigation.

‌



The Australian Border Force (ABF) technical outage caused major delays for international passengers at Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane airports on Friday morning, with an ABF spokesperson confirming the issue has impacted both outbound and inbound international travellers.

‌



As a result, huge queues formed throughout international terminals, with the tech outage causing headaches at the e-gates for outbound and some inbound flights.

‌



View 2 Images The issue has now been resolved (Image: Manchester Evening News)

An ABF spokesperson said specialist officers were being deployed to the affected areas to resolve the problem.

Article continues below

“The Australian Border Force is aware of a technical outage impacting E-gates for outbound and some inbound passengers,” the spokesperson said.

“Additional ABF officers are being surged into work areas to manually process passengers and provide as minimal disruption as possible.

“We appreciate travellers’ patience as we continue to work through the issue.”

News.title: Police share new information eight months after man found dead on Wolverhampton school field by young girl
News.content:
Police share new information eight months after man found dead on Wolverhampton school field by young girl

Police investigating the death of Neil Thompson, 45, who was discovered at Smestow Academy in Wolverhampton on January 19 by an 11-year-old girl have shared new information eight months on

View 4 Images Neil Thompson who was found dead in the grounds of Smestow Academy in Wolverhampton (Image: West Midlands Police / SWNS)

Detectives believe they may be a step closer to solving the tragic mystery of how a beloved dad was found dead on a school field after his e-bike ended up in a canal.

‌



The body of Neil Thompson, 45, was discovered at Smestow Academy in Wolverhampton on January 19 by an 11-year-old girl as she prepared for a PE lesson. An inquest heard the dad died from aspiration of blood caused by traumatic facial injuries and a serious head injury.

‌



Police initially launched a homicide probe, but officers now believe Neil may have suffered the devastating injuries when he crashed his e-bike.

‌



View 4 Images The new image of Neil Thompson's water-damaged electric bike (Image: West Midlands Police / SWNS)

The mystery took another twist after the water-damaged bike was later hauled from a canal and left propped against a bridge.

On what would have been Neil's 46th birthday, West Midlands Police released pictures of the rust-covered e-bike and appealed for the person who pulled it from the water to come forward.

‌



Detective Sergeant Amie Petford said: "His family are now asking that the person who got the bike out of the water to get in touch so that they can have a place where they can go to grieve.

"The bike was rusty and appeared that someone had pulled it out of the canal and left it by a bridge at a lock so it is likely it would have been near there, but his family are hoping to know exactly where so they can lay flowers."

View 4 Images Tributes have been paid to a 45-year-old man who was found dead at a school by a horrified 11-year-old pupil during a PE lesson (Image: Anita Maric / SWNS)

‌



Police believe Neil left home on his electric bike at around 8.17pm on January 18 to visit a friend. He set off for home at around 1am the following morning, with CCTV capturing him riding along a canal towpath at 1.26am.

A dog walker later photographed him in the grounds of Smestow Academy at around 7.15am after spotting him while walking through Smestow Valley Nature Reserve. Police believe Neil was still alive at that point, but what happened in the hours between remains a mystery.

A post-mortem examination found significant injuries to the left side of his face, evidence of a traumatic brain injury and a fracture around the left eye socket. Consultant pathologist Dr Brett Lockyer said the injuries were consistent with blunt-force trauma and suggested Neil could have suffered them in a heavy fall, but could also have been assaulted.

‌



View 4 Images Smestow Academy, Wolverhampton, where pupils discovered the body of a man in the grounds (Image: Anita Maric / SWNS)

However, police now believe he died as a result of injuries suffered when his e-bike crashed into the canal.

Following his death, Neil's family paid tribute, saying: "Our beautiful son, brother, father and friend Chuck, very much loved in the community of fishing, his one true love. His love for life and funny stories touched the lives of so many people."

Article continues below

The father of the 11-year-old girl who discovered Neil's body previously revealed how the youngster was left "really shaken up" by the ordeal. He said: "My daughter phoned her mum up, screaming, and told her that she found a dead body by the goal posts on the field.

"She's only 11 years of age. They went out for PE and it was very foggy. It's terrible what she's had to see."

News.title: F-16 crash - recap: US fighter jet explodes in Michigan during training exercise
News.content:
The F-16 was carrying out a routine training mission when it crashed

An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan, with images from the scene showing a massive fire engulfing debris in a field

An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan - moments after its pilot ejected and parachuted to safety.

The crash happened at around 2pm EDT (7pm BST) near County Road 633, between Jeffrey Place and Blair Townhall Road, in Green Lake Township. Dramatic images from the scene show a large fire and thick smoke rising from the wreckage.

The aircraft belonged to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing and was carrying out a routine training mission, the Texas Military Department said. Sgt Derek Gutierrez, of the 149th Fighter Wing, said the pilot is receiving medical treatment at a local hospital.

Traffic has been blocked and motorists have been urged to avoid the area. A shelter-in-place order has been issued for residents nearby.

News.title: Major update after UK airline plunged into administration – 'We are delighted'
News.content:
Major update after UK airline plunged into administration – 'We are delighted'

British freight airline European Cargo Limited entered administration on June 3, but its fleet of 16 Airbus A340-600 aircraft has since been rescued

View 2 Images European Cargo's aircraft have been acquired by European Aviation Group (Image: European Cargo Limited)

A huge fleet of cargo aircraft has been acquired after a British airline set up during the Covid-19 pandemic collapsed into administration.

‌



European Cargo Limited (ECL) - a freight airline based at Bournemouth International Airport - entered administration on June 3, with Stuart Morris, Robert Fishman and David Soden, of Teneo Financial Advisory Limited, appointed as joint administrators.

‌



Teneo Financial Advisory said the appointment followed a "period of significant financial pressure on the business, driven by reduced flying activity and working capital and fuel cost pressures". The administrators confirmed that ECL had ceased trading and that 178 employees had been made redundant.

‌



View 2 Images European Cargo Limited entered administration on June 3 (Image: European Cargo Limited)

EES delays update over 9 UK tourist destinations - key details READ MORE :

Flight to Manchester declares mid-air medical emergency after entering UK airspace READ MORE :

However, all of European Cargo's assets have since been acquired by European Aviation Group, which is led by Paul Stoddart, the former boss of the Minardi Formula One team.

The deal, announced in late August, includes ECL's fleet of 16 Airbus A340-600 aircraft, seven of which are understood to be flight-ready, as well as its Rolls-Royce Trent 553 and Trent 556 spare engines.

‌



Stoddart, chairman and chief executive of European Aviation Group, said: "We are delighted to have concluded our acquisition of all of the assets of ECL with the joint administrators.

"Whilst this is a massive investment from EAL, I feel totally confident that we can keep this excellent fleet of cargo aircraft flying for the foreseeable future."

Despite the sale of its assets, ECL remains in administration, according to Companies House.

Article continues below

European Aviation Group has not confirmed whether any of the 178 former European Cargo employees will be offered jobs as a result of the acquisition.

European Cargo began operations in April 2020 after its parent company at the time, European Aviation, responded to an urgent request from the UK Government to transport personal protective equipment (PPE) from Malaysia.

The carrier subsequently operated more than 400 charter flights carrying PPE and Covid-19 testing kits. Its aircraft were also painted in commemorative liveries paying tribute to the NHS.

News.title: Elderly lollipop man struck by car on crossing in front of primary school pupils
News.content:
Elderly lollipop man struck by car on crossing in front of primary school pupils

The crash, which involved two cars and a pedestrian, took place just outside Holy Family Catholic primary school as children and parents were heading home

View 2 Images The crossing outside the school (Image: MEN)

An elderly lollipop man was hit by a car in front of children and parents at a Greater Manchester school.

‌



The incident took place during pick up time as pupils and parents were heading home from Holy Family Catholic primary school in Sale Moor, Trafford, yesterday. The crash involved two cars, police said, and a pedestrian.

‌



A man, 45, was later arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving and drug driving and has since been bailed.

‌



Meanwhile, the crash victim, aged in his 70s, is understood to remain in hospital with a suspected leg fracture.

His injuries have been described as "serious" by the police.

View 2 Images A man was arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving and drug driving and has since been bailed. (Image: MEN)

‌



A statement from Greater Manchester Police reads: "We were called shortly before 4pm on Wednesday 16 September to reports of a (road traffic collision) on Old Hall Road, Sale, involving two cars and a pedestrian.

"Officers attended and a man in his 70s was taken to hospital with serious injuries.

"A 45-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving and drug driving. He has since been bailed pending further enquiries."

Article continues below

The school has emailed parents to inform them about the incident, saying the lollipop man is recovering in hospital, Manchester Evening News reports.

The crash took place on a pedestrian crossing on New Hall Road, a busy road between the M60 and Sale Moor village, located just outside the school.

A spokesperson for Trafford Council said: "This was a very upsetting incident and we are offering support to the school crossing patrolman who was injured, as well as to the school community. We are also supporting police with their investigation."

News.title: Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil
News.content:
Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil

A man described as 'bald and in his fifties or sixties' was reportedly spotted recording a pupil on Clover Road in Timperley, Greater Manchester, outside Wellington School

View Image The incident took place in the vicinity of Wellington School in Timperley (Image: Google Street View)

Parents of students at a school in Greater Manchester have been asked to be vigilant after a man was reportedly seen following and recording a pupil.

‌



The incident allegedly took place outside Wellington School, a mixed secondary and sixth form in Timperley.

‌



An email sent to parents described the man as "a bald male in his fifties or sixties".

‌



The warning added that he appeared to be recording the student in question on his phone.

It read: "We want to make all parents and carers aware of a report that an adult male in the area was seen on Clover Road yesterday appearing to follow a student and record them with his phone.

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday with 19 counties at risk READ MORE :

"He has been described as a bald male in his fifties or sixties, wearing glasses and a dark tracksuit."

‌



The school added that the incident has been reported to the police, Manchester Evening News reports.

The message continued: "Staff on the school gates have been alerted to this report so that they can remain vigilant as students are leaving site."

Parents have also been urged to contact the school should they have any further concerns and report any similar incidents to the police.

Article continues below

The concerning incident quickly attracted reaction from parents on social media, as the email was shared in an Altrincham Facebook group. The poster urged: "Please make your children aware."

One user replied: "These warnings feel far too frequent these days, so worrying."

Mirror Online has approached Greater Manchester Police for comment.

News.title: Twenty women had breasts removed unnecessarily during cancer treatment, NHS trust admits
News.content:
Twenty women underwent mastectomies unnecessarily while being treated for breast cancer, an NHS trust in north-east England has told the BBC.

They were among hundreds of patients who came to harm during treatment at the breast unit of the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust (CDDFT).

The admission comes in the wake of revelations about serious failures in the unit, as reported by the BBC last year.

Steve Russell, who has recently taken over as CDDFT's chief executive, says he apologises "unreservedly" for the harm the trust caused.

"There are no words I could use to convey how personally distressed I am," he says. "What happened was utterly unacceptable."

News.title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

News.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
News.content:
If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

News.title: US fans with Ed Sheeran tickets left 'torn' over Macklemore controversy
News.content:
The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.

Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.

All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.

"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".

Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.

Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.

News.title: British woman rescued in Malawi shootout that left four suspected kidnappers dead
News.content:
A British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi nearly a week ago has been rescued in a police operation that left four suspected kidnappers dead and a senior police chief wounded.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was freed on Thursday during an operation on the outskirts of the southern city of Blantyre, police said.

Officers exchanged gunfire with the suspected kidnappers, who police said were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a pistol.

"The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," the Malawi Police Service said in a statement.

Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira, who was involved in the operation, also sustained gunshot injuries and is being treated in hospital. The police statement said he was in a stable condition.

Osman was reunited with her family following the rescue and was also taken to hospital for treatment, and for physical and mental health assessments, local media reported.

Osman's younger brother, Shobi Jiwa, praised the Malawian police for securing her release, telling the UK's Sun newspaper that the family was deeply grateful for the force's efforts in investigating the kidnapping.

He also paid tribute to Kayira, the police chief who was shot during the rescue operation, describing him as the family's "hero" for putting his own life at risk to save her.

Police have not identified the four suspected kidnappers who were killed and have not provided further details about how officers located the group.

Osman was abducted by four unidentified men in Blantyre's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood on 11 September.

Police said she had been driving home when the men blocked her vehicle, forced her into another car and drove away.

Her disappearance prompted a major search operation, with authorities offering a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha ($17,000; Â£12,500) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible.

Osman, who is from Leicester in the UK, has lived in Malawi for several years and works for an auditing firm. She is married and has two young children.

The UK Foreign Office earlier told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

The case had puzzled investigators because police said there had been no known ransom demand or communication from the kidnappers following her disappearance.

Her family had made emotional public appeals for her safe return, describing the disappearance as deeply distressing and urging anyone with information to contact police.

The kidnapping also caused concern among Malawi's business community and British nationals living in the southern African country, where abductions of foreign nationals are relatively uncommon.

Police have not disclosed a possible motive or said whether they believe other people were involved.

They said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances surrounding the kidnapping and the subsequent rescue operation.

Authorities have urged the public to remain calm while the investigation continues.

News.title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
News.content:
A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.

The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.

But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.

Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.

News.title: UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs
News.content:
The UK's "dismal" record in selecting songs and acts for Eurovision is to be scrutinised by MPs.

In May, Look Mum No Computer came last with one point. In 2023 Mae Muller finished second from bottom and in 2021 James Newman came last - this time with "nul points".

The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC, sometimes with a record label or music management company.

The chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee, Dame Caroline Dinenage, said: "We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years [Sam Ryder to one side] is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else".

News.title: Badenoch says she is instructing lawyers to challenge government after Tory-run council's 94% tax hike
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.

She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous" but that "they're not doing it because they want to".

Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to see if an Â£84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.

The government has insisted it needs to reform the "outdated" council funding system to move money to where it is most needed.

Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over Â£1,000, compared to above Â£2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.

But this would nearly double with the planned Â£958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London.

There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.

Changes to the funding formula for councils announced last year will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. Wandsworth Council said it stood to lose Â£84m annually in funding by the end of the next three years.

Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".

"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.

"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.

"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
News.content:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden.

Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007.

Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context".

Lambeth Palace now says "comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led (us) to reconsider this award and we can now confirm that the award has been withdrawn".

In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance".

His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him.

He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie.

But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people.

Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden.

In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy.

But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2,000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s.

They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too.

Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands.

But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs".

The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities".

News.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into 'Made in Europe' industry scheme
News.content:
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses â wherever they are based across the UK â get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

News.title: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference
News.content:
Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend.

Two years on from their best ever general election result, conversations with those on the party's frontbench, its MPs, and backroom staff reveal a frustration at what many see as a failure to capitalise on that success.

Polling by YouGov in the build up to the conference highlighted the Lib Dems "have seen no real growth in support since the last general election" and if anything have slipped back.

"We lack the ability to say something new or interesting," said one senior Lib Dem MP.

"There is no energy, no excitement."

A frontbencher said: "With the possible exception of our position on Trump, you could characterise most of our press lines as 'a Lib Dem spokesperson said, steady on now, gently does it'."

Others describe the party's approach as "boring" and are spooked by the rise of the Green Party under Zack Polanski.

The party's leadership are aware of the anger. They insist this conference will be a "gear shift".

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader, told me it would be "a gloves-off kind of conference".

"You'll see a bit of fighting talk," she said.

Some of the caution until now has been deliberate. The party's leadership met over the last few months and discussed whether to copy Polanski's punchy, social media-focused style but decided it wouldn't appeal to the well-heeled areas of southern England that form the Lib Dem heartlands.

Those involved in that decision point to Polanski's recent struggles and feel vindicated.

But at all levels of the party there is an acknowledgement they lag behind other parties on grabbing attention on social media, highlighted by Andy Burnham's "social first" approach.

The party has only recently rolled out training for its MPs on making social videos, something senior figures despair at.

"When we have a success we're very good at getting a leaflet sent out to supporters straight away," one senior MP said. "But we don't do that for socials."

Digital and social media will be a focus of at least 17 fringe events at conference, as the party tries to improve its online communications.

But others worry that social media is just the medium and the problem is with the message.

News.title: Sunshine to return to parts of UK with warmer and drier weather on way
News.content:
Don't pack away your summer clothes just yet as warmer and drier weather could be set to return to the UK next week.

Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of England and Wales - several degrees above the average for the time of year.

Forecasts for early next week show an area of high pressure building near the UK. This will largely block Atlantic weather systems, which often bring wind and rain, from reaching the country.

North-west Scotland will see some rain but these systems are not expected to push across the rest of the UK, so this would mean drier weather with lighter winds and higher daytime temperatures for most.

The last few weeks have been very changeable with rain and strong winds in most parts of the UK.

Despite this, the whole of Wales and most of England are still in drought.

After stronger south-westerly winds are due to blow cloud and outbreaks of rain across from the west on Friday, the weather will start to settle down over the weekend.

The northern half of the UK will see a return to sunshine and blustery showers on Saturday, with most of the showers being in Scotland.

The southern half of the UK is likely to be more cloudy and have a muggy feel with the chance of light rain and drizzle.

News.title: Police hold press conference in search for girl, 13, missing for six days
News.content:
The mother of a 13-year-old girl who has been missing from home for six days has made an emotional plea for her safe return.

Lillia, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, was last seen on Saturday at the Trafford Centre shopping mall wearing a small black backpack.

Police said they believe she then boarded a bus to nearby Altrincham at about 13:50 BST, but it is not known where she got off.

In a statement read out by an officer during a police press conference earlier, her mother Jessica said: "Lil, I love you so much. My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe. We all need you back home safe and well."

Ch Supt Helen Critchley, of Greater Manchester Police, said: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe.

"You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home."

News.title: Andy Burnham to meet Irish Taoiseach for first time
News.content:
The Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Taoiseach (Irish PM) MicheÃ¡l Martin will hold their first official meeting in Manchester on Friday.

Martin will be the first international leader to visit Number 10 North, the government said ahead of the talks.

The men are expected to discuss further strengthening of the UK/Ireland relationship including boosting trade, security and working with the EU.

Burnham said he was "delighted" to be hosting the taoiseach and said it was an "historic and proud day for Manchester".

"No10 North is all about creating opportunities for working people, and our partnership with Ireland as we improve the lives of people in both of our countries is a key part of that," he said.

"There is so much we can achieve together: from our shared commitment to the Good Friday Agreement, to trade, to working with Europe and supporting Ukraine. We are the closest of friends, and I look forward to further strengthening that friendship."

Following their meeting, the leaders will visit a local Irish community centre to meet with representatives from the Irish community in Greater Manchester.

The visit comes days after US President Donald Trump made remarks supporting a "unified Ireland".

On his visit to Northern Ireland last month, Burnham said a border poll was "off the table", but later said he stood by the Good Friday Agreement.

It is also expected that the two leaders will discuss reform of the Stormont institutions as well as progress on replacing the controversial Troubles legacy act during their meeting.

News.title: Early Bowie music available to stream for first time
News.content:
Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read.

What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name.

From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream.

"They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist.

For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums.

He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons.

Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles.

"It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao.

In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time.

But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats.

News.title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
News.content:
A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.

Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.

The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.

Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.

In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising.

News.content:

A British mother of two who was abducted in the southern African nation of Malawi last week has been rescued, police say.

Inspector General Richard Luhanga, the head of the Malawi police, said Nusrat Osman, 47, was safe and had been reunited with her family following a police operation in the southern city of Blantyre on Thursday that left her four suspected kidnappers dead.

The Malawi Police Service said officers exchanged gunfire with the suspects, who were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol.

"The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," police said in the statement.

During the operation, Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira also sustained gunshot wounds and is being treated in hospital in a stable condition.

Osman's brother, Shobi Jiwa, had earlier confirmed to Malawi news outlet Nation Online that she had been rescued in an operation in which the police officer was shot and wounded.

open image in gallery Inspector General Richard Luhanga said 47-year-old Nusrat Osman was safe ( Handout )

Osman, who works for a local auditing firm, was abducted about 12.30pm local time last Friday, September 11, in a neighbourhood of the southern city of Blantyre.

She and her family moved to Malawi from Leicester after her husband set up a business in the country.

Malawi police had said they were looking for four men who had used a grey car to kidnap her.

The motive was not clear, police said, and the suspects had not contacted Osman's family or authorities.

Authorities had offered a reward of about £12,600 for information leading to Osman’s rescue and the arrest and conviction of the kidnappers.

Local politician Atupele Muluzi described the case as “deeply disturbing”, adding that it was one of an increasing number of similar incidents in the country.

“Kidnappings and abductions are becoming increasingly frequent in Malawi, a country where such incidents were previously largely unheard of,” he wrote in a post on Facebook.

At the time, the UK Foreign Office said it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities about the situation.

Thought all America’s downtowns were sterile business districts packed only with glass offices that become ghost towns after the working day ends? Think again.

There are some city centers packed with character that break the mold — and here we reveal seven of the most beautiful. What’s more, they are all highly walkable.

Venture to South Carolina for a city that feels like a living museum, with over 2,500 historic buildings in its downtown area. In Georgia, leave your car parked and set out on foot to explore the city with 22 park-like squares, while New Mexico’s capital has strict rules ensuring that its downtown will always be a mesmerizing mix of earthy tones.

Our downtown directory also includes a Wisconsin city with a spectacular setting on an isthmus between two lakes and the Rhode Island destination with a distinctly European vibe.

We also included a leafy Idaho city, along with a stunning spot in Virginia that in many respects is little changed from its 18th-century beginnings.

Most beautiful downtowns in America

1. Charleston, South Carolina

open image in gallery Charleston's downtown is packed with picturesque buildings, including the colorful houses of Rainbow Row ( Getty/iStock )

Charleston is akin to a living museum, with over 2,500 historic buildings dating to the 18th and 19th centuries clustered in the walkable downtown area, and dozens of church spires punctuating the skyline.

Among the most picturesque buildings are the 13 candy-colored Georgian row houses on East Bay Street. These are must-haves for your camera roll — along with the intricate wrought-iron balconies that embellish the facades throughout the district, the cobblestone streets and narrow leafy lanes, and the hidden passages that connect them.

One of the best viewpoints to take it all in from is the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge pedestrian path, which offers sweeping views of the skyline and harbor.

After that, review your photos at celebrated Southern restaurant Husk, located in a beautifully restored Victorian house.

Great place to stay: The Ryder Hotel (rooms from $300) is a boutique property with quasi-tropical design accents and an outdoor pool in the heart of downtown.



2. Savannah, Georgia

open image in gallery Savannah features 22 park-like squares, a grid plan that dates back to 1733. Pictured is the fountain at Forsyth Park ( Getty/iStock )

Savannah’s downtown is not only stunning, but a candidate for being one of America’s most walkable historic districts. A grid plan dating back to 1733 that features 22 park-like squares remains intact, and the atmosphere is enchanting.

The streets are lined with buildings that span 300 years of American architectural evolution, from Federal (think brickwork, centered doors and evenly spaced windows) to Greek Revival (ancient temple aesthetics), and from Gothic (steep gables and spires) to Italianate (ornate ironwork). Adding to the storybook vibe are vast oak trees draped in Spanish moss that form canopies over the roads.

One of the best viewpoints? Look north from the fountain in Forsyth Park along oak-lined Bull Street, which runs toward the river through several historic squares.

For a top dining spot, try The Grey, which is set inside a restored 1930s Greyhound bus terminal.

Great place to stay: The Marshall House (rooms from $250) is a beautiful landmark hotel dating to 1851 in the center of the historic district — you won’t need your car before you leave.



3. Santa Fe, New Mexico

open image in gallery Santa Fe has a strict architectural code that stipulates earthy adobe aesthetics ( Getty/iStock )

Santa Fe has a distinctive downtown look unlike any other, thanks to a 400-year history — the city is the oldest state capital in the U.S. — and a strict architectural code that stipulates adobe aesthetics: flat roofs and earthy, neutral tones such as tan, cream or yellow.

Adding to the vibrancy are over 250 art galleries, the majestic 17th-century Palace of the Governors (America’s oldest public building), and a skyline that’s framed by the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Head to the Cross of the Martyrs in Fort Marcy Park for a sweeping panorama of the city and the peaks beyond, and then to The Shed for some classic New Mexican fare, such as blue-corn enchiladas.

Great place to stay: Inn of the Governors (rooms from $250) is a short walk from downtown’s shops, galleries and landmarks.



4. Madison, Wisconsin

open image in gallery Madison’s focal point is the Wisconsin State Capitol, which features a magnificent granite dome ( Getty/iStock )

Madison’s downtown has a head start over many others simply because of its spectacular setting. The city sits on a narrow isthmus — formed 18,000 years ago by glacial activity — between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona.

Visitors are also wowed by its majestic centerpiece: the Roman Renaissance-style Wisconsin State Capitol, whose gleaming white granite dome towers above a cluster of handsome historic buildings.

Urban planning also plays a part in the appeal: there's State Street, a mile-long pedestrian mall, which links the University of Wisconsin campus to Capitol Square, and extensive lakefront parks.

For the best Instagram shot, head to the Frank Lloyd Wright-designed lakeside convention center Monona Terrace. From here, you can capture the Capitol dome rising dramatically above the water.

You can also admire the view from Graze, a popular Capitol Square bistro serving seasonal Midwestern dishes.

Great place to stay: The Madison Concourse Hotel (rooms from $220) is positioned right beside Capitol Square, with views of the grand surrounding architecture part of the package.



5. Providence, Rhode Island

open image in gallery Providence’s waterside downtown features elegant walkways and an intoxicating spread of architectural styles ( Getty/iStock )

The architectural grandeur of downtown Providence gives it a distinctly European feel, with Beaux-Arts, Greek Revival and Art Deco designs underpinning many of its civic buildings.

Your eye will be drawn to the Art Deco Industrial Trust Tower — dubbed the “Superman Building” due to its striking resemblance to the Daily Planet building featured in the 1950s Adventures of Superman TV series — and the neoclassical Rhode Island State House, which is topped by one of the largest self-supporting marble domes in the world.

The Westminster Arcade, with its huge Greek-style columns, also impresses. Built in 1828, it was the first enclosed shopping mall in the United States. Carve out time to stroll the elegant walkways alongside Providence River and take in the view of the skyline from Prospect Terrace Park on College Hill.

For food, book a table at Al Forno, a Providence institution famous for its wood-grilled pizzas and hand-churned ice cream.

Great place to stay: Graduate by Hilton Providence (rooms from $200) is soaked in vintage character and sits in the heart of downtown Providence on the edge of Kennedy Plaza.



6. Boise, Idaho

open image in gallery Boise has a tree-lined downtown with the foothills of the Rockies rising beyond the city ( Getty/iStock )

An oasis at the edge of the high desert, Boise’s downtown is blanketed in trees, a feature that has defined the city since its earliest days.

The name derives from the French “les boisés,” meaning “the wooded place,” coined by French-Canadian fur trappers who discovered the lush valley where the city was later founded.

The Boise River Greenbelt park and trail system is one of the most tranquil areas of greenery, while the handsome neoclassical State Capitol building anchors the skyline.

The best view of the latter is from Camel’s Back Park in the North End, from where you can look out beyond the city to the foothills of the Rockies beyond.

A can’t-go-wrong downtown food option is Fork, which serves locally sourced comfort food, from Wagyu smash burgers to “dirty buffalo wings.”

Great place to stay: The Grove Hotel (rooms from $220) sits right next to the Idaho State Capitol, with foothill views and a rooftop-level fitness club with pool and spa.



7. Alexandria, Virginia

open image in gallery Alexandria’s charming King Street runs through the heart of the city’s historic downtown ( Getty/iStock )

Downtown Alexandria, set along the Potomac River, is most commonly referred to as Old Town — and for good reason. Established in 1749, it’s a beautifully preserved colonial-era historic district.

It’s a haven where open-flame gas lanterns illuminate wrought-iron gates and cobbled streets are lined with historic row houses.

One of the most notable landmarks is Gadsby’s Tavern Museum, which in the 18th and early 19th centuries comprised a tavern and hotel visited by the likes of George and Martha Washington, Thomas Jefferson and the Marquis de Lafayette.

The district’s anchor is King Street, a mile-long thoroughfare lined with historic storefronts, boutiques, galleries, restaurants and independent coffee shops.

It leads down to the waterfront promenade, where you’ll discover gorgeous views of the harbor, river and the Washington, D.C. skyline in the distance.

For a good feed, head to Virtue Feed & Grain, set inside a lovingly restored 19th-century feed warehouse. Here you can refuel with the likes of shrimp & grits, oven-baked rockfish and rigatoni alla vodka.

Great place to stay: Hotel Indigo Old Town Alexandria by IHG (rooms from $250) has a waterfront setting and offers views of Old Town Alexandria, Washington, D.C. and the sparkling Potomac River from its rooftop courtyard.

News.title: Milestone banking hub to give ‘crucial access to cash and face-to-face banking’
News.content:

The 250th banking hub is opening its doors, as part of moves to help plug gaps in access to cash and banking services.

Cash Access UK, an organisation set up to protect access to cash, said the milestone had been reached with the 250th banking hub in Chepstow in Monmouthshire, Wales.

Like other banking hubs, Chepstow’s hub offers a counter service operated by the Post Office, where major banks’ customers can make regular transactions.

A community banker service will also be offered, enabling customers to speak to their own bank about more complex issues on the day their bank is in the hub.

The hub is located in the heart of the town centre in Beaufort Square.

Economic Secretary to the Treasury Lucy Rigby, who was officially opening the new hub on Friday, said: “This new banking hub means that local residents will still have access to important services they rely on.”

Referring to the commitment to deliver at least 350 banking hubs this parliament, Ms Rigby said: “We’re well on our way to opening 350 hubs across the UK – a manifesto commitment and a key part of our Financial Inclusion Strategy.”

Banking hubs have helped to fill gaps amid waves of bank branch closures, the rise of digital banking, and concerns that some parts of the UK were at risk of becoming cash “deserts”.

Cash Access UK shows that since the start of 2026, more than eight million transactions have been supported across banking hubs and deposit services, with cash withdrawals being particularly popular.

It said new services continue to expand across the UK, with 45 banking hubs opening in 2026.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

To date, 285 banking hubs have been recommended, with more openings planned in the coming months.

Gareth Oakley, Cash Access UK chief executive, said: “I’m happy to announce the opening of Chepstow as our 250th hub, ensuring crucial access to cash and face-to-face banking services for residents and businesses across the local community.

“The services are hugely popular, with a busy front desk to support cash transactions and a rotating community banker to support face-to-face banking needs.

“This year we’ve opened a new hub every week, so we see the real difference it makes to the local community and are proud to be bringing this service to Chepstow.”

open image in gallery 2SCAXE1 The Post Office Banking hub Dartmouth, Devon, UK

According to a recent report from UK Finance, cash made up 8% of payments in 2025, falling from 9% in 2024 and 45% in 2015.

By 2035, cash use is expected to account for just 4% of payments made in the UK, with around two billion transactions, UK Finance’s report said.

Natalie Ceeney, Cash Access UK chairwoman, said: “Every one of our 250 banking hubs exists because millions of people and small businesses across the UK need somewhere to walk in, deposit their takings, withdraw cash, or sit down with someone face-to-face about their banking.

“Since the start of 2026, more than eight million transactions have been supported across all banking hubs and deposit services, showing that face-to-face banking and access to cash is still vital for those that need it.

“We are working together with the major UK banks to provide this service and will continue to do so in order to support communities across the UK.”

John Howells, chief executive of cash access and ATM network Link said: “Access to cash and face-to-face banking remains vital for millions of people and businesses who rely upon these services.

“We are proud of Link’s role in recommending 283 hubs to date, alongside 192 other cash services to make it easier for businesses to bank cash.

“While cash may no longer be the default payment method for most people, we know that when payment and digital systems fail, cash provides the necessary resilience.”

Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said: “People and businesses across Wales want services such as banking to be available in their local communities – and that’s what we are delivering via the new hubs.

“The UK Government is determined to make local services work better for people, and I’m delighted for the people of Chepstow that this new hub will serve their community so that face-to-face banking continues long into the future.”

Ross Borkett, financial services director at the Post Office, said: “As we celebrate the opening of the 250th banking hub in Chepstow, it is clear just how important the model has become.

“Banking hubs now help thousands of people and businesses access everyday banking services locally, while also providing face-to-face support from major banks when it matters most.

“This milestone reflects the trusted role Post Office and postmasters continue to play at the heart of communities.

“We are proud to be working with Cash Access UK and our banking partners to keep cash and banking services on the high street, supporting local economies and ensuring customers can access the services they need close to home.”

News.title: I’ve been cancer-free for 14 years – here’s why I travelled to India to celebrate
News.content:
