A presidential ordinance of 13 September 2026 created the preliminary organising committee for the Democratic Republic of Congo’s national dialogue. Its coordinator, deputy coordinator and members are all appointed by the head of state.

What the Ordinance Does

The ordinance of 13 September 2026 establishes a preliminary organising committee under the direct authority of the head of state. Its coordinator, deputy coordinator and members are all presidentially appointed.

An eleven-expert technical secretariat supports it, also designated by the presidency. The structure was contested publicly within a day of its publication.

What the Dialogue Is

The process is formally titled the national dialogue for peace, cohesion and the refounding of the state. President Felix Tshisekedi announced it on 27 August 2026.

It provides for consultations in all 26 provinces, followed by national assemblies in Kinshasa. The whole process is capped at three months.

Who Is Not Invited

Armed groups considered to be backed by foreign interests are excluded, including the AFC and M23. Tshisekedi has said the Doha process remains the appropriate framework for dealing with them.

That draws a firm line between a domestic political conversation and an armed conflict negotiation. Whether the two can be kept separate is the central question critics raise.

The Objection to the Structure

Emery Okundji of FONUS, part of the Coalition Article 64, has objected to the committee’s composition. Jean-Claude Katende, president of the rights organisation ASADHO, has said the country is going in a bad direction.

The Kabila-aligned movement Sauvons la RDC has also objected. The common argument is that a body appointed by one office cannot convene a national conversation.

What One Civil Society Group Is Asking For

The public expenditure observatory ODEP set out its position on 14 September 2026. It wants the AFC and M23 at the table without granting them political legitimacy.

It also refuses committee members drawn from the governing coalition and demands independent facilitators. It urges that the process be modelled on Congo’s sovereign national conference.

That conference is the country’s reference point for an inclusive constitutional process. It was held in the early 1990s.

Where the Church Sits

On 16 September the Catholic bishops’ conference, through its justice and peace commission, hosted a panel on the conditions for the dialogue. Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya sat alongside the opposition figure Martin Fayulu and the former minister Marie-Ange Mushobekwa.

Convening government and opposition at one table is the church’s traditional role in Congolese politics. The panel discussed conditions rather than endorsing or rejecting the process.

A Claim We Are Not Repeating

A statement attributed to the bishops’ conference criticising the dialogue has circulated widely. Fact-checkers have established that the video dates from June 2026 and concerns a proposed constitutional change rather than the dialogue.

We are flagging it because it has shaped much of the coverage. The bishops’ conference has not issued the criticism being attributed to it.

Why the Composition Question Is Not Procedural

A dialogue’s legitimacy rests on who convenes it as much as on who attends. Participants who believe the outcome is predetermined tend not to come.

That is the practical risk of an entirely presidential appointment. Empty chairs are what turns a national dialogue into a government consultation.

What It Means for People in Congo

For citizens in the 26 provinces, the consultations are the stage they would encounter. No schedule for them has been published.

For anyone in the east, the exclusion of the armed groups means this process does not address the conflict there. That remains with the Doha track.

What Is Not Yet Known

The committee’s members have not been listed publicly. No start date for the provincial consultations has been announced.

It is also unclear whether any of the objecting parties will take part. None has formally declined.

What to Watch

Whether opposition parties agree to participate. That is the test of whether the three-month process can begin at all.

Watch also for any revision of the committee’s composition. Adjusting it is the most obvious way to answer the objection.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the ordinance do?

It created the preliminary organising committee for Congo’s national dialogue on 13 September 2026.

Who appoints the committee?

The head of state appoints the coordinator, deputy coordinator and all members, as well as an eleven-expert technical secretariat.

How will the dialogue run?

Consultations in all 26 provinces, then national assemblies in Kinshasa, over a maximum of three months.

Who is excluded?

Armed groups considered backed by foreign interests, including the AFC and M23.

Where are those groups dealt with?

Through the Doha process, according to President Tshisekedi.

Has the Catholic bishops’ conference criticised the dialogue?

No. A widely shared statement attributed to it dates from June 2026 and concerns a proposed constitutional change.

Sources: Presidential ordinance of 13 September 2026 and Congolese press reporting, 14 to 17 September 2026; ODEP statement of 14 September 2026; Balobaki Check verification of the attributed bishops’ conference statement.

World.title: Benin and Rwanda Sign a Round of Cooperation Deals on Trade Worth About US$126,500 a Year
World.content:
RWANDA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni met Paul Kagame in Kigali and signed cooperation instruments.

— What they cover Taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

— The trade behind it Two-way trade was about US$126,500 in 2024, counting both directions.

— What each sells Rwanda sent cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment, and Benin sent secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

— The earlier framework A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023, under Benin’s previous president.

— What the presidents asked for They directed their delegations to strengthen existing cooperation and identify new areas.

Seven areas of cooperation, two presidents, and a trading relationship worth less than a small apartment.

Kigali, where Benin’s president met Paul Kagame on 16 September (Photo: Emmanuelkwizera, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni met Rwanda’s president Paul Kagame in Kigali on 16 September 2026. The two countries signed cooperation instruments on the first day of a two-day official visit.

What Was Signed

The two governments signed cooperation instruments on the first day of a two-day visit. They cover taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

The presidents also directed their delegations to strengthen existing cooperation. They asked for work on the mobility of goods, services and skills.

The Number That Frames It

Two-way trade between Benin and Rwanda was about US$126,500 in 2024. That is the total in both directions for a full year.

Rwanda’s exports to Benin were about US$116,000 and Benin’s to Rwanda about US$10,500. These are not rounding errors in the figures; they are the figures.

What Each Country Actually Sells

Rwanda’s exports to Benin consist of cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment. Benin’s exports to Rwanda are secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

Neither list suggests an established commercial relationship. They read as occasional shipments rather than trade flows.

The Growth Rates, in Context

Rwandan exports to Benin grew about 47.5 percent a year between 2019 and 2024. Beninese exports to Rwanda grew about 8.46 percent a year.

Growth rates on figures this small are not meaningful in the usual way. A single additional tractor moves the percentage.

Why Two Countries Sign Anyway

Cooperation instruments create the legal machinery that trade needs before it can exist. A double taxation agreement, an air services agreement and an investment protection framework are preconditions rather than results.

Neither country can trade with the other at scale without them. Signing them is what turning intention into possibility looks like.

The Distance Problem

Benin is on West Africa’s Atlantic coast and Rwanda is landlocked in East Africa. There is no direct road route and very limited direct air freight.

An air transport agreement is therefore among the more consequential items signed. Connectivity is the binding constraint on everything else.

What Came Before

A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023, when Kagame visited Benin. Patrice Talon was Benin’s president at the time.

Wadagni took office this year. The current visit is described as moving from those accords toward concrete projects.

The Rest of the Visit

The first day also included a tribute at Rwanda’s genocide memorial. The two delegations took part in a five-kilometre walk.

Those elements are standard in Rwandan state visits. They signal the relationship’s tone rather than its substance.

What It Means for Business

For companies in either country, the useful question is whether an air freight route follows. Without one, the agreements remain paperwork.

For anyone watching African intra-continental trade, the case is instructive. Two willing governments and almost no trade is the normal starting point rather than the exception.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither government published the full text or a complete list of the instruments signed. No investment figure or project was announced.

It is also unclear when the agreements take effect. Ratification timelines have not been given.

What to Watch

Whether a direct air link or freight arrangement follows. That is the single change that would make the rest usable.

Watch also for the next trade figures. They are the only honest measure of whether any of this worked.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who met?

Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni and Rwanda’s president Paul Kagame, in Kigali on 16 September 2026.

What was signed?

Cooperation instruments covering taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

How much do the two countries trade?

About US$126,500 in 2024, counting both directions.

What do they sell each other?

Rwanda sends cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment. Benin sends secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

Was there an earlier framework?

Yes. A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023 under Benin’s previous president, Patrice Talon.

Were any investment figures announced?

No.

World.title: Guinea’s Media Regulator Issues a Formal Warning to France 24 Over One Word
World.content:
GUINEA · MEDIA

Key Facts — What happened Guinea’s media regulator issued a formal notice to France 24 on 16 September 2026.

— What it is not No sanction was imposed, and the broadcaster has not been taken off air.

— The wording at issue A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya using a term meaning coup-installed president.

— What the regulator said It called the description inappropriate and degrading toward Guinea’s institutions.

— What the broadcaster did France 24 acknowledged the wording and said it would apologise and issue a correction.

— What could still happen The regulator has reserved the right to impose sanctions later.

A formal notice, not a ban, over an adjective the broadcaster has agreed to withdraw.

Conakry, where the media regulator issued its notice Photo: Jcornelius, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Guinea’s media regulator has issued a formal notice to the French broadcaster France 24. The notice concerns a description of President Mamadi Doumbouya as a coup-installed president.

What Was Issued

Guinea’s High Authority for Communication issued a formal notice, known in French practice as a mise en demeure. It was dated 16 September 2026.

A formal notice is a warning that requires a response. It is not a suspension, and no immediate sanction was imposed.

Why This Distinction Matters

Several reports described France 24 as banned from broadcasting in Guinea. The regulator’s own statement says no immediate sanction was pronounced.

It does reserve the right to impose sanctions. That is a different position from having imposed one, and the difference is the story.

The Wording at Issue

A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya with a term meaning coup-installed president. The regulator called the description inappropriate and degrading toward Guinea’s institutions.

The objection is to a single characterisation rather than to a report’s facts. That is what makes the case a press freedom question rather than an accuracy dispute.

How the Broadcaster Responded

France 24 acknowledged the use of the expression. It said it would present its apologies and issue a correction.

That response is what a formal notice is designed to produce. It also removes the most likely trigger for a sanction.

The Facts the Term Refers To

Doumbouya led a coup on 5 September 2021 that removed President Alpha Conde. He then headed a transitional government.

He won a presidential election on 28 December 2025 with 86.72 percent of the vote, on a turnout of 82.86 percent. The Supreme Court confirmed the result in early January 2026.

Why the Description Is Contested

Supporters point to the election and the court confirmation as the source of his current mandate. Critics point to how he first took power.

Both facts are on the record. A regulator ruling on which one may be used in a description is regulating characterisation rather than fact.

What a Formal Notice Can Lead To

Under most West African broadcasting frameworks, a formal notice is the first step in an escalating scale. Suspension and revocation sit further along it.

Whether the regulator proceeds usually depends on whether the broadcaster complies. France 24 has said it will.

What It Means for Viewers and Journalists

For viewers in Guinea, the channel remains available. Nothing announced changes access.

For journalists working in the country, the case marks where the regulator draws a line. It concerns how the head of state is described rather than what may be reported.

What Is Not Yet Known

The exact broadcast date is not settled. Reporting places it on 14 or 15 September 2026.

Nor is it known whether the regulator will consider the matter closed once the correction airs. It has not said what compliance would look like.

What to Watch

Whether the correction is broadcast and whether the regulator then closes the file. That would settle the case.

Watch also for similar notices to other foreign broadcasters. One notice is an incident and a pattern would be a policy.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has France 24 been banned in Guinea?

No. The regulator issued a formal notice and imposed no immediate sanction.

What was the objection?

A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya using a term meaning coup-installed president.

How did France 24 respond?

It acknowledged the wording and said it would apologise and issue a correction.

When did Doumbouya take power?

He led a coup on 5 September 2021 that removed President Alpha Conde.

Was he elected?

Yes. He won the presidential election of 28 December 2025 with 86.72 percent of the vote.

Could a sanction still follow?

Yes. The regulator has reserved the right to impose sanctions.

Sources: Guinean High Authority for Communication notice of 16 September 2026, as reported by allAfrica, Tchadinfos and La Nouvelle Tribune.

World.title: Ghana’s Opposition Backs Some Constitutional Changes and Rejects the Process That Produced Them
World.content:
GHANA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Ghana’s opposition New Patriotic Party published its position on the review of the 1992 constitution.

— Who presented it Kojo Oppong Nkrumah, for the party’s policy coordination secretariat.

— What it supports Barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, a ceiling of 60 ministers, and electing local chief executives.

— What it rejects Expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats, and a five-year presidential term.

— The bigger objection The party says the package amounts to a new constitution and demands a constituent assembly.

— The scale involved The review proposes amending 147 of 299 articles and adding 59 new provisions.

Yes to a minister cap and elected mayors, no to a bigger parliament, and no to the process itself.

Accra, where Ghana’s constitution review has become a party-political dispute (Photo: NASA Astronauts, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Ghana’s opposition New Patriotic Party has set out its position on the review of the 1992 constitution. It supports several individual changes while rejecting the review process as partisan.

Who Is Speaking and From Where

The New Patriotic Party has been in opposition since losing the December 2024 election. John Mahama of the National Democratic Congress is president.

Kojo Oppong Nkrumah presented the position for the party’s policy coordination secretariat. The party notes that it rejected some of the same proposals when it was in government.

What the Party Supports

It backs barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, deputy ministers or regional ministers. It also supports a ceiling of 60 ministers.

It supports electing metropolitan, municipal and district chief executives rather than having them appointed. And it backs restricting members of parliament from sitting on public boards and procurement bodies.

What the Party Rejects

It opposes expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats. It also opposes moving to a five-year presidential term.

Those two are the changes that would most directly affect the balance of power. That is the pattern in its position.

The Objection to the Whole Exercise

The party argues that the package amounts to the overhaul of a constitution and, in substance, the enactment of a new one. It points to 147 of 299 articles being amended and 59 new provisions added.

It says that in the absence of a constituent assembly, an attempt to bundle the government’s preferred amendments will not receive its support. That is a procedural objection rather than an argument about any single clause.

Why Separating Ministers From Parliament Matters

In Ghana’s system, members of parliament can serve as ministers. Critics say that gives the executive leverage over the legislature that is supposed to scrutinise it.

Barring the practice would change how much independent oversight parliament can offer. Both major parties have supported the idea in opposition more readily than in government.

Where the Review Came From

The Constitution Review Committee delivered its report to President Mahama on 22 December 2025. The review covers the 1992 constitution, which has governed Ghana since the return to multi-party rule.

A constituent or consultative assembly is the mechanism Ghana used to adopt that constitution. The opposition is asking for the same route this time.

The Money Question in the Background

Research by the Ghana Center for Democratic Development has documented the rising cost of seeking office. Campaign spending averaged about 389,803 cedis per parliamentary seat in 2016, a rise of 59 percent on 2012.

By 2020 it reported figures reaching as high as four million cedis. Its researcher Jacob Tetteh Ahuno has warned that this trend points toward state capture, where campaign financiers dictate what the state does.

The Party’s Own Timing

The New Patriotic Party holds its national officer elections on 19 September 2026. Positions taken publicly in the days before an internal election are read in that light.

Sulemana Tampuli Alhassan, the member of parliament for Gushegu, has been among those speaking on the proposals. He holds no national party office at present.

What It Means for Ghanaians

None of this changes any rule today. A constitutional amendment requires its own legislative process and, for entrenched provisions, a referendum.

The practical question is whether the two main parties can agree a process. Without that, a package of this size is unlikely to pass.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not responded to the demand for a constituent assembly. No timetable for putting amendments to parliament has been published.

It is also unclear which provisions the government regards as entrenched. Those are the ones that would require a referendum.

What to Watch

Whether the government engages with the constituent assembly demand. That is the procedural fork the whole exercise now turns on.

Watch also for the outcome of the opposition’s internal elections on 19 September. New party officers could revisit the position.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the New Patriotic Party in government?

No. It has been in opposition since losing the December 2024 election. John Mahama is president.

What does the party support?

Barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, a 60-minister ceiling, electing local chief executives, and restricting members from public boards.

What does it reject?

Expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats and moving to a five-year presidential term.

What is its main objection?

That the package amounts to a new constitution and should go through a constituent assembly.

How large is the proposed change?

Amendments to 147 of 299 articles, plus 59 new provisions.

When was the review report delivered?

On 22 December 2025, to President Mahama.

Sources: New Patriotic Party position on the review of the 1992 constitution, 17 September 2026, as reported by MyJoyOnline; Constitution Review Committee report of December 2025; Ghana Center for Democratic Development research.

World.title: British Airways Makes Costa Rica a Year-Round London Route
World.content:
If you have ever tried to book a direct flight between Costa Rica and the United Kingdom in June, you already know the problem. The route has only existed in the European winter, which meant anyone travelling outside the high season connected through Madrid, Miami, Panama City or Atlanta and added most of a day to the trip.

That changes in October as British Airways confirmed today that it will keep its London–San José service running all year, with flights scheduled continuously through September 2027. The route also moves from London Gatwick to London Heathrow, the airline’s main base.

Frequencies split by season so between October 2026 and March 2027 the airline will fly five times a week, up from three. Between April and September 2027, when demand from Europe softens, the schedule drops back to three flights a week — but it no longer stops.

For the winter schedule, the flight leaves Heathrow at 11:10 a.m. and lands at Juan Santamaría International Airport at 4:40 p.m. The return departs San José at 6:40 p.m. and reaches Heathrow at 10:50 a.m. the following morning. The crossing takes roughly 11 hours in each direction.

British Airways will operate the year-round service with a Boeing 787-8 carrying 204 passengers — 31 seats in Club World business class, 37 in World Traveller Plus premium economy and 136 in World Traveller economy.

The airport change matters more than it sounds. Gatwick is a secondary base with limited long-haul connections, while Heathrow feeds more than 130 destinations British Airways serves directly. Someone flying in from Manchester, Edinburgh, Dublin, Frankfurt or Milan can now reach San José on a single ticket with one stop instead of hunting for a self-connection across London.

Heathrow also carries more freight. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute said the terminal switch will improve air cargo capacity between Costa Rica and Europe, which affects exporters shipping perishable goods on passenger aircraft.

Marcos V. Borges, executive president of the Costa Rican Tourism Institute, said the announcement represents a significant increase in seats and frequencies from London. Ricardo Hernández, executive director of AERIS, the company that operates Juan Santamaría, said the route’s year-round permanence resulted from joint work between the airport operator, the tourism institute and the airline. Tourism Minister William Rodríguez said earlier this year that negotiations with British Airways ran for roughly two years.

The United Kingdom is the third-largest European source market for visitors to Costa Rica, according to tourism institute figures. The institute reported 15,741 British arrivals by air during the first two months of 2026, and 319,552 arrivals from Europe overall, an increase of 8.8 percent over the same period a year earlier.

The timing is deliberate as the World Travel Market, one of the largest international tourism trade fairs, opens in London in November, and Costa Rica arrives with a confirmed year-round connection rather than a seasonal one. The tourism institute (ICT) has also been running its first pan-European marketing campaign, built around the tagline “live.life.now.”

Costa Rica is not the only beneficiary of a wider British Airways expansion announced the same day. The airline plans to increase Latin American capacity by 25 percent for the northern summer of 2027, moving London–Buenos Aires to a daily operation with an onward leg to Santiago, and taking Rio de Janeiro to daily service as well.

Fares for the new Heathrow flights are already on sale through the airline’s booking system. Travellers holding reservations on the Gatwick service for dates after the switchover should expect to be reaccommodated on the Heathrow departure, and anyone with tight onward connections at Gatwick will need to rebuild that leg.

What Costa Rica gains is a link that no longer disappears for half the year — steadier seat supply, a European hub with real onward reach, and cargo space on a wide-body aircraft twelve months out of twelve.

World.title: What Costa Rica’s Record-Low Dollar Means for Expats and Retirees
World.content:
The dollar fell to another all-time low on Costa Rica’s Foreign Exchange Market (Monex) on Wednesday. The drop extends a slide that is steadily shrinking the purchasing power of residents whose income arrives in U.S. currency. The session’s weighted average closed at ¢446.93 per dollar, according to the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR).

That was ¢0.41 below Monday’s ¢447.34 and marked the fifth consecutive trading session to set a record. Trading was paused over the weekend and for the September 15 Independence Day holiday. The streak began on September 9, when the rate fell to ¢448.17 and broke a low that had stood since August, as The Tico Times reported when the dollar hit a new record low in Costa Rica.

The declines are small day to day, but they add up for households that convert dollars into colones every month. A retiree converting a $2,000 monthly pension would have received ¢899,940 at the September 8 rate of ¢449.97. At Wednesday’s rate, the same transfer yields ¢893,860, a difference of ¢6,080 in just over a week. Rent paid in colones, utility bills, groceries at the feria and domestic staff wages do not fall when the dollar does. As a result, the gap comes directly out of discretionary spending.

The figures also understate the effect at the bank counter. The Monex weighted average is a wholesale benchmark. The rate banks pay customers who sell dollars typically sits several colones lower.

Remote workers paid in U.S. dollars and property owners who collect rent in dollars face the same squeeze. Tourists notice it as well: a restaurant bill of ¢10,000 now costs roughly $22.37, up from about $22.22 on September 8. The per-meal difference is modest, but it compounds over a two-week vacation and over years of dollar-based retirement budgeting in Costa Rica.

The trend works in the opposite direction for anyone holding colones. Businesses and individuals buying dollars for imports, travel abroad, or dollar-denominated loan payments now need fewer colones to cover the same obligations.

The Central Bank continued to intervene on Wednesday, purchasing $24.7 million through stabilization operations. BCCR stabilization purchases in September now total $133.7 million: $41.1 million on September 9, $2.8 million on September 10, $65.1 million on September 14 and $24.7 million on Wednesday. Stabilization purchases for 2026 have reached $1.14 billion, with no sales recorded in that category.

The BCCR uses these operations to moderate abrupt swings in the exchange rate, not to set a target level. The bank has said repeatedly this year that an extraordinary increase in the foreign exchange surplus has put additional downward pressure on the dollar. Wednesday’s session moved $58.9 million across 255 transactions.

For dollar earners, the practical question is whether the slide continues. The Central Bank’s steady purchases have slowed the decline without reversing it. Market conditions throughout 2026 have been marked by abundant dollar supply, and nothing in the latest data points to an imminent change. Residents who budget in dollars may want to review how much of their cost of living in Costa Rica is tied to colón-priced expenses.

World.title: ‘Tell Matura, I got 10… months’: Prince Copious sentenced for burglarizing attorney’s home but Audrey says ‘he should have gotten more’ because her stolen gun was never recovered
World.content:
‘Tell Matura, I got 10… months’: Prince Copious sentenced for burglarizing attorney’s home but Audrey says ‘he should have gotten more’ because her stolen gun was never recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Attorney Audrey Matura says the sentence handed down to her former handyman, Prince Copious, for burglarizing her home was too lenient, particularly because her licensed firearm remains missing and has never been recovered.

Copious was sentenced Thursday to 18 months in prison after pleading guilty to burglarizing Matura’s Chetumal Boulevard residence in April 2025. After credit for 224 days already spent on remand and other deductions, he has 10 months and 16 days left to serve.

Matura told Breaking Belize News that she believes the punishment amounts to little more than a slap on the wrist given the circumstances of the burglary.

“The sentence was lenient given the fact that he stole a licensed firearm which he refused to say where it is, other than to say to me he took it to Belmopan,” Matura said.

She also said that at the time Copious pleaded guilty, he was already on remand in connection with another burglary.

Matura further alleged that Copious had a lengthy antecedent history involving burglary and theft charges, but said many of those matters were never concluded because of repeated court adjournments and frustrated victims.

“His antecedent history shows many charges for burglary and theft but the court process so slow and frustrating that many of those cases were never heard as victims got tired of the adjournments,” Matura said. “That is why he had gotten away with so much and has graduated from petty theft to bigger items.”

Those claims relate to allegations and charges described by Matura and do not, by themselves, amount to convictions.

Matura said she had hired Copious to perform maintenance and handyman work at her home and business, placing him in a position of trust. Police later alleged that surveillance footage showed him using a makeshift ladder to access the second floor of her home through a bathroom window.

Among the property reported stolen was Matura’s 9mm Ruger pistol valued at $3,500, a magazine containing seven live rounds, jewelry, cosmetics, a knapsack and knives belonging to her son. The stolen items were valued at more than $6,000.

Matura said the firearm remains her greatest concern because it has never been recovered.

She also previously told reporters that while Copious was in police custody, he admitted the burglary to her and allegedly provided information about other persons to whom he would take stolen property. Matura said she recorded that conversation and was disappointed that police did not use the information to more aggressively pursue the missing items and firearm.

Copious initially pleaded not guilty following his arrest but changed his plea to guilty on August 11, 2026, after his trial had already begun.

As police transported him to prison Thursday afternoon, Copious reportedly waited until cameras stopped recording before calling out a message for Matura: “Tell Matura, I got 10,” before pausing and adding, “months.”

He will now serve the remaining 10 months and 16 days of his sentence at the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: Deovan Hall shot dead while riding home from event in Corozal; police seek two suspects
World.content:
Deovan Hall shot dead while riding home from event in Corozal; police seek two suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are seeking two suspects following the murder of Deovan Hall, who was shot multiple times while reportedly heading home on his bicycle in the San Antonio Village area of the Corozal District Wednesday night.

Police responded to reports of a shooting and found Hall’s lifeless body near a field along a feeder road with multiple gunshot injuries.

Initial investigations indicate that Hall had attended an event and was riding home when he was approached by persons in the area. Police say there appeared to have been a struggle before Hall was shot.

Hall was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police say Hall had previously been arrested for minor offences, but investigators have not confirmed whether his past encounters with the law have any connection to his murder.

Two suspects are being sought as the investigation continues.

World.title: 20-year-old Anthony Perry gunned down on Louise Bevans Street; police point to ongoing rivalry
World.content:
20-year-old Anthony Perry gunned down on Louise Bevans Street; police point to ongoing rivalry

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police believe an ongoing rivalry involving persons in the Louise Bevans Street area may be behind Wednesday night’s murder of 20-year-old Anthony William Perry in Belize City.

Perry was walking in the area when he was approached by a gunman who opened fire, striking him. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital but was pronounced dead on arrival.

Police say Perry was known to authorities and that investigators believe the murder stems from an ongoing rivalry involving persons from the area. Investigators are currently seeking two suspects and are reviewing surveillance footage that may assist the investigation.

No one had been detained in connection with the murder at the time of Thursday’s police briefing.

Perry’s age, full name and the location of the shooting were also independently reported Wednesday night by Breaking Belize News, which reported that he was shot on Louise Bevans Street before being taken to KHMH.

World.title: Honduran scrap-gold dealer allegedly lured to Faber’s Road and shot dead for money
World.content:
Honduran scrap-gold dealer allegedly lured to Faber’s Road and shot dead for money

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Honduran national who regularly purchased scrap gold in Belize City was allegedly lured to the Faber’s Road area Wednesday evening before being shot and killed after a demand for money, police say.

Police responded to the shooting at around 6:20 p.m. and found 42-year-old Dennis Guevara suffering from gunshot injuries. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed.

According to investigators, Guevara routinely purchased scrap gold from people in the area and had reportedly been contacted by someone who asked to meet him there.

Police say that during the meeting, the person allegedly demanded money from Guevara before shooting him several times.

Authorities have not yet confirmed whether robbery was the motive for the killing.

Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage from the area and are working to identify and locate suspects.

World.title: U.S. Ambassador André Bauer personally delivers school bags to students in Santana Village
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador André Bauer personally delivers school bags to students in Santana Village

By Breaking Belize News Staff: United States Ambassador to Belize André Bauer personally handed out backpacks filled with school supplies to primary school students during a visit to Zion Park Methodist Primary School in Santana Village on Thursday.

Bauer was joined by locally employed staff of the U.S. Embassy in Belmopan for the distribution, which also included supplies for teachers. In photographs shared by the Embassy, the newly appointed ambassador is seen interacting directly with the children and handing backpacks to students.

The Embassy described the initiative as part of its continuing commitment to education and opportunity across Belize.

Thursday’s donation continues a years-long pattern of U.S. Embassy support for Belizean students. In 2022, the Embassy provided 500 backpacks containing school supplies to students of Carmelita and Santa Martha Government Schools in the Orange Walk District.

In 2016, the Embassy donated more than 150 backpacks to a back-to-school drive for children in residential care facilities; records from that initiative indicate then-Deputy Chief of Mission Adrienne Galanek participated in the distribution rather than then-Ambassador Carlos Moreno.

And Bauer is not the first U.S. ambassador to personally get involved in handing the bags to Belizean children. In January 2023, then-Ambassador Michelle Kwan personally distributed backpacks and school supplies during a visit to San Jose Government School in Orange Walk. News 5 reported Kwan describing the experience of “passing out school supplies, backpacks to the students,” while the Embassy’s contribution of school supplies was valued at approximately US$8,000.

Bauer was sworn in as U.S. Ambassador to Belize in August and recently began his assignment in the country.

World.title: International News: U.S.-Mexico trade talks advance
World.content:
International News: U.S.-Mexico trade talks advance

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke by phone Wednesday as the two countries continue negotiations aimed at reaching an agreement on trade, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the conversation.

The call comes as Washington and Mexico move closer to an agreement on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

The two sources offered differing descriptions of the conversation.

The person familiar with the call, who spoke anonymously, described it as “so-so” and said new topics were introduced during the discussion, creating some uncertainty.

A U.S. official, also speaking anonymously, described the conversation as “constructive” and said the trade negotiations remain active and are moving in a positive direction, Politico reports.

Mexican officials believed the two sides were nearing an agreement addressing concerns surrounding the USMCA, the North American trade pact signed during Trump’s first term, according to the person familiar with the call. The ongoing review has involved increasingly detailed negotiations between Washington and Mexico over the future of the agreement.

The fourth round of formal U.S.-Mexico discussions has been rescheduled for September 28 and 29 in Washington. The talks follow a third round in July between Mexican officials and U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer, where both sides reported progress on areas including automobiles, steel and aluminum, agriculture, labor and economic security.

World.title: Trees, Climate action and conservation: Ministry brings sustainability to Independence Day parade
World.content:
Trees, Climate action and conservation: Ministry brings sustainability to Independence Day parade

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Sustainable Development will join Belize’s 45th Independence Day celebrations in San Ignacio and Santa Elena, highlighting its efforts to promote a healthier, more resilient and sustainable Belize.

The Ministry will participate with an Independence Day float showcasing its departments, programmes and national initiatives.

Featured initiatives will include the One Million Trees Campaign, the “Bin It” campaign promoting responsible waste management, climate action and resilience, and water conservation.

The float will also highlight efforts in biodiversity and protected areas, the Carbon Market and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Through the initiatives, the Ministry aims to raise awareness about environmental stewardship, responsible resource management and the importance of building communities that can adapt to a changing climate.

World.title: Team Belize set for 5-match FIFA U-15 World Cup Qualification campaign
World.content:
Team Belize set for 5-match FIFA U-15 World Cup Qualification campaign

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Football Federation of Belize announced Team Belize’s qualification-stage match schedule for the FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival 2026, which will take place in Azerbaijan from October 22–31, 2026.

Team Belize’s 5 qualification-stage matches will be played at the Hovsan Competition Complex. Belize has been drawn in Group F alongside Liberia, Curaçao, Morocco, the Philippines and Costa Rica.

Our Jaguars will open their campaign against Liberia on October 24, followed by two matches each on October 25 and 26.

TEAM BELIZE — MATCH SCHEDULE

Date Match Azerbaijan Time Belize Time Saturday, October 24, 2026 Liberia vs Belize 9:00 a.m. 11:00PM (Oct 23rd) Sunday, October 25, 2026 Belize vs Curaçao 2:30 p.m. 4:30AM Sunday, October 25, 2026 Morocco vs Belize 8:45 p.m. 10:45AM Monday, October 26, 2026 Philippines vs Belize 2:30 p.m. 4:30AM Monday, October 26, 2026 Belize vs Costa Rica 8:45 p.m. 10:45AM

Following the qualification stage, the competition schedule includes a rest day on October 27, with tournament-stage matches beginning October 28. Team Belize’s subsequent fixtures will be determined following qualification-stage results.

“Participation provides an important opportunity for Belize’s emerging footballers to gain international experience, compete against teams from different regions and proudly represent their country. It also supports the FFB’s continued commitment to youth football development,” FFB said.

The FFB calls on Belizeans at home and abroad to rally behind Team Belize as our young footballers prepare to wear the national colors on the world stage.

World.title: How Dis Mek: Ludo boards
World.content:
It’s a game that unites us, divides us, and can make us happy and vex us in equal measure.

For most of us, Ludo is played on age-old boards that we ‘born-come-see’, or a family member just came home with a board one evening.

The Jamaica Observer went to Olympic Gardens to find out the story behind the creation of these pieces on this episode of How Dis Mek?.

World.title: Holness elected CPA vice-chair, first Jamaican in 33 years
World.content:
Speaker of the House of Representatives, Juliet Holness

CAPE TOWN, South Africa — Speaker of the House of Representatives Juliet Holness has been elected vice-chairperson of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA), becoming the first Jamaican to do so in 33 years.

Holness was elected on Thursday during the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa.

Her election marks Jamaica’s return to the vice-chairpersonship for the first time since former Speaker of the House of Representatives Headley Cunningham served in the office from 1992 to 1993.

Holness previously served as chair of the CPA Caribbean, Americas and the Atlantic (CAA) Region and her tenure as regional chair culminated in Jamaica’s hosting of the 48th CPA Caribbean, Americas and the Atlantic Regional Conference from August 30 to September 5, 2026.

Reflecting on her election, Holness said she was deeply honoured.

“For Jamaica to return to this office after 33 years is a proud and significant moment for our Parliament and our country. I accept this responsibility with humility and with a clear sense of purpose. Leadership in the CPA is ultimately about service — strengthening the institutions through which we represent our people,” she said.

Holness gave special recognition to the presiding officers and other delegates of the CAA Region who worked actively in support of her candidacy.

“This achievement was not the work of one person or one Parliament. It was a tremendous regional effort, and I carry that support with me into this new responsibility. I remain committed to ensuring that the experiences and perspectives of our region, particularly those of small states and smaller jurisdictions, continue to inform and enrich the work of the CPA,” she noted.

Holness will serve as CPA vice-chairperson for a one-year term.

She assumes the vice-chairpersonship as the CPA advances its Strategic Plan 2026–2029 and transitioning to a new international legal status, following legislative measures in the United Kingdom designed to recognise the CPA in a manner more consistent with its character as an international interparliamentary organisation.

The 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference is being held in Cape Town, South Africa, from September 13 to 19, 2026 under the theme “Strengthening International Law and Parliamentary Democracy in a Changing World Order: Commonwealth Leadership”.

World.title: Bouncing back fast
World.content:
WILLIAMS...I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign.

CITING data that shows Jamaica 18 months ahead of schedule in recovering from the destruction Hurricane Melissa unleashed on several parishes last year, Finance Minister Fayval Williams on Wednesday painted a rosy picture of the country’s economy. She acknowledged, however, that “not everybody is feeling it just yet”, a nod to critics who have argued that the pace of the recovery and rebuilding is much too slow.

During her upbeat PowerPoint presentation at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet news briefing the minister reeled off data to support her claims.

“When I look at this chart, I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign,” Williams stated.

“And, no, this is not a picture of a recession. The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) already debunked that notion,” she added.

Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter, after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin) by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering. She argued further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

The finance minister highlighted that where it was projected that the fiscal deficit would have been 3.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) immediately after the hurricane, it instead came in at 2.5 per cent. At the same time the primary surplus was projected to be 1.3 per cent but came in at 2.3 per cent, while public debt-to-GDP was projected to rise to 68.9 per cent but came in at 65.6 per cent.

Regarding the public debt-to-GDP number, Williams said, “That number matters, it is not a one-off, it’s because we had stronger nominal GDP, the economy itself is bigger than we assumed, and that is the kind of improvement that will persist.”

She also pointed to the positions taken by the big three international ratings agencies with Moody’s upgrading its assessment of Jamaica just seven weeks after the hurricane, which it described as a “temporary setback”. Standard & Poor’s held its rating for Jamaica in December 2025 and moved the outlook to stable, while Fitch affirmed its BB-rating for Jamaica in February 2026 with a stable outlook.

Williams also pointed out that while unemployment rose from 3.3 per cent to 3.7 per cent following the hurricane, it remained at record lows. She acknowledged that unemployment in the hardest-hit parishes was higher.

“I want to assure them that the Government continues to work night and day to restore the west — to restore roads, water, housing, all the services, employment, schools and so on,” she said.

Williams also noted that the response from the Diaspora helped to stabilise the economy, as is evidenced in the record level of remittances that were sent to Jamaica in the aftermath of the hurricane. A breakdown of the numbers shows that, in November, the Diaspora sent remittances totalling US$273 million, up 16 per cent. December saw a record US$296 million being sent. The figure was up 16.3 per cent for the month. Of note is that all of the hardest-hit parishes received more in remittances than before the hurricane.

In the first three months after the storm, Jamaicans abroad sent home US$93 million more than they sent in the same three months a year earlier.

On the matter of inflation, the finance minister insisted that, while it was expected that food prices “would run away” following the devastating hurricane, they did not. She pointed out that inflation moved to 2.9 per cent in October 2025, 4.4 per cent in November 2025, and 4.5 per cent in December 2025 — all within the target range for the Bank of Jamaica. This, she said, was because agricultural production recovered faster than expected.

“Because of that, the price shock was contained,” the minister remarked.

However, Williams acknowledged that by July 2026 the picture had changed completely, with headline inflation surging to 7.5 per cent — the driver being the transportation division, which was up 13.6 per cent. She said based on figures released by Statin on Tuesday, whereas transportation had pushed up inflation in July, it was higher food prices, as a result of the ongoing drought, which drove inflation in August.

While transportation is still a factor, the finance minister said the August inflation number is directly attributable to the upheaval in international markets, driven by the United States war on Iran which has pushed up oil prices since February.

World.title: Blessing in disguise
World.content:
Sharon Logan, director of sales and marketing at Half Moon Resort, speaks during a JAPEX partner media update on Tuesday. (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

WHEN Hurricane Melissa swept through Jamaica last October it left tourism businesses counting losses and racing to recover. But nearly a year later, Half Moon resort and Chukka Jamaica are looking beyond the devastation, using the disruption to refresh their properties, redesign experiences, and rethink their operations.

For Half Moon, the forced recovery has gone beyond repairing hurricane damage. The Montego Bay resort has used the interruption to undertake a broad refresh of its property, while Chukka Jamaica says the experience forced it to examine its processes and find ways to operate more efficiently.

Speaking during a Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) 2026 Partner Media Update on Tuesday, director of sales and marketing for the Half Moon resort Sharon Logan said the hurricane created an opportunity for the resort to undertake work that would otherwise have been difficult to complete while guests were on property.

“One of the things that I look on is the silver lining behind the cloud, which is that we got the opportunity to do a complete refresh and regrowth of the property since the reopening,” said Logan.

She explained that while some projects, including renovation work on some of the resort’s villas, had already been under way before the hurricane, other major improvements came directly out of the damage caused by the storm.

“The villas were already a project that we were working on. But the other parts of the property, like the original part of the hotel, that has a complete refresh and that is all as a result of the hurricane,” added Logan.

The result, she said, has included improvements across much of the 400-acre property, including its rooms, meeting spaces, lobby, roadways, and pool areas.

One of the more unusual benefits, she identified, came from the movement of sand during the hurricane.

“There are so many open spaces. All the plants have been sprung up fresh and nice…We even got new beaches because we got sand that washed up. That would have cost the hotel millions of dollars to purchase. We got 30 truckloads of sand, free, so we have expanded beaches, so we’re excited about that,” explained Logan.

The resort, which reopened on April 2, is continuing a phased reopening of its facilities. Logan said half of the original Founders’ Cove section is already open, with the remaining section scheduled to open on October 1.

The hurricane also gave the resort an opportunity to tackle work that had previously required interruptions to operations. Logan pointed specifically to the pool at the Eclipse section, which had experienced problems with its tiles.

But while Half Moon’s gains have been visible in its physical transformation, Chukka Jamaica’s experience has produced a different kind of reset.

The attraction operator, which describes itself as a nature adventure company, was particularly exposed to the effects of the hurricane because its business depends heavily on the natural environment.

Group Digital Platform Manager Ilia Tomlinson said the recovery was especially difficult at Chukka’s river locations. At Good Hope in Trelawny, for example, the site was inundated and its river operations were disrupted.

Chukka began reopening locations in November, according to Tomlinson, with its final reopening taking place in June. She said the river-based operations were among the hardest to restore because of the overflow of the waterways.

But the disruption also prompted the company to scrutinise how it worked, with greater productivity emerging as one of the main lessons from the recovery.

“I would say the silver lining is…we operated a little bit more efficiently. We have had to. Nobody wants to cut back, it’s hard decisions to make, but cutting back and being efficient almost go hand in hand where there’s a middle spot where it’s productivity,” said Tomlinson.

“We have had to look at things we have never thought we have had to look at, and in a way we’re thankful for that. You know, it really has had us reflecting on our own processes and procedures and being more efficient in how we deliver our experiences,” added Tomlinson.

That reassessment has taken place alongside changes to Chukka’s tourism products.

In Ocho Rios, the company has redesigned parts of its offering following the hurricane and has expanded its portfolio through its acquisition of the Green Grotto Caves, which it took over just two days before Melissa struck Jamaica on October 28.

The caves, located near Discovery Bay in St Ann, are being incorporated into Chukka’s wider network of experiences in the resort area, adding a stronger history and culture component to its nature and adventure products.

Meanwhile, at Good Hope, the company has rebranded the attraction as a river outpost reflecting its location and the experiences offered there, including river tubing, bamboo rafting, ziplining, and dune buggies.

Tomlinson said the storm also reinforced the importance of preparation, particularly for a company whose operations are so closely tied to Jamaica’s landscape.

“We didn’t know we were so good at preparing. That was the lesson learned on the value of our standards of procedures and policies that we put into place that we probably otherwise take for granted,” she added.

World.title: J-House Vol 1 puts Jamaica on a new global dance floor
World.content:
Freddy Browne

There are collaborations, there are compilations — and then there are projects whose star-studded line-ups pack such a heavy punch that they position themselves for global attention long before anyone hears a single track.

Keen on taking Jamaican voices into the billion-dollar world of electronic music, Freddy Browne’s ambitious J-House Volume 1 is poised to do just that.

With Patra, Beenie Man, Tessanne Chin, Busy Signal, T.O.K, Agent Sasco, and more in the mix, the project, set for release on September 18, aims to take unmistakably Jamaican voices and personalities into the international house music arena.

Rather than simply placing Jamaican artistes over electronic beats and calling it fusion, Browne has been building J-House as its own musical proposition.

According to the American producer, DJ, and JHouse Entertainment CEO, the project stretches across generations of Jamaican music while refusing to stay comfortably inside any one of them.

Each artiste represents a different era in Jamaica’s rich musical history. Patra carries the weight of an artiste who helped push dancehall into mainstream international spaces during the 1990s. Beenie Man has spent decades as one of the genre’s most recognisable figures, while Busy Signal has built a catalogue around his ability to move between hard-core dancehall and broader musical territory. Ding Dong, meanwhile, brings an energy rooted heavily in dance and movement.

Then there is Tessanne Chin, whose victory on The Voice introduced her powerhouse vocals to millions internationally. T.O.K, whose harmonies became integral to dancehall’s crossover era; Richie Stephens, bringing decades of reggae experience; and Agent Sasco, one of the genre’s most respected lyricists.

Newer voices J’Calm and AcYn ensure the project is not only honouring Jamaica’s musical legacy, but also looking towards its future.

Browne, who has previously spoken about imagining artistes such as Ding Dong performing before audiences at major electronic music festivals, described J-House as an opportunity to carry Jamaican talent into spaces it may not traditionally occupy.

“This is crazy,” he said. “We’re creating a blueprint for other producers and record companies. The goal is to open doors for artistes, producers, and the industry as a whole.”

That ambition extends beyond the music itself. House music connects artistes to a vast international network of DJs, clubs, festivals, streaming platforms, radio, play lists, licensing opportunities, and electronic music audiences. J-House is designed to place Jamaican talent directly within that ecosystem, making the project as much about market expansion as it is about musical experimentation.

With J-House Volume 1 distributed through The Orchard/Sony Music the project also has access to an established international distribution network. And Volume 1 is not being treated as the endgame.

Browne shared that Jamaica represents the first instalment of a wider international concept. The United Kingdom is planned as the focus of the second volume, Japan the third, with Africa completing the four-part series. If the vision unfolds as planned, Jamaica will not simply be participating in another global musical movement. It will be the starting point.

World.title: Jamaica, US finalise operating procedures related to TCNs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that the United States and Jamaica have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding for TCNs that was signed earlier this year..

JAMAICA could soon receive its first batch of third-country nationals (TCNs) from the United States (US) as Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that both governments have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was signed earlier this year.

Jamaica now joins 30 countries, including several members of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), which have similar arrangements with the US Government amid its ongoing crackdown on illegal immigration.

“After internal consultations and thoughtful negotiations, both governments have now finalised operating procedures related to the MOU in order to settle the guard rails and parameters underpinning the agreement. The arrangements were also finalised, taking into account Jamaica’s capacity constraints and our belief in the principles of safe, orderly, and lawful migration,” said Johnson Smith, speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday.

The agreement, Johnson Smith clarified, will see 25 TCNs entering the country biweekly. While here, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) will provide basic services, like health care and counselling, to help with their transition.

The minister reiterated that under no circumstance will more than 25 TCNs be present in the island.

“We have also not agreed to receive 10,000 individuals. We have negotiated guard rails to address capacity constraints, and have, therefore, agreed to a maximum of 25 individuals per two-week period, which the IOM will, of course, be on a continuous basis making arrangements for their return.

“Furthermore, this arrangement will be suspended if 10 TCNs apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum procedures or other humanitarian applications. This, again, is specifically negotiated by Jamaica,” said Johnson Smith.

She further explained that TCNs were not deportees but the nationals of other countries who entered the US unlawfully and are being returned to their home countries through the IOM’s Assisted Voluntary Return Programme.

Johnson Smith added that while she is aware that some countries have opted to accept TCNs with criminal records, Jamaica will only facilitate those with no previous convictions.

“The Government reiterates its commitment to working with the IOM and the Government of the United States of America to ensure that all arrangements for the next stage of TCN implementation are appropriately governed and implemented in accordance with both our domestic laws and international law,” she said.

Additionally, while acknowledging Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang’s previous commitment to release the agreement, Johnson Smith explained that the MOU’s bilateral status prevents it from being made public.

“As indicated, this is not a unilateral arrangement; it is a bilateral arrangement, and one in which they [the United States] have not generally released their agreements, and they have not agreed to release this one,” she said.

“I give you every assurance as well that we have all shared all the relevant and material matters, provisions, in relation to the matter. So there’s nothing being hidden per se, but as you would note, even under the ATI [Access to Information Act], bilateral agreements, security agreements, arrangements that are sensitive to relations between countries and otherwise are treated differently from other agreements,” explained Johnson Smith.

Despite not being able to give an official start date for when the first TCNs are expected to arrive, Johnson Smith affirmed that Jamaicans will be regularly updated as conversations advance.

World.title: NEXT LEVEL
World.content:
Jamaica 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith competes in the women’s 4x100m relay heats during the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, Japan, on September 20, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

After breaking into the ranks of Jamaica’s fastest women ever, national 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith says she’s looking to carry her strong form into next season with the World Athletics Championships looming.

Smith ended her impressive 2026 season over the weekend at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, finishing fourth in the women’s 100m final and helping Jamaica land silver in the 4×100 metres mixed relay.

The 2025 North American, Central American and Caribbean (NACAC) 100m champion moved to 14th all time in Jamaica’s all-time list when she clocked a personal best 10.89 seconds at the Eugene Diamond League in July.

Prior to this year, Smith had never gone under 11 seconds in the event. However, she managed to dip under the mark six times, including at the Ultimate Championship where she registered 10.94 seconds both in the semi-final and final.

Smith, a finalist at this summer’s Commonwealth Games in Scotland and March’s World Indoor Championships in Poland, believes improving her confidence level was key in her success this year.

“I’m proud of myself [for] having confidence in myself,” she told the Inside Lane UK. “As good as last year was, it took me a while to start to trust my body and I feel like from day one this year in the background, I told myself that I was a champion and I was going to get what I wanted done and I think that’s what I’m most proud of, just being confident.”

The 30-year-old, who won 4x100m silver at last year’s Tokyo World Championships, says writing out her goals has helped change her perspective, which was on display at the recent Ultimate Championship.

“I journalled every day before practice and I had to do that [for the 100m final] also,” she said. “After the 4x100m, I felt bad because I really wanted us to win and I wasn’t able to pass [USA’s] Kayla [White]. She’s a phenomenal athlete, but I wanted us to win [0:44] to be honest, so I genuinely felt bad. My people were like ‘you split nine [seconds], that was so good’. But regardless, it was just like we didn’t win.

“So I went back to what I was used to and I journalled, I told myself that I’m a champion and I reminded myself what we were doing, trying to have fun and stuff like that. And I felt like that made me come out a whole lot more confident since the last month and the results showed.”

Describing 2026 as “phenomenal”, Smith says she’s excited for what’s to come in 2027.

“I got my 10.8, I got top three at the national trials and Ultimate finalist,” she said. “I just didn’t get [a] Commonwealth [medal] but that was out of my control, so I got to give myself some grace for that. But I feel like I finished off extremely well and I started even better indoors, so it’s a great thing to build off going into next season.”

Smith will likely be eyeing an individual spot at the 2027 World Championships in Beijing, having last done so in 2019 in Doha.

World.title: Shan’s Garlic, Thyme & Scotch Bonnet Butter Ribeye
World.content:
Shanice Gore completes the spread, serving up the garlic, thyme, and Scotch bonnet butter ribeye. (Photo: Alan Smith)

Get ready for a flavour-packed feast Mia Hair Artistry principal Shanice Gore shares her Garlic, Thyme & Scotch Bonnet Butter Ribeye recipe with Thursday Food.

“Ribeye is one of my favourite cuts of steak because of its beautiful marbling and rich flavour. In my home, we love our steak cooked medium rare, so I focus on getting a good, flavourful sear on the outside while keeping the centre juicy and tender. My garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet compound butter is the finishing touch — it melts beautifully over the hot steak and adds a delicious Jamaican kick,” says Gore.

Ingredients

•1 ribeye steak, approximately 1–1½ inches thick

• Salt, to taste

• Freshly cracked black pepper, to taste

• 1 tablespoon olive oil

For the Compound Butter:

• ½ cup unsalted butter, softened

• 2 cloves garlic, finely minced

• 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves

• ½–1 Scotch bonnet pepper, finely minced, depending on desired heat

Method

1. Begin by preparing the compound butter. Combine the softened butter with the garlic, thyme and finely minced Scotch bonnet pepper. Mix well until everything is evenly incorporated. Place the butter onto parchment paper, shape into a log, roll tightly and refrigerate until firm.

2. Remove the ribeye from the refrigerator about 30 minutes before cooking and pat dry with paper towels. Season both sides generously with salt and freshly cracked black pepper.

3. Heat a heavy skillet or cast-iron pan over high heat until very hot. Add the olive oil and carefully place the steak into the pan. Sear undisturbed until a deep golden-brown crust forms, then flip and sear the other side.

4. For a ribeye approximately 1–1½ inches thick, cook for approximately three to four minutes per side for medium rare, four to five minutes per side for medium, or six to seven minutes per side for well done. Cooking times will vary depending on the thickness of the steak, so a meat thermometer can be used for accuracy.

5. Once the steak has been seared on both sides, reduce the heat or remove the pan from the heat and place a generous spoonful of the garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet compound butter directly on top of the steak. Allow butter to melt over the hot meat, spooning the melted butter over the steak.

6. Remove the ribeye from the pan and leave it to rest for five to 10 minutes before slicing. Slice against the grain and serve with the melted compound butter spooned over the top.

Shan’s Tip: For the juiciest ribeye, don’t skip the resting time. And in my home, medium rare is the preferred doneness — the combination of the tender, juicy steak and the spicy, garlicky compound butter is hard to beat.

World.title: EU warns Turkey to clean up waste treatment or face trade ban
World.content:
While a suspension would be in line with EU rules on the shipment of waste, it would also jeopardize the bloc’s most important market for trash. Last year, Turkey received a third of the EU’s exported plastic waste.

The Commission assessment, dated Sept. 1 and obtained by POLITICO, reported a long list of concerns over Turkey’s treatment of EU waste, including the fact that only around 10% of plastic waste is recycled in the country, while the majority goes to landfills, is mismanaged or leaks into the environment.

The Commission official said the report pointed to “several instances” of plastic waste mismanagement, generating “serious pollution problems.”

Despite evidence of practices that could breach EU rules, the report said the Commission would hold off on suspending exports and instead engage with the Turkish authorities on these concerns.

The bloc’s Waste Shipment Regulation — which restricts exports of certain types of EU waste to third countries to curb pollution — says the EU can stop the export of waste to OECD countries that fail to show the waste is managed in an “environmentally sound manner.”

The law specifically requires the Commission to assess whether OECD countries importing large volumes of plastic waste are managing it without causing significant environmental or health damage.

World.title: Week Ender: Can Europe patch up the world in disorder?
World.content:
The old global order is breaking down. Ursula von der Leyen thinks Europe may have to start building something new around it.

In her State of the European Union speech, she floated closer ties with Canada — even “associate membership” — and a new European Security Council, as Europe looks for new ways to work with like-minded powers in an increasingly chaotic world. But both ideas immediately raised questions about whether von der Leyen was getting ahead of her own allies.

Host Sarah Wheaton is joined by POLITICO Executive Editor Carrie Budoff Brown, senior EU climate reporter Zia Weise and AI and technology reporter Pieter Haeck to unpack what von der Leyen’s speech tells us about Europe’s search for a role in this new global “unorder.”

They also look at her climate message — heavy on adaptation to heat, drought and fires, but lighter on new answers to Europe’s energy problems — and at her attempt to square AI regulation with the need to keep Europe in the global tech race.
