World.title: Germany and Spain go head-to-head in EU budget fight
World.content:
They are pressuring Ireland, in its position at the helm of the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, to cut hundreds of billions of euros in their next negotiating document due in October.

Officials involved in the negotiations who spoke to POLITICO and were granted anonymity because the discussions are confidential see more moderate cuts as the most likely outcome.

Debt time bomb

The EU’s seven-year budget, the multiannual financial framework, which governs EU spending from farmers’ subsidies to student exchange programs, is the subject of some of the fiercest negotiations in Brussels and pits different groups of countries against one another.

To try to bring their positions closer together, European Council President António Costa toured 25 EU countries in the past month to sound out leaders on the most sensitive questions facing the negotiations. He continued the trip in Dublin on Thursday.



In his bid to free up more budget funding, Cuerpo said he wants to delay repayment of joint debt issued in 2021 to tackle the economic fallout from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Around €300 billion must be repaid from 2028 to 2058. While interest repayments are set in stone, governments have more leeway to set the timeline for repaying the principal.

The current plan compels EU governments to front-load repayments and cough up €25 billion a year over the next budget cycle. Critics say this limits the funds available for other areas of spending and further constrains negotiations.

World.title: Germany’s Merz girds for a post-election fight for political survival
World.content:
It’s for this reason that Merz has arranged a meeting with CDU leaders to take place Sunday, just before polls close, at which he’s expected to gauge their support and attempt to convince them that he has a plan to turn things around. Merz has also canceled a planned speech at the United Nations General Assembly scheduled for Wednesday to remain in Berlin and address the domestic fallout from the CDU’s performance.

In an effort to rally support, Merz is emphasizing the importance of avoiding turbulence in Berlin during volatile times for Europe.

“All eyes are on Germany, on Berlin, on our role in the world,” Merz said at a CDU campaign event in Berlin on Thursday evening. “Expectations are placed on us to contribute to keeping this European continent stable.”

‘Hell breaks loose’

Despite his efforts to remain at the helm, Merz’s fate could be sealed by as little as a few percentage point shifts on Sunday in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polls show Merz’s conservatives collapsing to just 7% in the state, as its center-left premier takes on the leading AfD in an increasingly two-way contest between the strongest centrist force and the far right.

Hendrik Wüst, Minister President of North Rhine-Westphalia and seen as Merz’s most likely replacement, speaking during the 2026 Digital X at Rheinauhafen in Cologne on Sept. 8, 2026. | Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images

Should the CDU fall further, it would put the party at risk of failing to meet the 5% vote threshold required to enter the state parliament — a result that one conservative official, speaking on condition of anonymity to frankly discuss the mood inside the party, said would mean “all hell breaks loose.”

In Berlin, where the other regional election will be held this Sunday, the chancellor’s party is polling better — but things could still go poorly. The CDU is narrowly trailing the far-left Die Linke, or Left Party, at around 20% support, according to polls. That is still 8 percentage points below the CDU’s result in the last Berlin election — a decline that could see the conservatives ousted from the city government they currently lead and replaced by a coalition of left-wing parties.

World.title: Five EU leaders: Europe must spend better, not just more
World.content:
Budgets are where political priorities become real. Speeches, declarations and summit conclusions matter, but ultimately it is the allocation of money that reveals what governments are genuinely prepared to prioritize. Europe needs to become more competitive, more sovereign and better able to defend itself. There is no other choice.

Our budget must reflect that new reality.

The status quo of the current MFF cannot be the starting point. It is too focused on subsidies and transfers allocated largely in advance, leaving too little room for what Europe urgently needs: common investment in security and defense, competitiveness, innovation, and the fight against irregular migration. The next MFF will be the test of whether Europe has understood the message of Mario Draghi’s landmark report on European competitiveness. It will show whether our promises of more common European investment are real — or just rhetoric.

Mario Draghi addresses the audience during the conference ‘One Year After the Draghi Report’ at the EU Charlemagne building on September 16, 2025 in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images

That requires choices. And choices require political courage. This does not mean abandoning traditional policies, but we cannot just add every new priority to every old one and send the bill to taxpayers.

Almost every EU member country is making painful efforts to consolidate its public finances. Those that are not should concern us even more. There will be no European sovereignty without sound public finances.

We are doing our part: The group of net contributors that recently met in Berlin stands for almost 40% of the financing of the EU budget and provides around 70% of EU member countries’ bilateral support for Ukraine. We are investing heavily in our common security and defense. We are not tight-fisted. Nor are we hiding behind the label “frugal.” In fact, when it comes to supporting Ukraine, greater engagement by other member states is both reasonable and urgently needed.

World.title: A common budget that makes common sense
World.content:
Louder calls to slash the EU’s 2028–2034 financial framework will prevent Europe from acting on its own terms in a hostile world. The European Commission’s original proposal of almost €2 trillion varies little from the current spending plan once repayments of the post-pandemic recovery grants are excluded. That amounts to roughly 1.15% of the EU’s gross national income (GNI).

To get the debate back on track, Spain has proposed freeing up to €11 billion a year in resources that make both financial and political sense.

Instead of repaying the debt associated with the grant component of NextGenerationEU faster than required, the EU should link its service to its long-term economic capacity. An annual payment of about 0.06% of EU GDP would retire the debt by 2058, the deadline agreed by member states. Under the current plan, repayments would amount to between 0.09% and 0.11% a year over the next seven years.

Reprofiling the debt payment would free up nearly €70 billion over that period, which is equivalent to about one-fifth of the proposed European Competitiveness Fund that would channel investment into strategic sectors. It also amounts to roughly one-third of the aid the EU has sent to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.

This approach would not only release extra resources but keep the stock of EU debt broadly stable in the medium term while sending a strong signal to investors who are demanding more euro-denominated assets.

The proposal can also be seen as part of a more ambitious strategy to develop a European safe asset that drags down the liquidity premium that investors are asking for. Separately, Spain has proposed allowing the Commission to issue a portion of member countries’ debt on their behalf, helping to create a deeper common market for European debt. This could generate €25 billion in annual interest savings.

World.title: Centrist dads Carney and Burnham get ready to take on Trump
World.content:
There was even more excitement when Carney gave his own speech to the European Parliament a day later. Alas, there were fewer EU lawmakers present for Carney than there were for von der Leyen because of that long-standing MEP tradition of pissing off home at the earliest opportunity.

Between those Strasbourg meetings, Carney made a whistle-stop trip to the U.K. to watch the biggest football match of the calendar: Everton vs Wolverhampton Wanderers in the third round of the second-most important domestic cup competition (sponsored by an energy drink).

Carney went to watch football with Andy Burnham in what sociologists are already calling “Centrist Dad Overload.” While on the subject, what’s the collective noun for centrist dads? A podcast of centrist dads? A New Balance of centrist dads? A ‘have you got Oasis tickets?’ of centrist dads?

Of course, Carney and Burnham are sworn enemies of Donald Trump. The Canadian and U.S. leaders have been sparring for some time, with Trump wanting to make Canada the 51st state, and now it’s time for the British leader to get involved. The American president has already insulted Burnham, calling him the “mayor of a town.”

The two heads of state will likely cross paths at the United Nations General Assembly next week. They’ve spoken on the phone but have yet to meet in person, and it’s going to be a challenge for Burnham, whose traditional ice-breaker, “what’s your favorite album by The Smiths?” is unlikely to elicit much of a response from Trump, who only listens to “Y.M.C.A.” by the Village People on a loop.

Incidentally, Carney’s favorite album is “London Calling” by The Clash, the punk band who have a song called “I’m So Bored with the U.S.A.” As I write, EU bigwigs are seeing if they can use that song as the EU anthem instead of “Ode to Joy” without a treaty change.

World.title: Women offered less invasive or intensive treatment than men with the same conditions
World.content:
Women were less likely than men to be offered intensive treatments such as surgery or strong painkillers, a new review has found. While men and women are often treated differently by healthcare systems, the researchers noted that it is not clear whether these differences put either sex at a disadvantage.

 

Sex differences are evident throughout medicine and play a key role in the diagnosis and management of patients. Researchers at the University of St Andrews in Scotland found visible differences in the way men and women are treated.

“While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was”, said Miriam Veenhuizen, honorary lecturer at St Andrews School of Medicine.

Researchers analysed 41 studies published between 2018 and 2023 and found the same pattern in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care.

Women suffering from heart failure, heart attack and tachycardia were more likely to be managed conservatively with medication compared with invasive procedures such as coronary artery bypass grafting and percutaneous coronary intervention.

Among patients with Parkinson’s disease, men were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation devices, an implantable device used to manage symptoms. Women were also less likely to receive a liver transplant or be referred to surgery.

“For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption,” said Andrew O’Malley, co-lead of the study.

What is behind this difference?

While the trend was consistent across studies, the reasons behind it remain unclear.

“It’s not entirely clear why this is happening, but it is likely because women were under-represented in clinical trials until recent decades, so many guidelines rest on data from men,” said Veenhuizen.

The researchers called for further research to understand whether these differences reflect legitimate variations in clinical practice or wider inequalities, and to ensure patients receive equitable care.

World.title: Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979
World.content:
Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12.5 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979, raising global sea levels by around 3.2 centimetres, according to a major scientific study.

 

The researchers found that ice loss has accelerated in recent decades, particularly since the 1990s.

Most of the loss is linked to warmer ocean temperatures, which cause glaciers to discharge more ice into the sea.

Ice loss accelerated sharply during the 2010s

The study combines satellite observations covering more than four decades. It extends the record back to 1979 for Antarctica and 1972 for Greenland.

The data shows the ice sheets were relatively stable through the 1970s, 1980s and into the 1990s.

Ice loss then increased, with the strongest acceleration recorded during the 2010s.

“There is a clear trend that the ice sheets are losing more mass and it has been increasing from decade to decade,” says Inès Otosaka, an ice scientist at Northumbria University.

She says the changes were clearly linked to rising air and ocean temperatures.

Warmer oceans drive most of the ice loss

Around 84 per cent of the ice loss is linked to increased ice discharge into the oceans, the researchers found.

Surface processes account for the remaining 16 per cent. Warmer seawater can erode ice from below and around the edges of glaciers, increasing their flow towards the ocean.

In Greenland, the Jakobshavn glacier is retreating by up to 50 metres a day, Otosaka says.

Ice loss is raising sea levels

The ice loss has contributed around 3.2 centimetres to global sea level rise since 1979. Scientists say even small increases can have significant consequences for coastal areas.

For every centimetre of sea level rise, an estimated two to three million more people could face annual coastal flooding.

Ice loss slowed between 2020 and 2023, but researchers say this reflected short-term weather patterns rather than a change in the longer-term trend. They also warn that ice-sheet responses to climate change can take decades. This means ice loss could continue even if global warming were brought under control.

The study was published in the journal Scientific Data.

World.title: Premiumisation, industry recovery and AI: What’s trending in travel at ATM Dubai 2026?
World.content:
There’s no doubt about it, it’s been a tough year for the tourism industry – especially in the Middle East, where regional conflict and the knock-on effects have disrupted travel.

 

Despite a record-breaking year for global tourism in 2025, the geopolitical situation has impacted travel to the Middle East and Gulf in 2026, with visitor numbers, air capacity and hospitality bookings all taking a significant hit.

While much of the conversation on the sidelines at Arabian Travel Market (ATM) in Dubai centred on this year’s major disruptions, there were also signs of industry recovery.

Unveiled this week, the ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 revealed that international travel across the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia (MENASA) region is forecast to rebound by 17% in 2027, “more than twice the projected global growth rate of 8%”, according to Tourism Economics, which co-produced the report.

It's also expected that international visitor spending in the Middle East will increase by $116 billion (€100.58 billion), or 57%, between 2025 and 2030.

Speaking at ATM Dubai, Dave Goodger, Managing Director EMEA of Tourism Economics, was “optimistic” about the forecasts.

“Over the next five years we see travel expanding on a structural basis rather than just a cyclical rebound,” he said. “International travel has never mattered more. This year is disrupted by an uncertain economic and geopolitical backdrop, but consumers are treating travel as essential.”

As the industry looks towards recovery and the long-term, many trends are emerging that could shape the next era in tourism.

From the “premiumisation” of travel and rise of lesser-known destinations to the use of AI for trip discovery, we take a look at the report’s main findings and some of the other big talking points on the ground this week at ATM Dubai.

The ‘premiumisation’ of travel

Luxury remains an important part of the travel market, particularly in the Middle East and Gulf, where Goodger said nearly 80% of prospective visitors prioritise luxury when travelling. But “premiumisation” extends beyond traditional five-star hotels.

Travellers are increasingly willing to spend more on particular elements of a holiday that matter to them, from upgraded airline cabins to memorable activities.

“People want those luxury experiences, they want those premium experiences, but they will save money where they can,” Goodger said. The report also found that 35% of travellers were more interested in premium experiences than two years ago.

Value hunting and price-conscious travel

The search for value is happening alongside premiumisation rather than replacing it. In a separate interview with Euronews Travel, Goodger said greater price-consciousness was a “global challenge”, evident across Europe, North America, China and other Asian markets.

“People are price conscious, they’re looking for value, but they are looking for valuable experiences,” he said. That could mean spending less on accommodation to pay for the experiences that motivated the holiday in the first place.

“They’re not just saying… ‘I’m going to find the cheapest package holiday I can do’,” Goodger added. “They are saying, ‘I will downgrade on the hotel, but I still really want to do that experience that I’m doing while I’m there’.”

Dave Goodger, Managing Director EMEA of Tourism Economics, speaking at ATM Dubai RX Global

The rise of lesser-known destinations

Of the travellers surveyed, 56% are more interested in exploring new destinations than they were two years ago, rising to 68% among prospective visitors to MENASA.

While this creates opportunities for secondary cities and regions away from established tourism hotspots, it doesn’t mean that Paris, London and other tourism giants are losing their appeal.

Goodger said first-time international travellers still want to “stand in front of the Eiffel Tower” or “see Buckingham Palace”, while repeat visitors are increasingly venturing further afield.

“They’re the ones that are going to the new destinations, the new regions, the secondary destinations,” he told Euronews Travel.

Experience-first travel

Travellers are increasingly choosing an experience or passion first and building their trip around it.

Culture and authentic experiences are among the priorities highlighted by Tourism Economics, while travellers are showing greater interest in activities, food and sport.

“People are looking for experiences,” Goodger said at ATM. “They want new experiences. They want these cultural experiences.”

Overtourism and when people travel

Mass tourism is also beginning to influence travel decisions. Tourism Economics' research found that three in 10 travellers actively avoid destinations because of overcrowding concerns.

Goodger told Euronews Travel that overtourism remains particularly significant in Europe, although the shift away from crowded destinations is still “very subtle”.

One emerging trend is travelling outside the busiest months. “We are seeing a bit of a flattening of seasonality,” he said. “People are looking outside of peak season for travel, just so they can have that experience without the crowds.”

This could benefit destinations attempting to spread visitors more evenly across the year, as well as lesser-known places looking to attract travellers away from overcrowded hotspots.

Event tourism

Travellers are increasingly crossing borders specifically to attend events, adding further momentum to the rise of sports and music tourism. Three in 10 travellers surveyed said they were more interested in event-related travel than two years ago.

Goodger highlighted “sporting, cultural [and] religious events” as increasingly strong drivers of travel, particularly in the Middle East.

Business events are also important with association meeting attendance in the Middle East nearly doubling over the past decade.

AI for trip discovery

Perhaps the biggest change to how travellers discover and plan their next trip is the growing use of AI. Goodger said travellers interested in visiting the Middle East are particularly "tech-forward", with AI chatbots already playing a significant role in trip planning.

The report found that 28% of prospective visitors to the Middle East had used an AI chatbot to plan a trip, compared with 12% of travellers interested in other regions.

AI could also help bring lesser-known destinations into consideration as travellers move away from traditional keyword searches towards more conversational queries based on the type of holiday they want.

For destinations, Goodger said that means being visible in a rapidly changing discovery landscape. “It’s absolutely crucial for the destinations to be discoverable through those different platforms.”

World.title: The EU and Canada are getting closer than ever. And the world is watching
World.content:
With Canada, the European Union has opened the door to a new way for the European project to affiliate with third countries that aren't even on its own continent. The rest of the world will be watching closely.

 

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spearheaded the idea of an alliance of middle powers in his seminal speech in Davos earlier this year. A few months later, Canada might provide the blueprint for how the EU integrates third countries.

On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become "the first associate member of the European Union," proposing an unprecedented arrangement that still has to be fully defined.

Whichever framework Brussels and Ottawa manage to agree on will have consequences well beyond Europe, as there is international attention on whether the EU can create an attractive blueprint to pull other democracies into its orbit.

"A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies. An alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability," Carney told the European Parliament on Thursday.

Unprecedented arrangement

The EU does not currently envisage an "associate membership." The idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as an innovative way to integrate Ukraine into the EU, but the proposal was rebuffed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

So far, the Union has consisted solely of member states and candidate countries. Canada, meanwhile, has no intention of joining the bloc, as Carney has made clear, and its treaties would not permit it in any case, given that Canada is not a European country.

"The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," the Canadian PM said, arguing that what mattered was the substance.

The EU treaties do allow some flexibility, as they state that "the Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure."

What exactly this associate status would entail is still not clear. Carney proposed deep cooperation across the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.

But while the details remain to be hashed out, what appears clear is that whatever deal Brussels and Ottawa reach will be a highly influential precedent for how the EU engages with other partners.

Trusted partners

The idea of making Canada an associate member of the EU was first made public via a WSJ report earlier this week.

"We are on the same page," Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell told the Sydney Morning Herald. "We will take great interest in what Carney does."

In an exclusive interview with Euronews, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said that Australia and New Zealand might follow Canada's path, as the EU seeks to deepen ties with like-minded countries.

MEP Tobias Cremer (Germany/S&D) told reporters he was receiving an increasing number of media requests, not only from Canadian outlets but also from Australian, British and Japanese ones.

Meanwhile, the UK is reportedly feeling left out of Brussels' newfound love for Canada, as some in London believe the EU is more interested in closer relations with Canada than with the UK.

"We need to think of partnerships that go beyond EU membership," Austria's Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger wrote on X. "Let's make that a model for the future — one that Europe also offers to other partners: Norway, Iceland, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand."

In other words, the success of the special relationship with Canada might put the EU at the centre of a new international alliance, as democratic countries that have lost faith in the US as leader of the Western world realign.

International order

The newfound alignment between Brussels and Ottawa might be one step closer to the realisation of Carney's vision of an alliance of middle powers, meant to strengthen each other's sovereignty by weathering shifting geopolitical realities together.

"I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners," he said.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," Carney continued.

In Brussels, officials tend to point out that, while member states taken on their own might be middle powers, the EU as a whole is not, and might actually emerge as a leader of a democratic coalition to support the faltering rules-based international order.

"We are by definition a convening power of middle powers in the way we function. I think that makes us actually attractive to many other middle powers, because the EU, like no other global player, has in its DNA leveraging small and middle powers without trampling on their interests," Cremer said.

At the same time, as the EU pursues global ambitions to forge deeper ties with democracies on other continents, some fear it might lose sight of its most immediate neighbourhood.

Unsettled candidates

The acceleration of the EU-Canada partnership, and the entirely new format on offer, has fallen flat especially among countries that have been standing in line to join for decades, such as in the Western Balkans.

It is not the first time the EU has floated a new membership structure. Candidate countries have seen, in close succession, the growth plan, reverse enlargement, gradual integration and now a tiered form of membership.

There is also a risk that the move further strains transatlantic relations with the US, with President Donald Trump already threatening possible retaliation, which might put pressure on candidate countries to pick a side between the two blocs.

"I don't feel comfortable with the constant new ideas over membership and the lack of discussion concerning the acceptance of new members," Obrad Kesić, the head of Bosnia and Herzegovina's mission to the EU, told Euronews.

"Canada is a large country, it could have negative ramifications for small candidate countries if the discussion becomes too broad. It changes the contour of the debate," Kesić said. "Conceiving memberships as going beyond Europe opens up a new set of issues."

World.title: Analysis: Bruised by Trump, EU and Canada find solace in each other's arms
World.content:
Taunted, scorned, belittled, pushed aside, ditched – it is fair to say that the European Union and Canada each know how the other feels.

 

For the past 20 months, the two have been relentlessly subjected to Donald Trump's threats, demands and commands. Their experiences have been nearly identical: punitive tariffs, annexationist attempts, regulatory intrusion, bitter recriminations, all amplified in scathing personal attacks splashed all over social media.

The breakup has been painful, to say the least. After all, both the EU and Canada have long defined the United States as their closest ally, their main security provider, their trade partner of choice. But Trump's return to the White House abruptly overturned these long-held assumptions, forcing them to reckon with their place in a cruel, cold world.

This week, they found solace in each other's arms. In back-to-back highly publicised speeches, the EU and Canada brought their courtship into a full-fledged, out-in-the-open romance.

Ursula von der Leyen made the first move during her State of the Union address, inviting Canada to make history by becoming the bloc's first-ever "associate member" – a brand new legal status devised to accommodate Ottawa.

"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," the European Commission president said, in a thinly veiled swipe at Trump.

"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she went on. "We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible."

The announcement, which was not included in the embargoed speech sent in advance to the press, was met with thunderous applause inside the European Parliament. Smiling in the audience, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got up to kiss von der Leyen on the cheek.

Ursula von der Leyen. European Union, 2026.

The following day, she took a seat as he addressed the same audience himself.

"Europe and Canada are stronger together," Carney declared to more applause. "Let us now deepen these roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground."

The grand statements sent Europe's Canada fever into overdrive. Lawmakers in Strasbourg lined up to take selfies with Carney. The leader of the Greens, Terry Reintke, donned a Canada jersey for his speech; Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez tweeted a European flag with a maple leaf next to the 12 stars, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the EU and Canada were "destined" to closer bonds.

Roberta Metsola, the European Parliament president, went further and name-checked Australia and New Zealand as next in line to be the bloc's "associate members".

"I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door," Metsola told Euronews. "In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."

The other side was no less enthusiastic: a poll conducted ahead of Carney's trip showed that 56% of Canadians think they have more in common with the EU, which is one ocean away, than with the US, with which they share an 8,891 km land border.

Beyond the love, anxiety

Brussels and Ottawa have framed their fascination as self-evident.

The two see themselves as equally committed to liberal democracy, the rule of law and open markets, making them, on paper, a perfectly compatible match.

In their speeches, von der Leyen and Carney spare no effort in listing the multiple areas of cooperation in which the EU and Canada can thrive together: trade, energy, critical raw materials, batteries, AI, quantum, finance, defence, space, the Arctic.

Carney touted a scheme to grant young people freedom of movement to "live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic", while von der Leyen spoke of a "common prosperity and economic security space".

It is not by coincidence that these are areas where cooperation with the US has become increasingly difficult, at times prohibitive, under Trump, with whom Carney is currently embroiled in a trade war that could wreck key sectors of the Canadian economy.

They did, however, disagree on semantics.

Von der Leyen went all in on the headline-making "associate member" title, despite lacking legal precedent and raising more questions than answers. It was not clear how, or if, the Commission chief had consulted with capitals before her pitch.

Carney, meanwhile, opted for "alliance for the future", a less charged term. For the premier, "associate membership" carries the connotation of ceding sovereignty to Brussels, something he stressed would not be the case under any circumstance.

"The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," he said.

Beyond that hiccup, the two stayed very much on the same script, sometimes using the same words to lavish praise on each other.

Donald Trump. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

But underneath the smiles, the hugs and the adulation lay a creeping anxiety about what the future holds.

The EU and Canada are today trapped between adversarial forces – Trump's "America first" agenda, China's unfair competition, Russia's aggression – that risk undoing their wealth and plunging them into a spiral of stagnation. They can only watch as the global norms they seek to uphold are weakened from within.

Their friendship is therefore as much about thriving as it is about surviving.

Trump, in particular, has proven a powerful push factor forcing them closer together. His penchant for disruption has made the blossoming partnership feel almost inevitable.

The US president was quick to take note of the love fest and threatened to impose "very serious tariffs" if the "associate membership" were perceived as a "hostile act".

Carney insisted the EU-Canada alliance was a "positive initiative" and "not a reaction to something else". But in his speech, he implicitly chided Trump when he said Canada was not a "fair-weather" ally that pursues "zero-sum deals".

Penny Naas, the director of the Brussels office at the German Marshall Fund, believes the newfound EU-Canada affinity is but a "natural outgrowth" of the past 20 months.

"The US is moving away from anchoring and leading its traditional alliance of democratic countries. This is clearly motivating the look for new partners in an uncertain world," Naas told Euronews.

"Trade status and regulatory alignment are no longer background conditions for prosperity. They are the terrain on which power is being contested directly," she added.

"Any EU-Canada architecture will be judged, and attacked, on those terms from the start."

World.title: UN Security Council fails to adopt US-backed Iran sanctions resolution after Russia and China vetoes
World.content:
Russia and China have vetoed a United Nations resolution that would have allowed independent experts to continue monitoring sanctions reimposed on Iran over its nuclear programme, dealing a blow to international oversight efforts.

 

The United States had drafted the resolution to extend the UN expert panel's mandate for a year. It was defeated on Thursday at the UN Security Council by a vote of 11-2, with Somalia and Pakistan abstaining.

The UN Security Council sanctions, which were reimposed on 27 September last year under the snapback mechanism of the 2015 nuclear deal, remain in effect. They freeze Iranian assets abroad, restrict arms deals with Tehran and penalise the development of its ballistic missile programme.

France, Germany and the United Kingdom triggered the snapback provision, which restored the Security Council sanctions committee and authorised the panel of experts to monitor compliance. Thursday's veto removes that oversight without lifting the underlying sanctions.

The vote comes as the Trump administration pursues a broader campaign to isolate Tehran economically. Separately on Thursday, Washington moved against digital currency networks it says are being used to give sanctioned Iranian entities illegal access to the international financial system.

The moves also come amid a more than six-month-old war in Iran that has reached a stalemate.

The US Treasury and State Departments announced that they had targeted two companies — BitBank and the Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Co. — and three associates of BitBank’s previously sanctioned chief, Babak Zanjani, who are accused of playing a role in helping Iran evade sanctions.

At the United Nations, Iran’s UN mission thanked China and Russia for vetoing the US resolution, saying on social media that the countries “prevented yet another cynical attempt by the United States and its allies to abuse the Security Council for their political purposes.”

Since Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025, UN nuclear inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium.

The UN nuclear watchdog has said Iran maintained a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

Russian UN Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia reiterated Moscow’s claim that the “snapback” of sanctions against Iran was illegal, and therefore the resolution to extend the mandate of the panel of experts “was deeply flawed and did not have any legal basis.”

US fumes at veto, says it's in support of rogue regimes

Russia and China had strongly urged the US and its allies not to put the resolution to a vote, which would only increase tensions in the council, Nebenzia said, but Washington “decided to opt for confrontation.”

According to the French UN Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, the current council president, implementing sanctions is “a crucial instrument to encourage Iran” to return to its nuclear obligations. France will study how to ensure sanctions are enforced, he said.

One possibility would be to follow what happened after the North Korea panel of experts was abolished: establishing a monitoring team that includes France, Germany, the UK and the United States.

Washington's deputy ambassador to the UN, Jennifer Locetta, said Washington wasn’t surprised by the vetoes on Thursday because the experts “would have shone the light” on prohibited cooperation between Iran and its partners.

According to Locetta, the vetoes are part of a broader effort to prevent expert monitoring of sanctions and even the appointment of panel members "to stifle reporting that implicates their own activities in support of rogue regimes.”

In March 2024, a Russian veto ended UN monitoring of sanctions against North Korea over its nuclear programme. In Mali, sanctions were terminated, and Locetta said that in Yemen and the Central African Republic, expert appointments have been delayed or refused.

While the panel of experts for Iran was authorised a year ago and Secretary-General Antonio Guterres proposed members, they were never approved.

“Without an independent panel of experts, this council loses its principal source of impartial, evidence-based reporting on sanctions violations, creating a monitoring gap that only benefits the Iranian regime and those who profit from evading those measures,” Locetta warned.

World.title: Nigeria: At least 37 suspected illegal miners die in custody
World.content:
Dozens of suspects accused of illegal mining were found dead in custody in Nigeria's north-central Niger State. Officials blame disease, while reports cite overcrowding and poor ventilation.

At least 37 people believed to be illegal miners died Thursday while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC), according to the governor of Nigeria's north-central Niger State.

"This morning we woke up to the news that about 37 persons died in the custody of the civil defense here in Minna," Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago told reporters in the state's capital.

He called the incident "sad" and "tragic," adding that a committee of inquiry into the deaths had been established and was already working. The governor declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for the January elections.

The police in Niger State announced that they have launched an investigation and urged relatives of the victims to come forward with any helpful information.

What do we know about the incident?

The suspects have been detained since the security agency made arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday due to suspicions of illegal mining in the state, said Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, head of the NSCDC in Niger, in a statement on Thursday.

Aniviye said that although the agency suspects the detainees died of disease, their bodies were sent to a local hospital for a medical examination to determine the cause of death. He did not specify the type of disease.

However, according to the intelligence report, "preliminary information suggests the fatalities may have resulted from overcrowding and inadequate ventilation within a detention facility."

A 40-second video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men, most of whom appeared to be teenagers. Volunteers wearing gloves stood over the bodies, while veiled women tried to identify their relatives.

Dirty gold: Nigeria's toxic water threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Survivors describe a lack of ventilation

Dauda Shehu, one of the survivors, told the Associated Press that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell. "We were jampacked and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well," he said.

"All of a sudden, we realized that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air," Shehu added. The detainees tried to get the guards' attention by banging on the cell door, he explained.

Spanning more than twice the area of Belgium, Niger State is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most of whom are lured by the hope of striking gold.

According to officials and experts, the scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger State is also fueling violence by criminal gangs known locally as bandits. These gangs tax miners and demand a cut of the extracted ore in exchange for access to the pits.

World.title: Aztec manuscript returns to Mexico after two centuries, on loan
World.content:
For years, Mexico has demanded the return of a treasured manuscript. Now the Aztec relic is back home from France — but on loan.

The Azcatitlan Codex, a rare and prized manuscript that recounts the history of the Aztecs in vibrant pictograms, has returned to Mexico for the first time since 1840. It went on display in Mexico City on Thursday.

The codex is a 16th-century artifact and regarded as one of the most important visual records of Aztec history. It records the founding of the Aztec capital to its fall after the subsequent arrival of Spanish conquistadores.

It arrived in Mexico on loan from France's Bibliotheque Nationale, where it has been since 1898. The temporary loan is occurring as the two nations celebrate 200 years of diplomatic ties.

In return for the Azcatitlan Codex, Mexico will loan a different historical artifact to France Image: Carl De Souza/AFP

Reunited with history

As two folios from the document went on display inside a glass case at the National Museum of Anthropology, Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco said the exhibition was about "reuniting a population with its (collective) memory."

The pictograms "represent our history, the written voice of our ancestors, and the deep root of our identity," he said, speaking at the inauguration.

The codex was created in Mexico by an indigenous craftsman from the Otomi people Image: Carl De Souza/AFP

Mexico has demanded the treasured artifact be returned for years.

Members of an indigenous group reacted ecstatically to the display. "They hid our history from us, they stole it!" Emilia Mendoza of the Hnahnu community said at the opening exhibition.

"This is a battle won, a first step toward the restitution of these books that reside in other countries," she said.

What's in the Azcatitlan Codex?

Made up of Mesoamerican pictograms with European writing, the codex is divided into three parts.

It traces the Mexica's migration from Aztlan — the mythical birthplace of the Aztec civilization — to the founding of Tenochtitlan. That's the capital of the Aztec empire and is present day Mexico City.

The document also depicts the succession of the city's rulers, the arrival of the Spanish and the subsequent evangelization, according to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History.

All of this has been rendered in the codex in vibrant reds, blues, greens and yellows, depicting warriors in feathered headdresses and showcasing ritual acts in pyramid temples.

More than five centuries have now passed since Tenochtitlan fell to Hernan Cortes, the leader of the invading Spanish forces. As most histories of invasion go, Cortez and his allies looted and razed the city after conquest, ushering in three centuries of Spanish domination.

Historic megacity — the legendary Aztec capital To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"These codices are extremely important to us because they continue to give us identity and value as human beings during these very special times we are experiencing," said ​Maria Eugenia Castaneda, representative of the Mexica peoples. "They elevate our morale, our customs, our culture, and our sense of who we are."

According to Mexican historians, an indigenous craftsman from the Otomi people created the codex.

The document will remain on display until December. As part of the exchange, Mexico will loan France another important historical document — the Codex Boturini — which also depicts the migration of the Aztec people to the Mexican valley.

World.title: UN mission notes possible US war crimes in Iran strikes
World.content:
A United Nations fact-finding mission said it found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran.

Experts from the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, commissioned by the UN Human Rights Council, said they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including one that hit a school in the southern Iranian city of Minab.

In a report published Thursday , the experts also accused Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people.

Established in 2022, the mission is chaired by Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and consists of independent experts.

They were expected to present their findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday. The Council is made up of 47 UN member countries.

The mission examined US actions during the Iran war, which started in February, and the Iranian government's response to the nationwide unrest that began in late December.

Although it is not binding, the report contributes to the international evidence gathered about the Iran war and could eventually be used in attempts to bring legal cases to international courts.

How did the US react?

The Pentagon declined to comment on the mission's report. "Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the White House issued a strongly worded statement, with spokesperson Anna Kelly saying the UN top human rights body has "accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades."

"The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Kelly said.

US strikes in Minab and Lamerd

In the report, UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe that US forces were responsible for the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab on February 28.

Iranian officials said that more than 150 people were killed in the attack, including around 120 schoolchildren.

The mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate, causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure. This amounts to a war crime under international law, according to the report.

UN experts concluded that the school was clearly a civilian facility and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

They reached a similar conclusion regarding a strike on a sports center in Larned, also on February 28. The report stated that the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school, killing and injuring 22 civilians.

The report concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.

In a statement issued in March, US Central Command said that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd that day.

Evidence points to US role in deadly Iran school attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Crackdown in Iran

The UN probe also found that Iranian authorities carried out widespread and systematic attacks against civilians during the protests that erupted in late December.

These attacks included unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, the report said.

According to human rights groups, bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.

Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign adversaries, including the US and Israel.

The probe stated that it could not independently verify the death toll, but it believes that the number of deaths and injuries is likely far higher than the official count of 3,038 deaths and 25,000 injuries.

World.title: Trump hails 'major progress' in setting up US base in Poland
World.content:
The location of the permanent US military base in Poland could be announced "very soon," Donald Trump has said. The US president also praised the leadership of his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki.

US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland.

"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland.

"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post.

His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there.

How did Warsaw react?

Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation."

He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."

Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland.

In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory.

"We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP.

Can Poland hold NATO’s line against Russia without the US? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Poland secures NATO's eastern flank

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank.

Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis.

Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence.

In the meantime, Washington heavily criticized several European countries for refusing to allow US forces to use NATO bases in its war with Iran.

World.title: US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
World.content:
In a recent memo, the US government would no longer consider the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful.

The US government is planning a major reinterpretation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), The New York Times reported and officials confirmed to AFP on Thursday.

The policy shift was delivered in a new memo signed by Brian Nesvik, director of the Interior Department's Fish and Wildlife Service.

In it, the department will reduce the term "take," a term that relates to pursuing, killing or capturing of a species, to simply "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals."

This change would no longer treat the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful.

Wildlife deaths resulting from foreseeable risks posed by activities such as commercial fishing or logging would end up exempt from the landmark 1973 law.

A 'huge loophole'

The wildlife service has historically held people liable for accidentally harming protected species such as grizzly bears, manatees and spotted owls.

"This cuts against the entire history of the Endangered Species Act," Dan Ashe, who led the Fish and Wildlife Service under former President Barack Obama, told the Associated Press. "It just creates a huge loophole. It completely relieves people of any responsibility for their actions, even consequences that can be easily predicted."

The Interior Department confirmed the memo's authenticity to AFP.

"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department told AFP.

"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.

Illegal dolphin hunting poses serious threat to species To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Broad overhaul of Endangered Species Act

Last year, the Trump administration declared it would consider "economic considerations" when deciding whether to protect species at risk of extinction.

The move is the latest attempt to loosen the landmark ESA's rules. Combined, the changes overturn five decades of precedent in how the law is interpreted and applied.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has argued that the changes are necessary, claiming the ESA has been "weaponized" to stop economic projects, weaken competitiveness, undermine national security, and ultimately hurt Americans.

Among the changes to ESA is the redefinition of the term "harm," which would allow oil drilling, mining and other activities in endangered habitats as long as those activities do not directly kill or injure the animals.

The automatic application of endangered species protections to those listed as "threatened" was also halted.

Additionally, the Trump administration announced that it was shrinking two vast stretches of protected land in Utah by more than 90%, to open millions of acres of protected land for fossil fuel extraction and mining.

States sue the government

Last week, the attorneys general of 20 Democratic-led states, along with Washington, DC, submitted a lawsuit against the administration over its overhaul of ESA.

One lawsuit tackles the redefinition of "harm," while a second lawsuit challenges a rule that removes protections for newly threatened species, and the new business-related considerations taken into account when declaring "critical habitats."

"The Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people ‌who overwhelmingly support protections for endangered species," Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said.

"Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to ‌our water is one of exploitation," he added.

World.title: Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
World.content:
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and stricter regulations in Argentina, more and more Russians are choosing to travel to Brazil to give birth to children, who will obtain Brazilian nationality.

Yulia and Dmitri (whose names have been changed for reasons of safety) flew from Russia to Brazil this summer so that their child could be born there. Yulia was 32 weeks pregnant at the time of travel.

"Of course, we didn't say that I was pregnant at border control," Yulia told DW.

Her daughter was born at a private clinic in Santos, a city in southern Brazil. Anybody born in the country has an automatic right to Brazilian nationality. The family is currently preparing all the paperwork.

"We've achieved our minimum goal," said Dmitri. "With a Brazilian passport, our daughter will be able to travel without a visa to almost any country in the world. She won't have to apply for an expensive and time-consuming Schengen visa. We want her to be able to decide for herself where she studies, works or lives."

He said that a colleague of his had traveled to Brazil in early August with his pregnant wife for the same reasons.

Yulia and Dmitri said that they had spent the equivalent of about €10,000 (about $11,500) during the first six weeks of their stay in Brazil, which included the costs for several days of treatment for their daughter in intensive care. Dmitri quit his job at a bank for the trip and hopes to find work again after the family returns to their home in the Russian capital Moscow.

However, they are only planning to return once all the documents for their daughter are ready and that could take months. Other Russian families have decided to stay in Brazil permanently.

According to organizations and lawyers that provide support to Russians in Brazil, there has been an increase in immigration from Russia, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which visa requirements for Russian nationals entering certain countries were tightened.

Should EU countries grant fewer visas to Russians? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Argentina tightens visa regulations

Birth tourism to Brazil has also increased since Argentina, which used to be one of the main destinations for people wanting their children to be born in a country that automatically grants citizenship to newborns, tightened its regulations. People who want their children to obtain Argentinian citizenship now have to have resided in Argentina for at least two years. Since 2025, the access of people who do not have a permanent residence permit to free healthcare has also been restricted.

According to the Russian news outlet RBC, more than 7,000 Russians applied for a residence permit in Argentina in 2023. By mid-2025, the number had decreased to about 1,800.

Meanwhile, almost 500 Brazilian passports were issued to Russians in 2024 and more than 600 the following year. More than half of the new citizens were women.

The parents of a child born in Brazil can apply for a residence permit, which they can obtain within a year, under certain circumstances.

Almost anybody born in Brazil can obtain Brazilian nationality Image: Paulo Lopes/ZUMA/picture alliance

Yana (name changed) and her husband chose to do this in 2023.

"The events of 2022 certainly played a role, but we had already toyed with the idea of giving birth abroad," Yana told DW. "A lot can happen in Russia. I always wanted a second passport and to give birth to my child in another country. When I became pregnant unexpectedly, all we had to do was decide which country made sense."

Yana gave birth to a boy at a public hospital in Florianopolis, the capital of the southern state of Santa Catarina, and the family stayed in Brazil for about three years.

"It was important to get passports for us and our child. I really enjoyed living there, and I learned Portuguese," Yana said, adding that she and her husband have lived as "digital nomads" in various countries over the years.

Even though they no longer live in Brazil, they want their son to have a connection to his birth country: "We read Portuguese books and talk a lot about Brazil. I want him to be able to travel without a visa and remain open to the world."

Big Russian community in Florianopolis

One of the largest Russian communities in Brazil lives in Florianopolis, and it's growing. According to the local health authorities, 119 Russian women took advantage of prenatal consultations in the first six months of this year. In all of 2025, it was 136 Russian women.

A lawyer who preferred to remain anonymous told DW that Brazil neither expressly prohibited nor permitted foreign nationals to enter the country for the purpose of giving birth. Often pregnant women do not disclose their reason for traveling to Brazil at border control. And once they are in the country they have access to free public hospitals and medical facilities regardless of their immigration status.

Florianopolis is home to one of the largest Russian communities in Brazil Image: Anderson Coelho/DW

As Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases, a whole industry has emerged. Often, recent Russian immigrants to Brazil act as intermediaries and help others find housing or medical care. They provide assistance with complicated administrative procedures or the language. Depending on the level of care, the cost can reach into the thousands of dollars.

However, providers of such services, lawyers, and volunteers report stricter controls by Brazilian authorities, particularly in cities with larger Russian communities, such as Florianopolis. They say authorities are requesting more documents than in the past.

"The police are conducting more thorough checks to verify whether people actually live at the addresses they provide," one lawyer said, explaining that in the past, false addresses had been given by people hoping to obtain residence permits more quickly.

No evidence of Brazil systematically denying entry to Russians

But DW did not find any evidence to suggest that Russians were being denied entry to Brazil en masse.

In late July, the Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that 10 pregnant women had been "deported" from Russia. The information was later picked up by various media outlets. However, the Brazilian police denied the veracity of the report to DW, explaining that decisions to deny somebody entry to the country were always made on a case-by-case basis, and that pregnancy played no role in the process.

DW was only able to find one documented case of a pregnant Russian woman being initially refused entry into Brazil. She was allowed to enter the country after a lawyer intervened. According to the court records, the Brazilian border authorities had doubts as to how the Russian national would be financing her stay in Brazil.

The woman did not respond to the DW's inquiries.

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
World.content:
Fuel shortages, drone strikes and mobilization rumors are fueling anxiety and war fatigue in Russia. As support for peace talks grows among Russians, the Kremlin is watching closely ahead of parliamentary elections.

Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.

According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan , 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.

"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.

She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.

All 450 seats in the Duma are at stake in the upcoming election Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "

That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.

From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.

Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?

"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.

Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.

"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.

In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.

But many Russians appear to want the opposite.

"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.

That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center . Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.

Support for Yabloko has been rising

One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.

The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.

Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.

Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.

"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.

What will anti-war voters do?

Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?

Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.

Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.

Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.

Navalnaya (center) and Yashin (right) have different suggestions for how voters in Russia can show their discontent with the government (file photo from June 2025) Image: Alexis Haulot/European Union 2025 - Source : EP

"These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."

DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.

"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.

Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."

Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Germany: Third malaria death linked to Frankfurt Airport
World.content:
Two new malaria cases have been registered this week near Frankfurt airport, two months after cases first emerged.

A person living near the Schwanheim district of Frankfurt died of malaria, local authorities said on Thursday. The incident is the third such death after a recent cluster of malaria cases linked to Frankfurt Airport emerged.

Two airport workers died of the disease in July and August.

Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is not common in Germany.

Schwanheim district, which borders the airport, registered two new malaria cases on Tuesday this week. Neither of the two infected individuals, both living in different households, had previously visited a malaria-endemic area and they did not work at Frankfurt airport.

Frankfurt health authorities extended their condolences to the relatives of the latest victims and said the two latest cases in the Schwanheim district were linked to an infected Anopheles mosquito that arrived in Germany by plane.

Germany's public health institute, the Robert Koch Institute, said malaria mosquitoes can fly between 5 and 10 kilometers (3 to 6 miles). The registered infections occurred some 5 kilometers away from the airport.

What is airport malaria?

Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. But in this instance, the cases are attributed directly to Frankfurt Airport.

Airport malaria can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area.

The RKI describes such cases as very rare, with the last documented case at Frankfurt Airport having been recorded in 2023.

Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual.

Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin.

Still, Frankfurt Airport urged employees at the airport to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms.

World.title: Crisis en Ceuta y actualidad política, en directo | La Policía organiza por grupos a los migrantes tras la estampida inicial en el traslado desde las playas al puerto de Ceuta
World.content:
Migrantes de la playa de El Trampolín y la playa Benítez esperan a ser trasladados a las instalaciones del puerto de Ceuta, este viernes.

Antes de que se desplazara a la zona el operativo completo, los migrantes han empezado a correr hasta la nueva instalación

Decenas de unidades de la Policía han controlado este viernes a los migrantes tras la estampida inicial en el operativo de traslado desde las playas al puerto de Ceuta. Los agentes han empezado a organizarlos por grupos para su traslado a pie a la instalación del puerto. A través de un megáfono han llamado a la calma, y los migrantes esperan su traslado tras el fuerte cordón policial. Por el momento, los migrantes pertenecen al asentamiento de Playa Benítez, vecina al asentamiento de Trampolín, más numeroso. La operación ha arrancado poco antes de las 7.00. Cuando solo se encontraban en la zona algunos operativos de Guardia Civil, los migrantes han comenzado a correr hacia la ubicación del Puerto, provocando una avalancha de gente en avance por el paseo marítimo de Ceuta. La Audiencia Nacional denegó ayer la suspensión temporal del campamento de migrantes en el Puerto de Ceuta, solicitada por un sindicato policial.
