World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.title: Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.content:
A zone in Beijing has launched a program asking several banks to extend billions of yuan in credit to multiple companies across the AI industry chain, partly based on their token usage.

Termed “token loans,” the financing scheme was recently implemented by the Beijing Economic and Technological Development Zone, also known as Beijing E-Town, in the city’s southeast, and involves extending nearly 2 billion yuan ($300 million) in credit to several AI companies, domestic media reported Monday.

A token is the smallest unit of data an AI large language model can process. In March, the National Data Administration officially adopted “ciyuan” — combining “word” and “currency” — as the Chinese term for “token.” The move was largely seen as putting an economic spin on AI-led computing power.

In June of this year, China’s daily token consumption already exceeded 500 trillion, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. A Saturday report by the China Telecom Research Institute estimates that that number could rise to 100 quadrillion, or 200 times that figure by year-end.

Six domestic banks, including the Agricultural Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, Industrial Bank, Bank of Beijing, China Minsheng Bank, and Huaxia Bank, provided the loans. The credit is intended for AI companies with “high research investment and high technological barriers,” as well as growing computing needs, but without the physical assets or profits typically required to obtain bank financing.

In addition to token consumption, the banks also awarded the loans based on technological barriers, team strength, and companies’ business development prospects.

Guoqi Zhikong, a developer of automobile-focused connected cloud platforms and autonomous driving vehicles, received a 30-million-yuan credit line from China CITIC Bank. Meanwhile, Shenzhou Guangda, which provides computing infrastructure and enterprise-level AI agent solutions, received the same credit amount from Industrial Bank.

The rapid growth of the AI industry has created a dilemma for tech startups, which often struggle to obtain traditional loans, an anonymous staff member from Beijing E-Town’s business and finance bureau told domestic media. Conventional lending models rely heavily on collateral and corporate profit statements, so even companies with strong technological capabilities often lack physical assets to pledge. In contrast, their opportunities for technological development and business expansion are constrained by profits that have yet to fully materialize.

In August, Bank of China’s branch in the southern city of Guangzhou launched the country’s first token loan scheme. Aimed at small- and medium-sized computing companies, it covers token supply, applications, and related services, with successful applicants eligible for up to 30 million yuan in credit.

Looking ahead, Lou Feipeng, a researcher at the Postal Savings Bank of China, said that before such loans can be adopted more broadly, the country must address several major issues, including exaggerated token-use data, inaccurate assessments of computing power consumption, and overestimation of borrowers’ repayment ability.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.title: From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.content:
In the classic Chinese novel “Journey to the West,” little demons are nobodies. They serve powerful demon kings, perform menial tasks, and are easily dispatched by heroes like Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King. Most do not even have names.

But increasingly, these once-forgotten characters are moving to the center of the story. Across Chinese films, TV shows, games, and books, little demons are being transformed from anonymous supporting characters into protagonists in their own right.

Take Black Myth: Wukong, the Chinese AAA video game that became a global hit. The game features a compendium of 203 supernatural creatures, including 90 classified as “little demons,” each with its own biographical profile. It is almost like an archive assembled from the gaps in “Journey to the West,” a who’s who of forgotten characters.

Another example is 2024’s “The Great Nobody,” a Chinese comedy series spinoff that grew out of the variety show “Amazing Night.” In it, a group of little demons living on the fictional Flower Neck Mountain waits in vain for the monk Tang Sanzang and his disciples to arrive on their pilgrimage to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. The reworking of the classic tale becomes a commentary on supporting comedians struggling to make their mark in the entertainment industry.

But perhaps the most striking example is “Nobody,” a Chinese animated film that grossed 1.7 billion yuan ($240 million) at the box office last summer. Expanded from the first episode of “Yao-Chinese Folktales,” an animated anthology series released on the video platform Bilibili in 2023, the film follows a “knock-off” pilgrimage team of demons comprising a pig, a toad, a weasel, and a gorilla.

Seen in the broader history of “Journey to the West” adaptations, this renewed interest in little demons represents the third major approach to interpreting the classic since the turn of the millennium.

The first was what might be called “post-revolutionary interpretations.” Emerging in the late 1990s, this approach is represented by Stephen Chow’s “A Chinese Odyssey” (1995) and the online novel “The Legend of Wukong,” which began serialization in 2000. These works focused on Sun Wukong’s struggle for individual autonomy, symbolized by his decision over whether to don the golden headband, a device used by Tang Sanzang to rein in his mischievous nature. At their core was the tragic rebellion of the neoliberal individual against the grand narrative of the pilgrimage, as well as a playful deconstruction of earlier “revolutionary” interpretations of “Journey to the West.”

The second consisted of “gothic interpretations,” represented by films including “Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons” (2013), “The Monkey King 2” (2016), and “Journey to the West: The Demons Strike Back” (2017). Through digital spectacle, these films created fantastical worlds and recast the classic as a monster movie. Their dark, horror-filled atmosphere can be seen as a cultural expression of the crisis of neoliberalism.

The third approach is what I call “system-based interpretations.” These works portray the Heavenly Palace and Vulture Peak, the respective seats of the Taoist and Buddhist hierarchies, as parts of a vast network of relationships. Tang Sanzang and his disciples’ pilgrimage to obtain the scriptures becomes a meticulously planned project, while the 81 trials they encounter along the way are recast as conspiracies orchestrated by the powers that be.

Ma Boyong’s bestselling novel “The Annoyance of the Gods” (2023), for example, portrays Taibai Jinxing, a deity associated with the planet Venus, as a project manager exhausted by office politics. In doing so, the novel reframes the pilgrimage as an internal struggle within a sprawling bureaucracy characterized by maneuvering, competition, and checks and balances.

The focus on little demons emerged from this same “system-based” approach. Rather than subverting the logic of the original text, these works stand in the shadows of its grand narrative and construct detailed accounts of the lives of those who remain nameless.

This interpretation is closely connected to the current social mood. Since 2020, growing uncertainty has weakened faith in nixi, or the idea that ordinary people can beat the odds and dramatically improve their fortunes. As economic growth has slowed, such aspirations have increasingly given way to greater empathy for ordinary workers simply trying to get by.

If the era in which little demons were ignored corresponded to a period of economic expansion, when workers believed they too could “retrieve the scriptures and achieve Buddhahood,” then the era of empathizing with them belongs to the period after that peak. Ordinary people stuck on the periphery of systems recognize themselves in these little demons: operating at the margins, with limited control over events, and little guarantee that their efforts will be rewarded.

Take “Nobody,” for example. Close-ups of the little demons’ vacant eyes and sluggish expressions reflect the mental state of some workers today. Their circumstances , to a certain extent, closely mirror contemporary workplaces: routine and often modest tasks, represented by scrubbing pots and making arrows; shifting expectations and promises that do not always materialize; and the risk of being treated primarily as a functional part of a larger operation.

Identification with these little demons reflects a changing sense of where ordinary workers locate themselves within larger systems. Rather than always imagining themselves as protagonists destined to rise above their circumstances, they may find greater resonance in supporting characters who navigate constraints, make compromises, and carve out limited forms of agency within the roles available to them.

This sense of being a supporting character also underlies the popular idea that “the world is just a ragtag troupe.” Some individuals may struggle to fully identify with the current situation while also finding it difficult to imagine viable alternatives. For those who remain within these structures, a common response is to learn how the rules operate and navigate the available room within them in order to maintain a workable position.

This shift toward accepting a supporting role has already manifested in forms of spectatorship common online. “Roasting” other people’s stories allows individuals to mock them from a safe distance while releasing some of the psychological pressure they themselves face.

Posting “bullet comments” that scroll across videos in real time creates a more distanced form of viewing while giving spectators a sense of collective belonging. “Eating melon,” a Chinese internet expression for following gossip and online drama as a bystander, similarly turns public events into spectator entertainment. Rather than emphasizing individual agency, these forms of spectatorship encourage people to watch from the sidelines.

This consciousness has also spread into contemporary cultural production, with little demons being just one example. In the 2024 web novel “The Diary of a Female Zombie’s Hiking Adventure,” the protagonist has no desire to become involved in other people’s storylines and instead chooses simply to observe. Meanwhile, in the animated film “Chang An” (2023), the figure who guides the audience through the splendor of the Tang dynasty (618–907) is the diligent and orderly poet Gao Shi rather than Li Bai, the personality who most fully embodies the era’s poetic spirit. Through Gao Shi’s eyes, Li Bai’s wildness and romanticism are viewed with a sense of incomprehension and detachment.

The audiences for these works are people navigating rapid social change, uncertainty, and shifting forms of connection. They are not merely digital natives, but individuals searching for a sense of place and meaning in this “era of supporting characters.”

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: Visuals from Douban and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.title: After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.content:
Hyrox has amended its official rulebooks after the winner of a recent Beijing event experienced bowel incontinence mid-race yet continued competing. The incident sparked widespread debate in China over sportsmanship and the organizer’s handling of potential hygiene risks.

On Monday, Hyrox updated its online rulebook to state that a race director may withdraw an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces pose a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers.”

The change comes in the wake of controversy surrounding the women’s solo elite race on Saturday, in which Australian athlete and Hyrox world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk finished first with a time of 1:01:23. Footage circulating online showed fecal matter staining Wietrzyk’s clothing and legs as she performed various exercises.

Hyrox has recently surged in popularity across China. Founded in Germany, the sport features eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by strength training stations including sled pulls, rowing, and burpees. China’s first official race was held in Beijing in 2024 and drew 1,700 entries. Participants at this weekend’s Beijing event exceeded 11,000, with standard individual registration costing roughly 800 yuan ($125).

Competitors and social media users questioned organizers’ decision to let Wietrzyk continue racing. The Women’s Pro division won by Wietrzyk began at 2:40 p.m. Saturday, with other heats scheduled until 8:40 p.m. and another full day of competition Sunday.

“As someone who works in the public health sector, my biggest concern is that if she had a bacterial or viral infection, contamination like this could spread pathogens very quickly,” a Beijing-based athlete in her 20s, surnamed Wang, whose race began about an hour after Wietrzyk, told Sixth Tone.

Toilets were available at the venue, she noted, but using the bathroom counts toward an athlete’s total race time.

In a post made via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo Saturday night, Hyrox’s China division said organizers had “immediately” closed and disinfected affected areas and removed contaminated equipment. Wang said she had seen nothing “noticeably unusual” on the course.

Wietrzyk later posted an Instagram Story of herself receiving an intravenous infusion from what appeared to be a hospital. An accompanying caption read: “a win is a win.”

This drew further criticism from some Chinese social media users, who saw the remark as dismissive of concerns over other competitors’ health and safety.

Italian Hyrox pro-athlete Sara Gandola, who competed in the same race, told Sixth Tone that Wietrzyk should not be blamed for the incident.

Gandola said the responsibility of athletes is to perform at their highest level within the rules, while “it is the sport’s responsibility to set those rules and define what is acceptable.”

“If you disagree with the rules, debate the rules,” she said. “But attacking an athlete for doing exactly what elite athletes are supposed to do is completely backward.”

On Monday, Hyrox’s global headquarters issued a statement on Instagram, describing the incident as an “unforeseen situation” and adding that those who threatened its athletes would be permanently banned from future events.

However, Chinese social media users criticized their stance for not directly acknowledging failures in how it handled the incident at the time.

Later that day, Hyrox China admitted on Weibo that the incident exposed “shortcomings” in its competition rules and said it had proposed revisions to its global headquarters. The previous Hyrox rulebook imposes a two-minute penalty for littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose onto the floor, but does not address fecal incontinence.

Hyrox China added that the venue’s carpets had been replaced and that the entire venue had been deep-cleaned overnight, pledging to disinfect both venues before future events and any shared equipment.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste also issued an apology via Instagram on Monday, admitting that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.”

In a Sunday commentary, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the incident highlighted a growing tension between the “rapid expansion” of commercial sporting events and “gaps in competition rules.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.title: The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.content:
A new Chinese dating app is betting that AI can do more than keep users chatting — it wagers it can see them married in three years or less.

If it fails, the team behind Liangpei — roughly “good match” in Chinese — promises to refund the user’s one-time fee of 2,000 yuan ($275). The guarantee comes as marriage rates fall in China, with only 6.76 million couples tying the knot in 2025, about half the number a decade earlier.

Launched this past July, Liangpei begins with a roughly 20-minute voice conversation with an AI matchmaker. Users answer 25 questions about their relationship history, marriage plans, and even whether they intend to buy property. The system then uses their answers to build a detailed profile, calculate compatibility scores, and recommend potential partners.

Once two people match, they can talk only until one decides to move on, a restriction the app’s developers say is intended to keep them focused on one relationship rather than constantly searching for alternatives.

“We want to get the users off the platform as soon as possible,” founder Zeng Xinxun told Sixth Tone.

Before launching Liangpei, the 32-year-old worked on AI search technology at Kimi, one of China’s best-known generative AI platforms. His 18-person team now uses similar technology to draw out information that basic dating-app tags such as age, occupation, and location cannot capture.

Approximately 91% of users who start Liangpei’s interview finish it, Zeng said, going on to create profiles averaging 516 Chinese characters, about four times as long as those on several major Chinese dating apps.

About one in 10 users has reached an exclusive one-on-one match, according to Zeng. Those conversations last more than 10 days on average and run to more than 200 messages.

“One-on-one allows both parties to invest more focus and effort into building a relationship,” Zeng said. “Even if it doesn’t work out, it’s a conclusion reached after genuine communication.”

So far, he said, Liangpei has more than 9,300 active users across 300 cities. Men account for 57% of users, and women 43%. The two largest age groups are 26 to 28 and 29 to 31.

China’s established dating and social platforms operate at a much larger scale. Tantan, one of the country’s oldest dating apps, had 10.7 million monthly active users in March 2025, while Soul draws large audiences with broader offerings that combine dating, social discovery, entertainment, and shared interests.

Liangpei also requires real-name registration, a marital status check, and live photo verification. The company has blocked 487 people found to be married, Zeng said. It also uses AI to watch for signs of fraud once conversations begin.

Wang, a Shanghai-based user who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, has tried more than 10 dating apps. Liangpei was the first on which she was willing to answer so many questions.

“It has helped me understand myself better and clarified exactly what I’m looking for,” she said.

Within a week, Wang entered an exclusive one-on-one match. She said the format made online dating less exhausting and allowed her to focus on getting to know her counterpart. But with no other matches to turn to, the arrangement depended on that person keeping the conversation alive.

“Once matched, your slot is locked,” Wang said. “If the other person isn’t proactive, you’re left waiting with nowhere for the conversation to go.”

On Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, Liangpei has drawn sharply mixed reactions. Some users described it as a welcome option for people anxious about finding a spouse, while others questioned whether treating marriage as a fixed target made dating too rigid.

Free users can send only one “like” a day, according to posts reviewed by Sixth Tone. The app also prominently displays compatibility scores, which some users said made them more reluctant to start conversations.

Despite the compatibility score, several users admitted they still ended up judging potential partners by appearance.

Three-year itch

Six years ago, Zeng said he became frustrated trying to meet someone online — a period that lasted a year. He wrote a lengthy profile, but few people seemed to read it, and even fewer replied.

“Profiles were too bare to spark interest,” he said. Zeng eventually expanded his own to around 2,000 Chinese characters, then came across a woman whose profile was just as detailed.

“We quickly went from strangers to a close connection,” Zeng said. By the time they met in person, he thought the relationship might go somewhere.

They are now married. And Liangpei uses that same outcome as its measure of success.

His team had considered a first date or the start of a relationship instead. Marriage, Zeng said, was different: “It’s legally verifiable and undisputed.”

The three-year cutoff came after his team interviewed 150 couples obtaining marriage licenses at a civil affairs bureau in the southern city of Shenzhen. More than 70% said they had married within three years of meeting, Zeng said.

Liangpei has been operating for only a few months, so none of its users have yet to reach that deadline. For now, the company is reviewing the data it does have, including whether higher compatibility scores are associated with more likes, replies, and longer conversations.

“For example, among 1,500 users in Shenzhen, the AI can directly rank the top 10 people most likely to succeed with you,” Zeng said. “You don’t have to browse everyone — just start with the highest scores.”

To address relationship anxiety, Liangpei offers an “icebreaker” feature that suggests questions when a conversation stalls. An “AI wingman” can also analyze an exchange and offer advice.

But the “AI wingman” will not compose replies. Zeng said someone who struggles with online banter might still make a good partner in person, but AI should only carry early exchanges far enough for both people to find out.

Du Shichao, an assistant professor of sociology at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Liangpei’s focus on marriage could appeal to people who already know what they are looking for. He also saw value in matching people using more than surface-level information.

“It may not address everyone’s pain points, but it can at least solve problems for some people and offer them more choice,” Du said.

But he was more cautious about AI taking on a larger role in relationships.

“This ‘enhancement’ can easily slide into ‘replacement,’” Du said. “When this kind of use is taken to an extreme, people need to be wary of ceding their capacity for emotional connection to technology.”

Whatever help an AI assistant can provide online, he said, people still have to learn about each other in person. “Ultimately, people must rediscover each other and themselves through real-world interaction.”

Du said technology may help with some of the difficulties individuals face in meeting and communicating with partners, but it cannot address the forces shaping marriage more broadly, including demographics, economic pressure, and family expectations.

“It may benefit some, but won’t significantly change China’s marriage patterns,” he said.

Zeng is making a more modest claim. “We don’t need to serve everyone,” he said. “We can’t help those with particularly poor prospects, or those with unrealistic expectations. If the people in between can find success in Liangpei, that’s good enough.”

Whether they do will become clear in 2029, when Liangpei’s first users reach the end of its three-year guarantee.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Apurva.

World.title: China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.content:
China has approved the weight-loss drug Wegovy, a brand name for the medication semaglutide, to treat a severe form of fatty liver disease, making it the country’s first and only glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drug approved for the condition.

The drug, approved Sept. 10 by the National Medical Products Administration, covers adults with moderate to advanced liver damage from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — the result of inflammation caused by excess fat — but no cirrhosis, or permanent scarring.

The move comes as obesity drugs become more widely available internationally and growing competition pushes drugmakers to differentiate products to treat a broader spectrum of diseases.

China has one of the world’s largest burdens of fatty liver disease, affecting about one in three adults and over 80% of people with obesity. An estimated 6.7% of Chinese adults have MASH, the disease’s more severe form, and may not qualify for GLP-1 drugs under previous weight-management indications.

The share of global liver cancer cases caused by MASH is forecast to rise from 8% to 11% by 2050, according to a report by the Lancet Commission on liver cancer published last year.

Effective drug options for fatty liver disease have long been limited, with treatment until now largely dependent on patients making lifestyle changes, Jia Jidong, director of the Liver Research Center at Beijing Friendship Hospital, told domestic media. He added that approval of the drug could help to raise public awareness of fatty liver disease, as the illness can be “silent and asymptomatic” in its earlier stages.

Semaglutide was originally developed to treat diabetes but has become widely used for weight management in recent years. It does so by mimicking the hormone GLP-1, released in response to eating, binding to the hormone’s receptors and suppressing appetite.

The medication is sold by Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk as Ozempic for diabetes and at a higher dose as Wegovy primarily for weight management. Wegovy was approved in China for weight management in June 2024.

The latest approval was based on a trial involving 1,197 MASH patients with moderate-to-advanced liver scarring. About two-thirds of patients who took semaglutide saw their MASH resolve, while slightly more than a third experienced reductions in liver scarring.

Other drugmakers are also exploring GLP-1 medications as potential treatments for fatty liver disease, with Chinese regulators fast-tracking approval for U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in January.

Chinese biotech firm Innovent Biologics has also reported fatty liver reduction with its drug mazdutide, which was approved in the country for weight management last year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: FACT CHECK: Davao City received funds from nat’l government under Marcos admin
World.content:
Malacañang said Davao City received national government support for programs and projects, citing data from the budget department

Claim: Davao City did not receive any funds from the national government under the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook page named “Wing Jusayan Vlog” posted the claim on August 22. The post featured images of Marcos and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte.

Text overlaid on the graphic reads: “Davao City survived without funds in 4 years, why are you looking for the project that was not funded by government? The worst part inangkin nyo ang project na hindi naman sa inyo (you took credit for the project that wasn’t yours).”

As of writing, the post garnered over 11,000 reactions, 2,300 comments, and 5,400 shares. Similar posts bearing the same claim are also circulating online. Several commenters, believing the claim, further asserted that Davao City has good leadership and governance while shaming the national government for supposedly withholding funds.

The claim appears to stem from Duterte’s comments that the city allegedly received no funding from the national government for years.

The facts: Davao City received yearly funding from the national government, according to Malacañang, citing records from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).

In a statement, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that Davao City and its barangays received a combined P53.11 billion in national tax allotment (NTA) and other national government allocations from fiscal years (FY) 2022 to 2026, as reported by the Philippine News Agency on September 4. This contradicts the misleading posts’ claim that Davao City received “no funds” over a four-year period.

Of that total, approximately P41.63 billion went directly to the city government, while P11.17 billion was the combined NTA of the city’s barangays. There was also an additional P314.48 million that came from releases under the General Appropriations Act.

Malacañang, through Castro, had previously refuted similar allegations during a May 25 press briefing, explicitly denying claims made by Duterte that the city received zero funds from the national government.

Castro presented an official statement from the DBM that said Duterte’s claim “is not supported by the national government’s released data.”

The DBM records, according to the Palace press officer, show that from FY 2023 to 2026, as of May 17, Davao City received at least P7.856 billion in total national government financial support for its programs and projects. This includes national tax allotment, special shares, fire code fees, and regular operating requirements.



Moreover, Castro said that the P7.440 billion came from identified national government agency programs and projects for health, education, infrastructure, and transport modernization projects.

In addition to regular national funding allocations, Rappler also reported that Davao City held the largest confidential budget among all local government units (LGUs) in Southern Mindanao for 2023 and 2024, amounting to P1.06 billion.

Lack of context: On September 6, Duterte clarified that he was specifically referring to the alleged lack of congressional district allocation. In an interview and report by GMA News Online, Castro explained that her refutation of Duterte’s claim was made in response to specific inquiries regarding “the NTA allotment, her assessment of the claim that Davao City had received no funds from the national government, and whether there were pertinent records to support the claim.”



Under Article X, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, local government units are legally guaranteed a just share of national government revenues, which must be automatically released directly to LGUs.

Debunked: Rappler has debunked a similar claim associating the supposed non-release of government funds to political reasons. – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is journalist based in Baguio and Bicol, and an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Philippine media watchdog CMFR is closing
World.content:
CMFR will close on September 30, its executive director Melinda Quintos de Jesus says

MANILA, Philippines – For nearly four decades, the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) stood as a watchdog over the watchdogs of Philippine democracy.

It will close on September 30, its executive director Melinda Quintos de Jesus said.

The decision was not about the work, but about whether there were enough resources left to keep doing it.

The CMFR board made the decision after confronting a funding environment that had become increasingly difficult, Quintos de Jesus said.

For years, Philippine and international funders had financed the center’s work. But that support had become harder to secure, leaving the organization without the resources required to continue operating.

The CMFR, for 37 years, had occupied a distinctive place in Philippine journalism. It had examined the conduct of the media even as it defended the press against those who sought to intimidate or silence it.

It also documented attacks and threats against journalists and news organizations, promoted media ethics, honored excellence in journalism, trained reporters to cover women, children and minority groups, as well as disasters, elections, and periods of political and social crises.

The closing of the center thus marks the disappearance of an institution whose work was, in part, to remember what happened to Philippine journalism – who was threatened, who was attacked, how the press responded, and what standards were expected of those who wielded its power.

In announcing the decision, Quintos de Jesus thanked those who had supported CMFR’s undertakings. – with a report from Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

World.title: What is in the EU’s planned KIDS Act?
World.content:
EU AND SOCIAL MEDIA. An EU flag and smartphone with displayed social media app icons in this illustration taken February 3, 2026

Here are the details of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which will require approval from European Union governments and the European Parliament and could be revised before it is enacted

The European Commission has proposed banning under-13s from social media and requiring platforms to design online services that are safe for all children’s accounts.

Here are the details of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which will require approval from European Union governments and the European Parliament and could be revised before it is enacted.

Age categories

The proposed regulation bans social media accounts for those aged under 13, allows parent-supervised “mini accounts” for children aged 13 and 14, and independent accounts only for those 15 years and older.

For 13- and 14-year-olds, a guardian would be able to set up a limited account that the guardian will control, with a daily limit of up to an hour of age-appropriate social media and video-sharing platforms.

For teenagers with existing accounts, platforms would have to check — within six months of the rules applying — whether existing account holders will have to disable the accounts of children under 15 or for those whose age cannot be established.

Checks would not be required if platforms can tell with high confidence that users are adults.

Age will be verified with certified solutions independent of platforms, including a planned European Digital Identity Wallet.

What social media companies must do

The EU KIDS Act sets obligations for all social media, video sharing, online video games, AI companions, and chatbots for users below the age of 18.

These include bans on addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds and personalised ads or algorithms based on past activity. The Act would prevent infinite scrolling without breaks, reward ‘tricks’, unsolicited contact from strangers and push notifications during sleeping hours, defined as eight consecutive hours between 10 pm and 8 am.

AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default. Profiles for children must be private by default, with geolocation, camera and microphone access turned off.

The burden of proof will be on platforms to show they are safe for children. Platforms with 45 million or more active monthly users in the EU will have to present compliance plans before coming into contact with children.

What will happen to existing national rules?

The provisions of the EU Kids Act are designed to replace a patchwork of different rules in separate EU countries with the same level of protection across the bloc.

France has pushed for an EU-wide ban for under-15s after France’s Constitutional Court struck down a national bill before it was due to take effect in September, saying it infringed on freedom of expression. – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines still among top countries in bullying – PISA 2025
World.content:
BAD WEATHER. Students go to school as it rains in Manila on August 3, 2026.

No longer the world’s ‘bullying capital’? The Philippines’ bullying index is still higher than average in the latest Programme for International Student Assessment results.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines saw a lower bullying rate in 2025, but it continued to have one of the highest rates among participating countries in the latest edition of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).

PISA data show that 47.2% or nearly half of 15-year-old Filipino students reported experiencing “at least one form of bullying a few times per month or more.”

It was more than double the 20% average rate of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the institution behind PISA.

Around three out of 10 Filipino students or 31% were also considered “frequently bullied.”

Who are more likely to report being bullied in the Philippines? Here are the PISA 2025 results:

Boys than girls

Disadvantaged students than advantaged students

From disadvantaged schools than socioeconomically average or advantaged schools

Located in rural areas or villages than towns or cities

From public schools than private schools

In 2025, the Philippines was no longer the country with the highest index of exposure to bullying, but it still ranked third, following Rwanda and Kenya. It was the first time the two African nations participated in PISA.

The Philippines had been dubbed the world’s “bullying capital”, as noted by observers including the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2), due to its results in global assessments like PISA.

Still, the Department of Education (DepEd) said “there are encouraging signs of improvement,” as it compared the findings from the country’s first PISA participation in 2018, rather than the COVID-19 pandemic era in 2022.

In 2018, 64.9% of Filipino students reported experiencing an act of bullying at least a few times a month or more.

Comparing the 2018 and 2025 PISA cycles, there were declines in reports of students being made fun of by other students, being hit or pushed, being threatened, and being victims of nasty rumors.

Threat of cyberbullying

PISA results also showed 13.9% of Filipino students reported being cyberbullied in 2025. It was the second highest among participating countries, just behind Rwanda’s 21.7%.

It was way beyond the OECD average of 3%.

PISA asked students if “upsetting” information about them had been published online, without their consent, at least a few times a month during the year prior to the exam.

The report also found that students who spend more time on digital devices are more likely to report incidents of cyberbullying.

“Although cyberbullying is less frequently reported than other forms of bullying, it often occurs in addition to other forms of bullying, and research suggests that it is associated with poorer well-being and mental health outcomes,” the OECD warned.

According to the assessment, cyberbullying victims also tend to experience significant achievement deficits.

In the Philippines, those who were cyberbullied scored 49 points lower in science than their peers, on average.

Cyberbullying is also being tracked by the DepEd in its anti-bullying campaign.

However, if the self-reported rates in PISA results are to be believed, the figures are quite distant from what the agency has recorded. Is bullying still “underreported” in the country?

What DepEd promised

The emphasis on mental health is even greater now following two fatal school shootings this year.

“The current goal of the DepEd is to…foster a more safe and welcoming environment for our students. It should not only be academic. They (the students) should look forward to school, to seeing friends and teachers, and look forward to that day’s lesson,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a news conference after the PISA results announcement on September 8.

Education Undersecretary Carmela Oracion also said the DepEd does not want to be reactive when it comes to school violence.

“There are urgent things to do like [strengthening] the security measures. But apart from that, we want to bring this in through values education…. We are really strengthening that,” she told reporters.

As it stands, it would be an uphill battle for the DepEd amid lack of funding to address the shortage of security guards, CCTV cameras, and metal detectors in public schools.

The agency’s proposed 2027 budget also lacks allocations to train teachers in spotting red flags in student behavior, as well as to fully implement its mental health and counseling program.

The DepEd already signed the revised implementing rules and regulations of the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013 in August 2025, to provide clearer definitions of bullying, set the responsibilities of various sectors, and strengthen school-level response. Budget constraints, however, could be another obstacle. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Puso at Diwa] Anti-political dynasties: When democracy belongs to the people
World.content:
The ultimate issue is larger than the Marcoses, Dys, Dutertes, Aquinos, Villars or any other political clan. It is whether public office belongs to the people.

For nearly four decades, the Philippines has carried in its 1987 Constitution a command that Congress conspicuously failed to implement: “The State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law.”

Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution was meant to open political competition and prevent public office from becoming a family inheritance. Yet it took the Lower House 39 years to produce an enabling measure. And when it finally did, the measure itself became controversial.

The House of Representatives approved House Bill No. 8389, the Anti-Political Dynasty Act, in June by an overwhelming 267-20 vote. It was principally authored by Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander “Sandro” Marcos, the President’s son.

Play Video

The irony has not been lost on its critics. But the more important issue is not who authored the bill. It is what the bill actually prohibits.

Critics argue that the House measure is too narrow, particularly because its restrictions are focused on close relatives and particular circumstances of simultaneous occupancy of elective positions. Such a framework could permit political families to reproduce themselves through succession, more distant relatives, changes in jurisdiction, substitutions or political allies.

This is precisely why three different but complementary initiatives have emerged.

Three initiatives

Congress has acted. Civil society has challenged it. The Supreme Court has now compelled Congress to finish the job.

The first response came from Congress itself. Its supporters argue that HB 8389 is a realistic and enforceable beginning after decades of legislative paralysis. But a law can be politically achievable and still fall short of the constitutional purpose it is intended to serve.

The second response is Dapat Isa Lang (D1L), a multisectoral people’s initiative seeking what its proponents call a genuine anti-political dynasty law. Its proposed measure extends the prohibition to relatives within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity and would limit a political family to one national and one local elective position. It also addresses successive occupation of positions, substitution, switching of positions and a cooling-off period after term limits.

Image from Dapat Isa Lang Movement FB

Bishop Gerardo Alminaza of San Carlos has urged Negrenses and Filipinos to support the movement. His intervention is important because the issue is being framed not as an assault on a particular political clan but as a question of the common good: whether public service remains genuinely open to citizens beyond established political families.

The third, and now decisive, development is the intervention of the Supreme Court.

On Wednesday, September 16, the Court announced its unanimous ruling on the consolidated petitions led by the 1Sambayan Coalition, including retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Antonio Carpio and former Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales.

The Court held that Congress has a mandatory constitutional duty to define and prohibit political dynasties and that its failure to enact an enabling law for 39 years constituted grave abuse of discretion. It directed Congress to discharge that duty with “utmost urgency.”

This changes the terrain.

The question is no longer whether Congress should enact an anti-dynasty law. The constitutional obligation has now been judicially affirmed. (READ: Why the SC is telling Congress to do its job on political dynasties)

Enacting a law consistent with constitutional intent

The harder question is whether Congress will enact a law faithful to the constitutional objective, and whether that law can survive the ingenuity of political families determined to preserve their influence.

Political dynasties are not merely genealogical arrangements. They are networks of name recognition, financial resources, political machinery, local alliances and institutional access. A prohibition confined to immediate relatives may therefore be circumvented by succession through cousins, nephews or other relatives; by moving family members across constituencies; by having relatives alternate positions; or by using political allies and substitutes to preserve control.

The test of an anti-dynasty law is thus not simply whether it prevents two members of one family from holding two offices simultaneously. It is whether it prevents the perpetuation and concentration of political power.

This matters because political competition is itself an institution.

Democracy is more than the periodic counting of votes. It requires genuine contestability: the possibility that incumbents can lose, that newcomers can compete, and that citizens without inherited political machinery can seek public office.

The empirical literature does not justify claiming that political dynasties alone explain Philippine underdevelopment. Indeed, the evidence is more nuanced. A 2016 study found a worsening effect of dynasties on poverty particularly outside Luzon. A 2022 study found that dynasties exacerbated poverty in resource-rich non-Luzon provinces, while the relationship was weaker in Luzon where more competitive business environments provided a counterweight. More recent research similarly emphasizes that the effects vary with local economic and institutional conditions.

Evidence supports institutional concern

But the evidence does support a broader institutional concern. Political inequality, or concentration of elective positions among dynastic families, has been associated with weaker development outcomes. And the latest Philippine policy research notes that dynastic concentration can limit political competition, weaken accountability and influence the allocation of the national budget.

The economic backdrop makes this institutional question more urgent.

The Philippines grew by 5.7% in 2024, but growth slowed to 4.4% in 2025 and to just 2.6% on average in the first half of 2026, based on first- and second-quarter Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) data. This does not establish that political dynasties caused the slowdown. Development depends on many factors including productivity, investment, human capital, infrastructure, governance, and external conditions. But it does sharpen the question of why the country has struggled to translate decades of economic growth into stronger productivity, investment and institutional performance.

That is where political reform becomes an economic issue.

Institutions that permit prolonged political concentration can weaken competition and accountability. And where political and economic power overlap, the capacity of government to allocate resources impartially, enforce rules consistently and execute long-term development plans can also be compromised.

Two-fold challenge

The challenge now is therefore twofold.

First, can Congress produce a law that genuinely fulfills the Supreme Court’s constitutional directive rather than merely satisfying it formally?

Second, can the law be designed so that political dynasties cannot simply adapt around it?

The answer will depend on details that are easy to dismiss as technical but are actually fundamental: the degree of relationship covered; simultaneous versus successive occupancy; territorial restrictions; substitution; term limits; cooling-off periods; enforcement; disclosure of family relationships; and the treatment of political surrogates.

After 39 years, the Philippines should be wary of celebrating legislative movement as constitutional fulfillment.

The Constitution did not promise equal access to public service eventually. It commanded it.

Congress now has its mandate from the Constitution and its marching orders from the Supreme Court. Civil society has offered another route through the D1L movement. And the people retain their constitutional power to participate directly in legislation.

The ultimate issue is therefore larger than the Marcoses, Dys, Dutertes, Aquinos, Villars or any other political clan.

It is whether public office belongs to the people—or whether, over time, it becomes something that political families can inherit, reproduce and defend.

That is the real test of political democracy. And after 39 years, it is a test the Philippines can no longer postpone. – Rappler.com

ALSO ON RAPPLER

References:

Ronald U. Mendoza, Edsel L. Beja Jr., Victor S. Venida, and David B. Yap. (2016). “Political Dynasties and Poverty: Measurement and Evidence of Linkages in the Philippines.” Oxford Development Studies, 44(2), 189–201.

Ronald U. Mendoza, Jurel K. Yap, Gabrielle Ann S. Mendoza, Leonardo Jaminola III, and Erica Celine Yu. (2022) “Political Dynasties, Business, and Poverty in the Philippines,” Journal of Government and Economics, Vol. 7, Article 100051.

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.

He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

He also serves as principal advisor for New York-based GlobalSourcePartners. He remains in the advisory board of ASEAN Macroeconomic Research Office and Singapore Management University’s Sim Kee Boon Institute for Financial Economics.

He is the senior pastor of the Fullness of Christ International Ministries in Mandaluyong.

World.title: SAGIP BATA bill takes aim at ‘sadistic extortion,’ online recruitment into violence
World.content:
ROBLOX. Senator Risa Hontiveros welcomed Roblox’s commitment to cooperate with Philippine authorities as she emphasized the importance of requiring online platforms to appoint a legal representative in the country, as the Senate prepares to amend its online child sex abuse law amid threats of online violent radicalization and grooming

The proposed SAGIP BATA Act expands the anti-online child sex abuse law to cover grooming, violent recruitment, and other technology-facilitated abuse amid recent school shootings

MANILA, Philippines – Amendments to Senate Bill (SB) No. 1819 proposed earlier this week seek to strengthen Republic Act No. 11930 or the law on online sexual abuse or exploitation of children and child sexual abuse or exploitation materials.

Among the amendments is a new proposed name — the Safeguarding Against Grooming, Inducement and Predation, and Building Accountability for Technology-Facilitated Abuse Act, or SAGIP BATA Act — reflecting its expanded protections after the the two fatal school shootings in Tacloban and Zamboanga in June and August, respectively.

These incidents have intensified scrutiny of the online spaces young Filipinos inhabit as authorities probe possible links to nihilistic violent extremism (NVE), leading to Senate hearings on violent digital communities and child safety, and these proposed updates to existing laws and other new bills.

Beyond sexual abuse

One of the SAGIP BATA’s most significant proposals is a proposed offense called “sadistic extortion of a child,” moving beyond just sexual abuse. It would cover the use of threats, manipulation, blackmail, deception and similar means to compel children into grave, cruel, degrading or harmful acts.

The amendments also propose to create a separate offense for online recruitment, coercion or inducement of a child to commit a serious violent act.

In the bill’s current form, the offense could be committed through either recruitment or mere attempt to persuade a child. The child would not have to agree to participate, and the planned violent act would not have to actually take place for the act to be a crime.

The amendments also spell out possible indicators of grooming: asking a child to keep a relationship secret, moving conversations from public or supervised channels to private ones, offering gifts or money in exchange for continued engagement or silence, and isolating children from family or peers.

Recruiting, coercing, or inducing a child into serious violent activity carries a penalty of reclusion temporal in its maximum period to reclusion perpetua and a fine ranging from ₱1 million to ₱5 million. If the recruitment results in the child actually committing the violent act, the offender is also additionally liable for the penalty prescribed for that specific crime.

Another update explicitly covers AI-generated and synthetic child sexual abuse or exploitation materials, including wholly artificial depictions that appear to show a child nude, engaged in sexual activity or being sexually exploited, even when no actual child’s image was used.

More obligations on platforms

The proposed law also adds age-assurance and age-verification provisions and new obligations for technology platforms. Amendments set a 24-hour deadline for platforms to act on identified content depicting serious violent activity or sadistic extortion after notice from authorities, and 48 hours for material glorifying or promoting groups involved in recruiting children into serious violence.

Journalists, documentarists and academic researchers who encounter active online sexual abuse or exploitation of children material in legitimate work would also receive specific protections, generally subject to notifying authorities within 48 hours while reserving the right to preserve confidential sources.

The jurisdiction gap

Another major focus is a problem Philippine cybercrime investigators have repeatedly raised: foreign platforms are often outside their direct jurisdiction.

Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) chief Aboy Paraiso told senators in August that authorities often have to rely on foreign platforms’ internal rules when seeking information or action. Similar problems surfaced in Rappler’s investigation of an online forum sharing non-consensual intimate content, where the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group said going after the overseas-hosted forum itself was more difficult and could require international cooperation.

Under the SAGIP BATA proposal, online platforms would have to designate a Philippine-based legal representative who could receive subpoenas, takedown and blocking orders, requests for account information and other lawful directives. Roblox, a platform that could allegedly be used by certain actors to recruit or manipulate children, has told Hontiveros it is open to appointing such a representative.

House targets addictive features

A parallel House proposal, the consolidated Children’s Social Media and Online Gaming Safety Bill, takes at the features that keep children addicted, apart from social media bans.

House leaders say children under 13 would be completely barred from social media, while those aged 13 to 17 would have access but face restrictions on potentially harmful or addictive features, including short-form video and group chats. Covered social media and gaming platforms would also have to register in the Philippines, bringing them within Philippine jurisdiction.

That focus on product design comes as addictive social media features face growing scrutiny abroad. Meta agreed in August to pay up to $18 billion to settle lawsuits by nearly all US states alleging that Facebook and Instagram were designed to addict children while parent company Meta admitted no wrongdoing.

Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa has argued that age restrictions alone do not address the underlying problem.

“We know this is harmful, so you should remove the addictive features, not just for teenagers, but for all of us,” Ressa told Reuters.

The House also summoned Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Thursday, September 17, over child safety issues on Meta platforms.

Another bill would penalize parents

A separate Senate proposal, SB 2424 filed in August, would generally prohibit children under 16 from using covered age-restricted social media platforms and would also require foreign platforms to maintain a local office and legal representative in the Philippines.

Unlike the other measures, it also expressly penalizes parents or guardians who knowingly help a child bypass age checks or create an account, or whose gross negligence results in repeated violations.

Proposed penalties range from P5,000 to P50,000 and may include mandatory digital-parenting programs. Mere failure to supervise would not be enough without willful intent or gross negligence.

The new bills or amendments happen amid a broader regulatory shift worldwide. Australia has required covered social media platforms to prevent under-16s from holding accounts since December 2025.

And on September 17, the European Commission proposed an EU Kids Act that would restrict social media access by age while also targeting addictive design features such as infinite scrolling and reward-based engagement. The proposal still has to go through the EU legislative process. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Come sit with us at Rappler’s Culture Desk
World.content:
Hey there!

If you’ve ever found yourself falling down a rabbit hole over a hyper-niche hobby, a specific coffee order, or a local spot you can’t stop recommending — welcome home!

My name is Julian Cirineo, editor for Culture Desk, Rappler’s new home for stories about the things we enjoy, the stuff we’re secretly geeking over, and the hidden reasons we love the things we love. This is our refreshed editorial approach to covering culture because we know that the way we live, spend our time and money, and log off has changed.

Our team of writers, researchers, artists, and curious minds will be your enablers in doing what you’ve always wanted to do, or finally visiting that new restaurant you’ve saved on IG. We’ll be your go-to whenever you have questions on trends, products, or whatever is taking up your headspace. We’re that friend in the friend group who always has something new and cool for you to try.

To kick things off, the team has a roundup of stories that we’re sure will get you off your desks and out of the house. Grab your favorite drink and get ready to share these with the group chat.

Our ‘non-AI’ field guide to cozy spots in Kapitolyo

When was the last time you took a walk just so you could add a bit of whimsy to your life and experience finding things by chance? We did precisely that right in Rappler’s own neighborhood — Kapitolyo! The result? A list of some of the coziest places we’ve tried, including a matcha bar great for cooling down, a “dopamine-decked” maximalist cafe, and our next favorite brunch spot.

🍵 Watch where we ended up on this non-AI-guided Kapitolyo crawl

🍵 Read the full experience here

8 independent spaces to experience Manila’s creative scene

Where do you go to get a feel for Manila’s creativity? It’s not exactly a category you can easily search on Google, but a crop of places do come to mind. In this list you’ll find places that teach art, keep print alive, provide intimate film-viewing experiences, open spaces for music and dance nights, and more.

🔖 Pin these places to get to know their communities

Why Romblon’s islands deserve more love and attention

Laid-back and underrated, Tablas in Romblon has made it into our list of travel destinations for intimate and quiet getaways. Life was enticingly slow in Tablas. It was full of experiences, flavors, and stories from local members of the community. Our writer, Chau, wrote a love letter to Romblon.

🏖️ View our virtual postcard/love letter to Tablas, Romblon

How ‘Filipiñana’s’ slow burn exposes the Philippines’ class divide

Filipinos have a complex relationship with the tropical heat. In the Filipino film Filipiñana, though, heat isn’t only a villain; it’s a catalyst for exposing bigger evils. The satirical debut feature of Rafael Manuel — who also wrote and edited the film — follows Isabel (played by Jorrybell Agoto), a 17-year-old “tee girl” who’s new to the job in an exclusive country club. We felt a lot of things about the film, so we wrote about them.

☀️ Read what we thought of the film Filipiñana

Seeing the many things ube can become at Ube Fest

Some stayed close to ube’s OG dessert roots, while others treated it as a starting point — playing with its color, texture, and aroma in many unconventional ways. The result was part food festival, part small-business showcase, and part answer to the question: How many things can ube become?

🟣 Read our recap of the recent Ube Fest here

You should start junk journaling too

It’s not a common thought for everyone to save that small piece of gum wrapper in your pocket or that crumpled receipt you kept from a night out with friends. Yes, even that movie ticket you have from that time you went out with a failed situationship. The little pieces of scrap we usually overlook can easily become meaningful mementos — sometimes in ways that a photo on your phone cannot.

🔖 Here’s how to start your own junk journal

What we’re cooking up next

We’re filled to the brim with culture stories we want to share. We’ll give you more trend breakdowns, product reviews, and what to do in the city. Here’s a little taste test to get you looking forward to the rest of the menu. In the coming weeks, we’re taking a look at how millennials and Gen Z are choosing solo living over staying with their parents. We’re also diving into why it’s so hard to stop watching Chinese microdramas, what makes a good iPad case, what the iPhone Duo will bring to the world of foldables, a cafe that’s only open on the weekends, and what in the world squishies are and why people are buying them.

We want to hear from you, too

Growing Culture Desk won’t be an easy feat, but it will definitely be a fun one — and we want you to sit with us at our desk. We want to know what experiences excite you, what’s making you laugh, and what drink you grabbed as you read through our stories, because you and your daily rituals are at the heart of what we cover.

So tell me, what’s the one thing that you can’t stop recommending to your friends and family? Consider this your official permission to yap about your latest hyper-fixation. Let me know via email at julian.cirineo@rappler.com — maybe we’ll write about it next!

Julian Cirineo

Culture Desk Editor

World.title: Expert: Investment Headquarters Highlights Gaps in Kazakhstan’s Investment Infrastructure
World.content:
ASTANA – The Investment Headquarters is an important mechanism for resolving investors’ problems, but its continued role also shows where Kazakhstan’s investment infrastructure still has “rough edges,” financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov told The Astana Times.

He described the Investment Headquarters as a useful “diagnostic” tool, saying that its cases could provide insight into which regions and sectors resolve investor issues more quickly and where decisions take longer.

“If we collect all the data from the Investment Headquarters and understand in which regions or sectors decisions are made faster and where they take longer, we need to understand which regions are working poorly and in which sectors we have poor legislation,” Rysmambetov said.

From resolving individual problems to identifying systemic barriers

Over the past three years, the Investment Headquarters has held 69 meetings, addressing issues related to 309 projects with a combined value of more than $154 billion, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Sept. 16.

Its work covers different stages of project implementation, including land allocation, infrastructure connections, permits, raw material supplies, financing and preparation for construction.

In 2025, decisions by the Investment Headquarters enabled 12 projects in nine regions to proceed to construction and installation works, representing more than $1.5 billion in invested capital.

Rysmambetov said the mechanism is particularly relevant because investors can face difficulties when moving from central government institutions to regional authorities. He identified coordination between central and regional authorities as a key challenge, noting that central-level decisions can face delays when investors move to the regional level.

Investment agreements expand the pipeline

The Government has also increased its use of investment agreements, intended to give investors greater predictability about the conditions for implementing large projects.

In 2025, 41 investment agreements worth $29.8 billion were signed, compared with six agreements worth $2.2 billion in 2024. Since the beginning of this year, another 25 agreements worth about $11 billion have been concluded.

The figures indicate a substantial expansion in the number and value of projects receiving this form of state support. The more important measure, however, is how many of these projects progress from agreements and investment decisions to construction and eventually operational production.

Several projects already moving through the implementation process illustrate the potential economic impact.

From raw materials to higher-value production

The projects illustrate how investment support can translate into new production and jobs. In Balkhash, the $1.5 billion Qazaq Smelter project is expected to produce 300,000 tons of cathode copper annually, process up to 1.5 million tons of concentrate and create nearly 1,600 jobs.

In the Mangystau Region, a $287.6 million multifunctional terminal at the Port of Kuryk is planned to handle 15 million tons and create around 500 jobs, adding capacity to the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route.

Other projects focus on domestic processing. Advanced Processing is developing a $100 million ammonia and ammonium nitrate plant in the Atyrau Region, while QazCoilPro is investing nearly $256.8 million in a full-cycle aluminum plant in the Turkistan Region, with more than 1,000 jobs expected across the project and related facilities.

Measuring implementation, not only commitments

These projects also highlight why resolving administrative barriers matters: investment agreements and announcements must ultimately translate into construction, production and jobs.

Rysmambetov said the Investment Headquarters helps “break through this ice” and reach the core of issues at the regional and ministerial levels. But its continued role also indicates that Kazakhstan’s investment infrastructure still has gaps.

“The fact that there is still work for such things as the Investment Headquarters means that the investment infrastructure is not yet fully developed,” he said.

Tracking the problems brought before the headquarters could help identify recurring regulatory and regional barriers and show where systemic reforms are needed.

Rysmambetov expects the Investment Headquarters to remain necessary for at least the next five years. Its longer-term value, he suggested, will depend on whether the problems it now solves project by project can eventually be addressed through improvements to the broader investment system.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands International Air Connectivity With New Routes to Türkiye and UAE
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is set to expand international air connectivity with new and resumed passenger and cargo services linking the country with Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as airlines increase capacity on key routes.

Turkish airline SunExpress plans to launch regular flights between Astana and Izmir with flights scheduled twice a week on Wednesdays and Saturdays using Boeing 737 aircraft, while increasing the frequency of its existing Almaty–Izmir service.

The plans were discussed during a Sept. 15 meeting between the Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee and representatives of SunExpress, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport.

Meanwhile, Air Astana plans to resume regular flights between Kazakhstan and Dubai in October. The Almaty–Dubai service is scheduled to restart on Oct. 1, followed by the Astana–Dubai route on Oct. 2. The airline plans to gradually increase frequencies during the month, with Almaty–Dubai flights rising from four to 12 per week and Astana–Dubai flights from three to 10 per week by the end of October. The airline said the schedule could be adjusted depending on developments in the Middle East.

The expansion also includes air cargo connectivity between Kazakhstan and the UAE. FlyDubai plans to launch weekly cargo flights on the Almaty–Dubai route from Oct. 2 using Boeing 737 aircraft. The service will transport both import and export cargo between the two countries, according to Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee.

The new cargo route is expected to provide additional logistics options for Kazakh businesses and support trade and economic ties between Kazakhstan and the UAE. Kazakhstan’s Transport Ministry has identified the development of air cargo transportation as a priority for strengthening the country’s transport and logistics potential, increasing its transit attractiveness and supporting the development of aviation hubs.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Face Thailand in Davis Cup Tie With First World Group Place at Stake
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s tennis team will face Thailand in a Davis Cup World Group 2 tie in Astana on Sept. 18–19, with the winner advancing to the World Group 1 playoffs. The official draw has determined the order of the singles and doubles matches at the National Tennis Center’s Arena.

The official draw for the tie was held in Astana on Sept. 17, determining the order of the five matches. The tie consists of four singles matches and one doubles match, reported the Kazakhstan’s Tennis Federation.

The first day on Sept. 18 will feature two singles matches, beginning at 1 p.m. Astana time. Kazakhstan’s Alexander Shevchenko will face Thailand’s Maximus Parapol Jones in the opening match. He will be followed by Timofey Skatov, who will play Kasidit Samrej.

The second day will begin with the doubles match. Kazakhstan will be represented by Denis Yevseyev and Beibit Zhukayev, who will face Thanapet Chanta and Pruchya Isaro.

The final two singles matches are scheduled to follow, with Shevchenko facing Samrej and Skatov taking on Jones. The tie will conclude on Sept. 19, with play starting at noon.

The winner of the Kazakhstan–Thailand tie will advance to the World Group 1 playoffs for the 2027 Davis Cup season. Kazakhstan currently occupies 42nd place in the Davis Cup rankings, while Thailand is ranked 60th. The two teams are meeting in the Davis Cup for the first time since 2009.

Ahead of the tie, Zhukayev said he had spent about three weeks preparing for the competition and was looking forward to partnering with Yevseyev in the doubles match.

“I prepared for this Davis Cup for about three weeks. I am looking forward to our match with Denis against Thailand. We had good training sessions, played practice sets and worked on different exercises. Overall, I feel good on court and hope we can produce a quality performance,” Zhukayev said.

Yevseyev highlighted the pair’s familiarity with each other as one of their strengths.

“This year has been difficult for us. We lost in February, and now it is important to draw the right conclusions and show what we are capable of. Beibit and I have known each other for a long time and have played together many times in both singles and doubles. We understand each other on court, and I consider that an advantage. We will try to make the most of our opportunities and give everything for the victory,” he said.

The matches will be played on hard courts at the National Tennis Center in Astana.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s National Fund Sees Investment Income Nearly Catch up With Oil Taxes, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s National Fund is increasingly generating income not only from the country’s oil sector but also from the capital accumulated over years of resource revenues, with investment returns in the first half of 2026 coming close to the amount raised through oil-sector taxes, Kazakh economist Ruslan Sultanov writes in his Telegram channel, analyzing Kazakhstan’s national statistics.

The National Fund received 3.21 trillion tenge (US$7.1 billion) in the first six months of 2026. Oil-sector taxes accounted for 55.6% of total inflows, while investment income reached 43.7%.

The figures point to an important shift in the role of the fund: as its accumulated assets grow, returns generated by investing those assets can become a source of income comparable in scale to current revenues from the oil sector.

Capital itself is becoming a source of income

The 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.13 billion) investment return exceeded the revenue generated by any individual oil-sector tax during the period.

The largest individual oil-related contribution was corporate income tax from the oil sector, which amounted to 798.9 billion tenge (US$1.78 billion). The mineral extraction tax generated 267.2 billion tenge (US$596.6 million), while the rent tax on exports brought in 172.5 billion tenge (US$385.1 million).

Against these figures, the investment return of 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.13 billion) represents a separate and increasingly significant source of resources for the National Fund, according to Sultanov. The scale of the underlying capital is central to this development. The fund’s assets stood at 37.34 trillion tenge (US$83.9 billion) at the beginning of 2026.

The investment income generated during the first six months was equivalent to approximately 3.8% of that starting capital. This means that even a relatively modest percentage return on a very large asset base can translate into hundreds of billions or trillions of tenge.

The fund financed the budget while its capital grew

The National Fund simultaneously continued to perform its traditional fiscal role during the first half of the year. A total of 1.87 trillion tenge (US$4.05 billion) was used from the fund, of which 1.86 trillion tenge (US$4.03 billion) went to the national budget as a guaranteed transfer.

At the same time, the fund’s capital, Sultanov writes, increased from 37.34 trillion (US$80.88 billion) to 38.68 trillion tenge (US$83.80 billion). The combination is significant: despite the transfer to the budget, the fund’s capital increased during the period. Investment income played an important role in that outcome.

From oil revenues to an asset-based model

The National Fund was created to accumulate part of Kazakhstan’s natural-resource revenues and provide a financial buffer for the economy. Its traditional role has therefore been closely associated with oil: when hydrocarbon revenues rise, the fund receives more money; when the economy requires support, part of those savings can be transferred to the budget.

The latest figures illustrate another dimension of that model. Once the fund reaches a sufficiently large asset base, the accumulated capital itself begins to generate significant income. The source of that income is therefore no longer directly tied to the production or taxation of another barrel of oil.

That distinction matters for the long-term role of sovereign savings. Oil revenues are linked to production volumes, commodity prices, export conditions and the fiscal regime. Investment income, meanwhile, depends on the size and composition of the portfolio, asset performance and the quality of asset management. As the capital base expands, the second factor becomes increasingly important.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wants More Oil Refining: Its Next Challenge Is Securing Feedstock
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to more than double its annual oil refining capacity to 39 million tons by 2040, seeking to move the energy sector toward deeper processing and higher-value products. But the scale of the planned expansion also raises a fundamental question: how will the country secure sufficient economically viable crude supplies for its future refineries while maintaining incentives to invest in exploration and production?

The issue was highlighted at the 13th annual Central Asia and Caspian Oil and Gas Petrochemistry and Refining Summit 2026, where the Ministry of Energy presented the main provisions of Kazakhstan’s Concept for the Development of the Oil Refining Industry for 2025–2040.

The concept envisages increasing annual crude processing from 18 million to 39 million tons and raising the ratio of oil production to refining from 5:1 to 2.5:1.

Refining expansion depends on a growing resource base
