World.title: Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s transit plan finds new momentum in S. Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. The Central Asia–Republic of Korea Summit, which opened in Seoul on September 16, marked a new stage in economic cooperation between Turkmenistan and the Republic of Korea. During President Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s state visit, the two sides signed 13 bilateral agreements and memoranda, including an agreement on the mutual protection of investments, as well as arrangements covering rail transport, shipbuilding, the construction of new cities, water management, artificial intelligence, and science.

The economic dimension also constituted one of the central areas of discussion at the regional level. Following the meeting of the leaders of the five Central Asian states, President of the Republic of Korea Lee Jae Myung called for expanding cooperation beyond raw-material trade to encompass the entire value chain, from resource development and processing to the joint production of high-tech goods. Seoul likewise reaffirmed its intention to deepen cooperation with Central Asia in the fields of energy, infrastructure, technology, and supply chains.

For Turkmenistan, this agenda is particularly significant. The agreements reached correspond closely with the areas of transport, industry, technology, and investment that have assumed increasing importance in President Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s foreign economic policy in recent years. In this broader context, the summit may be viewed as another element of the country’s long-term strategy to strengthen its position as an energy, industrial, and transit hub of the region.

At the same time, the practical returns of such initiatives are becoming especially visible now. As Trend previously noted in its analytical piece "Inside Turkmenistan’s investment cycle: How Turkish contractors anchor a new phase of economic expansion," the country is entering a new investment cycle, triggered by the start of the fourth phase of development at the Galkynysh field - one of the world's largest gas deposits. In April 2026, Turkmengaz and CNPC signed an agreement to build new facilities that will allow processing of up to 10 billion cubic meters of additional gas per year. A project of this scale creates a multiplier effect across the economy: demand rises for construction work, industrial equipment, engineering solutions, transport infrastructure and logistics. Against this backdrop, international agreements take on added practical weight, giving foreign companies the chance to take part not only in individual contracts but in a much larger cycle of economic modernization.

Viewed against South Korea's existing footprint in Turkmenistan, many of the areas outlined in Seoul turn out to rest on solid practical ground. South Korean companies have been involved in the development of Turkmen industry for many years, chiefly in gas chemicals, infrastructure and machine building. One of the best-known examples remains the gas-chemical complex in Kiyanly, built by a consortium led by Hyundai Engineering with the participation of LG International (now LX International), which produces polyethylene and polypropylene.

This cooperation has not been limited to facilities already completed. In 2024, Hyundai Engineering signed new agreements with Turkmengaz on further development of the Galkynysh field and the rehabilitation of a polymer plant, with the value of potential orders estimated at roughly $6 billion. Korean companies are thus continuing to operate precisely in the segments that are gaining additional momentum under Turkmenistan's new investment cycle.

It is the transport dimension, however, that best illustrates the link between industrial cooperation and Turkmenistan's push to become a transit hub. In May 2026, Turkmenistan commissioned the Gadamly dry cargo ship, the first vessel of its kind to be fully built in the country. It was constructed at the Balkan Shipbuilding and Ship-Repair Plant together with South Korea's Koryo Shipbuilding Industry Technology Co., Ltd. Korean specialists took part in technology transfer and the training of local personnel. The vessel has a deadweight of 6,100 tons and can carry up to 240 twenty-ton containers.

In May, the Gadamly made its first voyage to Azerbaijan and now operates on a regular line between the ports of Turkmenbashi and Baku. In effect, Korean technology has been built directly into a working transport route linking Turkmenistan's Caspian coast with Azerbaijan's transport infrastructure. Turkmenistan also plans to commission a second dry cargo vessel, the Menzil, currently under construction with the involvement of the same Korean partners.

This is why it was significant that, ahead of the summit, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung specifically tied Turkmenistan's potential to its geographic position. He said the country's abundant resources could become the basis for high-value-added industries, while its location linking the Caspian Sea and Central Asia could turn it into a new hub for logistics and trade. During talks with President Serdar Berdimuhamedov, the two sides also agreed that the "Revival of the Great Silk Road" concept could serve as a new driver of growth connecting Central Asia with the Caspian Sea.

Seen in this light, the Gadamly route shows how a single industrial-technology project can become a building block of the Trans-Caspian transport system. Baku plays a pivotal role in this scheme for Turkmenistan: Azerbaijan is developing the port and rail infrastructure of Baku, along with other elements of the East-West corridor, which runs from Central Asia across the Caspian and through Azerbaijan onward to Georgia, Türkiye and Europe, thereby linking Asia with Europe. Azerbaijan has officially stated that developing this route creates opportunities for Turkmenistan and other Central Asian countries to reach European and global markets.

Korean involvement in Turkmen shipbuilding thus offers a fairly clear example of how industrial cooperation can evolve into transport infrastructure, which in turn feeds into international logistics. It is precisely this sequence that allows the current Korean-Turkmen dialogue to be viewed as part of building a route in which Turkmenistan serves as the Caspian link connecting Central Asia with Azerbaijan and, further on, with Europe.

Still, viewing what is happening in Seoul solely through the lens of bilateral relations between Turkmenistan and South Korea would be incomplete. For Ashgabat, the summit is another element of the C5+1 format, which gives the five Central Asian states a platform to discuss economic, technological and transport issues jointly with major outside partners. The most illustrative and comparable examples in terms of the issues covered have been the C5+1 summits and meetings held with the United States, Japan and now South Korea.

Over the recent period, this model has developed consistently along several tracks. At the first Central Asia-Japan summit in Tokyo in December 2025, a dedicated section was devoted to transport and digital connectivity. In the final declaration, the leaders stressed the need to expand Central Asia's access to international markets and backed the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route as a tool for strengthening the region's connectivity and its access to global markets. The parties also agreed to develop cooperation in artificial intelligence and digital technologies. Trend examined Japan's strategy in Turkmenistan in more detail in its article "Serdar Berdimuhamedov's investment strategy: Role of Japanese business."

The American track has developed around a somewhat different set of interests. Within the C5+1 format, discussions in Ashgabat in early September 2026 focused on expanding cooperation between the five Central Asian countries and the United States in critical minerals, trade and transport, while a seminar held on September 15-16 was devoted to artificial intelligence, digitalization, cybersecurity, satellite communications and data centers. This shows that, even where specific priorities differ - from mineral supply chains to digital infrastructure - the central element of engagement remains connecting the region to international economic and technological chains.

The Korean summit looks like the next link in the same chain of events. Seoul is placing its emphasis on combining Central Asia's industrial potential with Korean technology, investment and manufacturing expertise. In the outcomes of the first summit, the parties agreed to develop joint value chains in critical minerals and energy, and to expand cooperation in industry, artificial intelligence, science and technology. Seoul has also established a separate mechanism for meetings between the industry ministers of Central Asian countries and Korea.

For Turkmenistan, the significance of this sequence lies in the fact that the country is acting simultaneously on several external fronts, drawing on different areas of expertise to serve its own development goals. At the same time, the C5+1 format gives each Central Asian country an additional platform to advance its interests as part of a region with a combined population of roughly 80 million people. This is not about creating a single market in an institutional sense, but about a regional platform that allows the shared infrastructural, resource, and economic potential of the five countries to be presented as an interconnected space.

This is precisely where the interests of Turkmenistan and its external partners converge. For the United States, Japan and South Korea, Central Asia is becoming a space where they can simultaneously work with resources, industry, technology and new transport routes. For Turkmenistan, these partnerships allow it to consistently attract the investment, technology and expertise needed to carry out President Serdar Berdimuhamedov's policy course as the country enters a new investment cycle. And the development of ties across the Caspian adds another important element to this system - a route for Central Asia, via Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan, to transport infrastructure leading further on to European markets.

In this sense, the Seoul summit can be viewed as a closing point in the current stage of Turkmenistan's efforts to build a new economic and transit configuration. The country has steadily attracted investment, technology and industrial expertise, while simultaneously developing its own production base and the infrastructure needed to access international transport routes. These strands are now beginning to converge into a single chain, in which industrial development generates cargo volumes, technology ensures their efficient movement, and the Caspian route together with the partnership with Azerbaijan opens the way to markets further to the west.

For Ashgabat, the next challenge is to make this accumulated potential function as a single system. New industrial projects need to generate sufficient cargo volumes, the development of ports and the fleet needs to ensure their movement across the Caspian, and international partnerships need to sustain a steady flow of investment and technology. If this chain is consistently put into practice, the current investment cycle could become the foundation for cementing Turkmenistan's role as a transit link between Central Asia, the Caspian, and the European direction.

World.title: VDMA sees potential for technology transfer, training in Kyrgyzstan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Technology transfer, training and local partnerships could provide new opportunities for cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and the German mechanical engineering industry as the country's market develops, the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA) told Trend.

"Looking ahead, opportunities may emerge in areas such as technology transfer, training, and local partnerships, should the market continue to open and develop within this broader regional context," VDMA said.

The association also linked Kyrgyzstan’s prospects to economic developments across Central Asia, noting that stronger regional growth could improve the outlook for smaller markets.

"A positive and stable economic development across the wider Central Asian region could also have a favourable impact on the outlook for the smaller markets such as Kyrgyzstan," VDMA said.

According to VDMA, the development of the regional economic environment will therefore be an important factor in shaping the prospects for deeper engagement between European machinery companies and Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan has been pursuing economic development and diversification, with efforts focused on strengthening industrial capacity, improving infrastructure and attracting investment. The country is also seeking to expand cooperation with foreign companies and international partners in areas including manufacturing, technology and skills development.

At the regional level, Kyrgyzstan is part of broader efforts to improve economic connectivity and cooperation across Central Asia. The development of transport infrastructure, trade links and industrial cooperation is contributing to the gradual expansion of opportunities for businesses operating in the region.

Germany and other European countries are among Kyrgyzstan’s potential partners as the country works to develop its industrial base and integrate more closely into regional and international value chains.

World.title: Iran’s Mahirud border terminal sees 90% rise in transit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Transit through Iran’s Mahirud border terminal in the northeastern South Khorasan Province increased by 90% during the first five months of the current Iranian year (March 21-Aug. 22, 2026) compared with the same period of the previous year.

Javad Zaker, head of the South Khorasan Province Road and Transportation Department, made the remarks, according to the department.

"During the five-month period, 684,000 tons of cargo were transited through the Mahirud border terminal in South Khorasan Province. This represents a 90% increase in cargo transit compared with the same period last year," he said.

Zaker said cargo transported through the Mahirud border terminal to Afghanistan mainly included oil, spare parts, sugar and medicinal plants. The cargo entered Iran through the port of Bandar Abbas from the UAE, Indonesia, India and China before being transported to the Mahirud border terminal.

The official noted that 373,000 tons of products were exported through the Mahirud border terminal during the five-month period, up 44% from the same period last year. The main exported products included cement, iron products, ceramics and greens. The products were mainly exported from Iran’s South Khorasan, Isfahan, Razavi Khorasan, Yazd, Kerman and Fars provinces.

According to Trend’s analysis, the increase in transit through the Mahirud border terminal to 684,000 tons indicates that the terminal is strengthening its position as an important transit hub for Iran’s trade with Afghanistan and Central Asia. In particular, the transportation of cargo from the UAE, Indonesia, India and China, entering Iran through Bandar Abbas and then moving to Afghanistan via Mahirud, highlights the expansion of Iran’s logistics capabilities linking its seaports with land border crossings.

The 44% increase in exports to 373,000 tons also indicates that the terminal is playing a growing role not only in transit but also in facilitating access for Iranian products to the Afghan market. This trend could create favorable conditions for expanding trade flows along Iran’s eastern border, increasing the use of logistics infrastructure and boosting cargo transportation among countries in the region.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan maintains strong economic momentum in 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. The real growth rate of Kyrgyzstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) stood at 11.1% in the first seven months of 2026.

According to the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan, President Sadyr Japarov made the statement on September 11 at an event in Talas dedicated to the 35th anniversary of the independence of the Kyrgyz Republic.

"The real growth rate of gross domestic product amounted to 11.1% in the first seven months of 2026. This is one of the highest economic growth rates not only in Central Asia but also in the world," he said.

The president emphasized that one of the main achievements of recent years has been the strengthening of the country’s economic foundation.

"Over the past four years, the average annual economic growth rate has stood at 10.2%, demonstrating a sustainable trend," the president added.

Trend's analysis indicates that if Kyrgyzstan maintains strong investment activity, construction momentum and domestic demand, the economy could record GDP growth of around 9–10% in 2026, despite a gradual moderation in the second half of the year. This would keep the country among the fastest-growing economies in the region and provide a strong base for further expansion.

In 2027, GDP growth could remain at around 7–8% as major infrastructure, energy, transport and industrial projects continue to support economic activity. By 2028, growth could stabilize at approximately 7%, reflecting a transition from exceptionally high expansion rates toward a more sustainable growth model based increasingly on investment, productivity and export capacity.

World.title: Think you've dodged the flu this year? Don't be so sure
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia is facing an abnormally late surge in influenza numbers this year, but the total amount of cases is predicted to be far fewer than 2025.

Last year, the nation recorded a grim record, with over 1,700 Australians dying from influenza — the most this century.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Dr Michael Wright said the good news was that numbers this year would be lower.

Dr Wright said last year saw two influenza peaks, with the second peak coming from a new strain of the virus.

This year's influenza vaccine covers that new strain — something Dr Wright attributes to the lower numbers recorded this year.

But he has warned against complacency.

"There may still be another peak coming," Dr Wright said.

"And really, it's not too late to still get your flu vaccine."

The Australian Centre for Disease Control tracks the number of laboratory confirmed influenza cases across the country.

This year, it shows there has been far fewer cases than the previous year.

A spokesperson for the centre said although the rate of flu activity had increased nationally, it had slowed in recent weeks, suggesting the national peak may be approaching.

Since the pandemic, flu season has typically aligned the winter months, however the spokesperson said a peak in early-September is consistent with pre-pandemic flu seasons.

States record upticks

At the start September, data from Queensland Health showed an unusually late uptick in influenza cases across the state, with abnormally low reports of the disease so far this year.

Experts warned the peak may continue to rise, with data from last week showing there were about 3,435 people diagnosed with influenza in Queensland.

Experts warn of late-season uptick in influenza Influenza statistics have jumped in Queensland, with experts urging people to get vaccinated before the free program ends on September 30.

Looking at other Australian jurisdictions a bit more closely, the data shows that influenza cases are also lower than compared to the same time last year.

In Victoria, influenza notifications have increased by around 400 per cent over the past seven weeks, with influenza A making up most of the cases.

The state's emergency departments have experienced a 25 per cent increase in acute respiratory infections over the past six weeks, mainly from children.

Victoria's Chief Health Officer Dr Caroline McElnay said the season has arrived later than previous years.

"While it can be difficult to predict exactly when flu activity will peak, cases are expected to remain high over the coming weeks, including through the school holidays," Dr McElnay said.

In New South Wales, Health Department data shows reported cases have decreased, but remain at a high level.

While cases remained lower over the winter months than the previous year, the state has recorded an uptick towards the end of August and start of September.

In August, South Australia's Chief Public Health Officer also predicted a late-flu season.

So far, the number of influenza cases reported in South Australia is well below figures at the same time last year.

In Tasmania, cases are also on the rise, but remain at "moderate" levels, according to the state's Health Department.

Dr Wright said higher-risk individuals — those with chronic health conditions, children under five, and older Australians — should seek medical advice on whether a vaccine was needed.

Self-reported respiratory illness activity (defined as fever and cough) in Australia shows a recent uptick in reports. (Supplied: FluTracking)

FluTracking Australia releases its own weekly national data on self-reported flu-like symptoms.

Its latest report from the week ending September 13 shows respiratory illness, defined as a fever and cough, has plateaued this month, and the surge has occurred later than in previous years.

World.title: Breaking: Simon Carman pleads not guilty in first court appearance
World.content:
Simon Peter Carman, the Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager Tunchanok Donhomla in June, has pleaded not guilty to all charges in his first court appearance since the girl's death.

Mr Carman fronted the Pattaya Provincial Court in Thailand today.

He is facing four charges including murder, concealing a corpse, and abducting a minor for indecent purposes.

The 45-year-old pleaded not guilty to all charges and told the court he had acted in self defence.

He also urged the court to grant him bail and said that he did not pose a flight risk.

Prosecutors objected to the bail application.

The next court date is set for October 12.

Thai police have accused Mr Carman of picking up Ms Tunchanok along Pattaya's popular Beach Road in June, then killing her and discarding the body.

The 17-year-old was last seen alive on CCTV walking hand in hand with Mr Carman into the elevators of his condo building on June 25.

Police found her body, which had been stuffed into a suitcase and dumped along railway tracks near Mr Carman's accommodation, two days later.

World.title: Murder accused appears in court over death of 48yo man
World.content:
Dominic Alexander Carbonari has appeared in a Tasmanian court charged with the murder of a 48-year-old man in the state's north-west.

The 42-year-old Tarleton man appeared in the Devonport Magistrates Court via video link from Risdon Prison on Friday afternoon.

Tasmania Police have alleged emergency services arrived at a Railton home on Wednesday morning after receiving reports that a man had been assaulted.

In a statement, police said the accused left the scene and was arrested nearby shortly after.

Mr Carbonari was charged on Thursday, after the Railton man died at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

Police said the men knew each other.

Magistrate Duncan Fairley adjourned the matter to October 26.

Mr Carbonari will remain in custody until then.

World.title: A beginner's guide to growing flowers to decorate your home
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Flowers can be a great way to bring more colour into your home, but store-bought varieties can also be expensive and have a big environmental footprint.

Growing your own cut flowers (blooms bred for use in vases and arrangements) is a fun way around this, and while it might sound intimidating, incorporating blooms into your garden space or even pots can be simpler than you think.

Filling a vase with flowers grown in your own garden can be very satisfying. (ABC News: Tegan Osborne)

Royal Botanic Garden Sydney horticulturalist Madeline Ward grows flowers at work and at home, where she usually has something in bloom.

"For beginners … if you start with one or two species [of flowers] and you really get to know them as friends … then you can expand from there," she says.

Madeline Ward grows flowers at work and has her own cutting garden at home. (Supplied: Botanic Gardens of Sydney)

Step one: Choosing the best spot

To grow flowers, the first thing you need is sunshine.

Madeline says ideally, you want an area with full sun that's close to a tap or hose for watering and in a spot with easy access so you can actually enjoy the garden once it gets going.

Bec Shelley owns a family-run seed company outside Hobart/Nipaluna and also grows her own flowers.

She says you don't need to make a formal garden bed.

"I think you can incorporate little patches of cut flowers in between your landscaped bits … it can still be pretty," Bec says.

Step two: Prep your soil

Once you've chosen your spot, you want the soil to be loose and free of weeds, Madeline says.

She recommends getting into the soil and weeding by hand to make it easy for your seedlings to send down roots.

"Once you've cleared the bed … and you've turned it over a little bit, you want to give it a nice healthy dose of compost over the top," she says.

Madeline recommends hand-weeding your the area to familiarise yourself with the soil. (Unsplash: CDC)

Madeline says store-bought compost is good for beginners, and homemade compost is also fine, as long as it's "well rotted and well turned".

But she says don't worry about manure, as this can over-complicate things.

Madeline also recommends making sure your bed is free of big rocks and debris, which can obstruct root growth, and using a rake to create a smooth surface to sow into.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Step three: Choosing and planting your flower seeds

With so many beautiful cut flower varieties available, choosing which to grow first can feel overwhelming.

But there are a few easy-to-grow exotic and native varieties that are ideal for beginners, depending on your climate zone.

These climate zones are based on simplified versions of the Bureau of Meteorology’s climate maps. (ABC Organic Gardener Magazine)

As many cut flower varieties, including the ones mentioned in this article, are hardy and don't need a lot of care, they can become weeds if they spread outside of gardens. So, before you get started, it's important to check with your local council whether that is the case in your area.

Click into the cards below to explore the flower types Bec and Madeline suggest, and growing tips for each.

Zinnas Read more Read more Zinnias are exotic annuals (plants that flower then die), mostly native to North and South America, with the kind of round flower heads you see in children's drawings. Species bred for cutting can grow almost a metre tall and come in a huge array of colours. "They'll come up pretty quickly and they're easy to look after," Madeline says. Zinnias are good for beginners because they need little care once established. (Supplied: Veggie & Flower Garden Seeds) Zinnia seeds are best planted in the warmer months (see climate zone map for your area) in moist, well-drained soil, and the plants don't like frost. While not illegal to grow, Zinnia peruviana is considered a weed in parts of Australia, including Queensland and northern NSW. If they are in your location, try growing the equally gorgeous Zinnia elegens. Climate zone When to sow Tropical April to July Subtropical February to December Temperate August to December Cool September to December Arid January, August to December Cosmos Read more Read more Comos is an exotic annual with classic round flower heads and soft petals, primarily in white, pinks and purples, originating in North and South America. Cosmos varieties bred for cutting can grow up to 2 metres tall, with flower stems of up to 60 centimetres. Bec says cosmos seeds germinate quickly and the plants are "quite low maintenance". Bec says cosmos are another great cut flower for beginner growers. (Supplied: Veggie & Flower Garden Seeds) Plant them in a protected sunny position with moist, well-drained soil, and sow the seeds about 6 millimetres deep. Cosmos bipinnatus and Cosmos sulphureus are considered emerging weeds in some states. If they are where you live, try the more subdued chocolate cosmos (Cosmos atrosanguineus), with blooms that smell like their namesake. Climate zone When to sow Tropical April to October Subtropical All year Temperate August to December Cool September to December Arid August to December Billy buttons Read more Read more Billy buttons are wildflowers native to inland and eastern Australia, with a striking yellow, spherical flower head. The most common species grown in gardens is the perennial Pycnosorus globosus. "It's an Australian native and so it's super hardy … a little bit trickier to start from seed but once that gets going you don't have to do a lot," Bec says. They're best grown in full sun or part shade and are drought and frost-tolerant once established. Shallow sow with just a millimetre of soil on top, as they need sunlight to germinate, and be sure to keep the soil moist. Climate zone When to sow Tropical April to September Subtropical February to May, August to November Temperate January to April, September to December Cool January to May, September to December Arid January to April, August to December Sweet peas Read more Read more Sweet peas are another classic exotic that are easy to grow. They come in a range of colours, have soft, frilly petals and are native to Sicily, southern Italy, and the Aegean Islands. "I would really recommend people look at the heirloom varieties and the ones that have a strong scent. The most beautiful thing about sweet peas is how gorgeous they smell," Madeline says. They are best grown in full sun and well-drained soil, and will climb on a trellis. Check your seed packet for sowing depth, as this can vary. Bec Shelley grows sweet peas on trellises. (Supplied: Veggie & Flower Garden Seeds) Lathyrus latifolius sweet peas are considered an environmental weed in parts of Australia (including Victoria and Lord Howe Island) and is an emerging weed in other states. If they are considered weeds in your area, the less aggressive Lathyrus odoratus may be an option. Climate zone When to sow Tropical February to May Subtropical March to May Temperate February to April, August to September Cool January to April, September to October Arid February to June Paper daisies Read more Read more Paper daisies (Xerochrysum bracteatum) are a perennial Australian native found in the wild in parts of every state and territory. They have round flower heads with papery, pointed petals and come in yellows, whites, reds, pinks and purples. "They're really great. Super easy for beginner growers," Madeline says. "They work really well as a dried flower, and they have a lot more longevity in a garden than some of our exotic species, so they'll last a lot longer … right through the summer." Paper daisies are best grown in full sun and need very well-drained soil. Sow seeds 1mm deep in moist soil. Climate zone When to sow Tropical Not appropriate for this climate Subtropical April to July Temperate February to March, September to December Cool January to April, September to December Arid February to April, August to October

A note on sowing seeds

To keep things simple, Madeline recommends sowing seeds for the above flowers directly into the soil.

While you're still getting a feel for flower growing, you can follow the depth and spacing instructions on your seed packets.

But Madeline says you can also be a bit more relaxed.

"I think it's so much fun to cast seed out into a garden and see what and where it pops up," she says.

Distributing your seeds in a carrier mix of vermiculite or sand will help distribute them more evenly, she says.

If you live somewhere chilly or are keen to observe the germination process close up, you can also sow your seeds in a punnet and spout them in a greenhouse or a sunny spot inside.

Bec Shelley from Veggie & Flower Garden Seeds in Tasmania prefers to sow in punnets first. (Supplied: Veggie & Flower Garden Seeds)

For cosmos, zinnia and sweet pea planted in punnets, Bec recommends using good quality potting mix and then hardening the seedlings off so they don't suffer transplant shock.

"You let them spend a few hours outside [each day], building up to a whole day over a week's time," she says.

How to replace your lawn with native plants Many of us are looking to create a native garden as a lower maintenance, more sustainable and often cheaper alternative.

"Then plant the seedling into your garden at about six weeks of growth, which is generally when they have two sets of leaves."

For both direct sowing and sprouting in punnets, watering every day is important. You want to keep the soil moist, but not wet enough to wash away or damage the seeds.

If you live in an apartment or without a yard, Bec and Madeline say cut flowers can be sown and grown in pots, but get the largest ones you can find and water religiously, as soil in pots dries out rapidly.

If growing from seed sounds too tricky, nurseries also sell seedlings for some of the species listed above. But be sure to check the label to make sure what you're buying produces flowers with stems long enough for cutting.

Step four: Growing responsibly and harvesting

Once your plants are established, give them a daily drink. Your seed packet should tell you roughly how long your flowers will take to bloom.

"Once they're in the ground [and no longer in the seedling stage], they're pretty low maintenance … you'd want to mulch around the base of the plant and watch out for any pests and disease," Bec says.

"But generally, [with] those easy-to-grow flowers, you can sort of let them go and they'll just keep growing."

To keep new flowers coming through, it's important to deadhead regularly. (ABC News: Tegan Osborne)

When your flowers arrive, cutting your blooms regularly to bring inside will ensure more grow in their place. But if you've got more than your vases can handle, deadheading (cutting the flower heads off once they droop) will do the same job.

Deadheading before your flowers go to seed will help ensure they don't escape the garden and become a weed problem in your neighbourhood.

Madeline says avoiding seed mixes that don't list the flowers included can also help stop the spread of weeds.

Madeline's final advice for new flower growers is to have fun and "be prepared to fail".

"Plants will die … do weird things … get disease," she says.

World.title: Police continue search for potentially armed man in rural Queensland
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A potentially armed man remains missing after he disappeared more than six days ago on a rural highway.

Marcus Bismark, 44, was last seen walking along the Gregory Developmental Road in the Greenvale area, about 250 kilometres west of Townsville, on Saturday afternoon after his vehicle broke down.

Marcus Bismark went missing on September 12. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

He is believed to be in possession of a firearm and travelling on foot.

Queensland Police launched a search operation and deployed specialist police to the area earlier this week.

Mr Bismark is described as being approximately 180 centimetres tall with a solid build and dark complexion.

He was last seen wearing long, black pants and no shirt.

His family hold concerns for his welfare due to a medical condition.

Members of the public are being warned not to approach Mr Bismark but to report any sightings to Triple Zero (000).

Police are also appealing to anyone with dash cam footage that may show Mr Bismark in the region to come forward.

World.title: Social service body says Qld's breach bail laws were made in 'echo chamber'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Queensland's peak social service body has accused the state government of making laws in an "echo chamber".

The LNP administration's latest measure to curb crime, breach bail, go to jail, is being examined by a parliamentary committee.

The policy proposes that adults and children who commit serious crimes while on bail face a mandatory 12 months behind bars.

The committee today heard evidence from experts on the impact of the legislation.

But the Queensland Council of Social Services (QCOSS) and other community organisations were not called to appear.

Qld breach bail laws criticism Experts from policing, legal professions, and advocacy services have widely criticised the legislation.

Chief executive Aimee McVeigh was scathing in her assessment of the exclusion.

"The approach that's being taken is the development of law inside an echo chamber," she said.

"We won't have robust laws and policies made without hearing diverse voices.

"We are working together with some of the most vulnerable people in the community, and so our voices are really important, and we have an important contribution to make to public policy."

The criticism comes after the government was last month accused of gagging frontline community organisations, for fear of losing state funding.

'What comes next?'

The parliamentary committee heard from groups including victims' advocates and legal experts.

Commissioner of the Queensland Family and Child Commission, Luke Twyford, also fronted the hearing, backing the core aim of breach bail, go to jail, in increasing community safety.

Queensland Family and Child Commission principal commissioner Luke Twyford. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

But he noted the key way to achieve that was through changing behaviour.

"I don't believe we can punish our way to behaviour change. We actually need interventions," he said.

"What is going on for them [children] that they are engaging in repeat behaviour?

" And as a society, locking them up for mandatory periods might be one solution, but is it going to change their behaviour and what comes next? "

The government consistently said it's been responding to what the community wants in the next step of its hardline youth justice approach.

Attorney-General Deb Frecklington said on Friday she was open to change on the legislation but would not be deterred from improving community safety.

"Now adult crime, adult time may seem tough to some, but it's working. Now we know that there is a lot more work to do, but we've seen those breaches.

"The independent data is telling us that crime is gradually going down, and that is what we need to see more of."

Deb Frecklington said she was open to change on the legislation. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Also fronting the committee was Queensland Human Rights Commissioner Debbie Platz, who raised concerns about the long term effect of the proposed laws.

"The available evidence suggests that the proposed breach bail offence and mandatory sentencing scheme will not reduce offending, except for in the short term.

"The evidence suggests greater gains are actually achieved through early intervention, rehabilitation and diversion."

The parliamentary committee will hold several regional hearings before handing its report to the government.

The premier has pledged the policy will be law by the end of the year.

World.title: Man busted with 9kg of methodone at Melbourne Airport
World.content:
A Geelong man has been charged over trying to import around 2,500 methadone pills into Melbourne after arriving on a flight from Thailand.



The Australian Federal Police (AFP) said the 48-year-old was arrested at Melbourne Airport on Wednesday, after Australian Border Force officers X-rayed his luggage.

Police said a subsequent examination found five plastic bags containing nine kilograms of the opioid hidden inside.

The man appeared before the Melbourne Magistrates' Court yesterday. (Supplied: AFP)

AFP Detective Superintendent Celeste Johnston said the quantity seized equated to more than four times the commercial quantity threshold.

"Australia's border is not an open door for people seeking to import bulk quantities of controlled drugs," Superintendent Johnston said.

"Quantities of this scale have the potential to cause significant harm if diverted into the illicit market."

The man was charged with importing and possessing a commercial quantity of a border-controlled drug, with both charges carrying a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

He appeared before the Melbourne Magistrates' Court yesterday, where he was granted bail and scheduled to appear before court again on January 7.

Police arrested the man at Melbourne Airport on Wednesday. (Supplied: Melbourne Airport)

Australian Border Force Acting Superintendent Costas Karatzas warned that travellers who attempted to unlawfully import border-controlled drugs faced severe penalties.

"Our message to anyone who thinks it's a good idea to smuggle illicit substances into Australia is to think again," he said.

" Such poor decisions will ultimately land offenders with lengthy jail time, including up to life imprisonment. "

Acting Superintendent Karatzas said the harm casued to the community by illicit and controlled drugs was "profound".

"Lives are cut short, and it brings with it a whole range of long-lasting health impacts and adverse societal outcomes," he said.

"We will continue to work with our law enforcement partners, including the AFP, to prevent these illicit substances from entering Australia and target those who attempt to bring them in unlawfully."

World.title: Inbred owl faces extinction without genetic rescue, scientists warn
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Researchers are warning a rare owl descended from a single breeding pair on Norfolk Island could die out unless new birds are brought in from New Zealand.

The entire population of the Norfolk Island Morepork owl, also known in Australia as the Norfolk boobook, is descended from one female after the species nearly died out in the 1980s.

About 25 owls are thought to survive on the island.

Monash University ornithologist Rohan Clarke said the window for action was closing.

"I think it can probably be measured in years," Associate Professor Clarke said.

" I would be pretty confident that we're going to be in a substantially worse position in 10 years if translocations haven't happened. "

In 1988, a male Morepork from New Zealand, which is a close relative to the Norfolk Morepork, was transported to save the species.

Norfolk Island science ranger Allie Andersen said the reproduction rate climbed after the first translocation nearly 40 years ago.

Experts believe the reproduction rate of the Norfolk Island Morepork has slowed due to inbreeding. (Supplied: Parks Australia )

By the late 1990s, the population grew to around 50 owls.

"Lots and lots of breeding was happening, nestlings were coming out of nests and that really restored the population," Dr Andersen said.

However, Dr Andersen said due to inbreeding, the growth had stagnated.

"Probably the single largest threat would be their very small population size and high inbreeding," Dr Andersen said.

"Every single owl that we have now is derived from just those two individuals.

"Sometimes we'll have a year where we don't see any breeding."

Hanging by a thread

Dr Clarke said infertility was common among highly inbred populations.

"All of those reproductive challenges are classic signs of inbreeding depressions in populations that have gone through extreme bottlenecks," he said.

A 2021 study showed there were only about 26 owls left on the island, many of which experts believed to be part of the older generation.

Dr Clarke said there may only be one single breeding pair out of 15 total pairs.

"Our knowledge is that the total number of young being produced is really small," Dr Clarke said

"If it's only one single with every loss of an adult bird and with the generation of more young from that single pair, the population continues to get more inbred because you've only got one female and one male contributing to the overall genetics of the population."

Another threat for the Morepork owl is secondary poisoning through chemicals intended for rats and house mice.

"If we lose even one owl to secondary poisoning that can have a real impact on the population," Dr Clarke said.

Dr Andersen said the community was worried about the future of the Morepork owl.

"I think we're all concerned," Dr Anderson said.

"It's a beautiful species.

"It means a lot to the community."

Rangers believe there are years where there are no new Morepork chicks being born. (Supplied: Parks Australia)

Last chance

The last hope for the Norfolk Island Morepork is to increase genetic diversity by integrating more New Zealand Morepork owls.

In New Zealand, the Morepork owl is listed as "not threatened" according to the local Department of Conservation.

Community consultations with the Norfolk Island community have already been completed.

However, more work still needs to be done before the translocation can happen, including talks with the Maori people as the traditional custodians and with various environmental agencies for any potential biosecurity risks.

A Parks Australia spokesperson said "substantial ecological, genetic and practical challenges need to be addressed before it could proceed".

Dr Andersen said the Norfolk Island community had not lost hope.

"While I think everybody is concerned, there's a lot of hope because we have such an incredible group of passionate people both on the island and off the island, a lot of researchers and a lot of wonderful research partnerships that have seen so much success in the past," Dr Andersen said.

Embattled Sydney developer Bathla Group has secured a 12-month extension from the NSW Supreme Court to finalise construction projects, but it is dependent on securing additional funds from lenders.

World.title: How Matilda Scholz became a football powerhouse, feminist and TikTok sensation
World.content:
SportAFLAFLW How Matilda Scholz became a football powerhouse, feminist and TikTok sensation Kelli Underwood September 18, 2026 — 3:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matilda Scholz is a towering presence. At 189 centimetres she’s the third-tallest player in the AFLW. Matilda Scholz is a formidable physical presence. AFL Photos via Getty Images Throw in a ruthless streak on the footy field – and she can spell trouble for opponents. Former Port Adelaide coach Lauren Arnell recalled having to step in at training to separate Scholz and her veteran teammate Gemma Houghton.



Arnell had encouraged the players to bring their physicality to the session. Scholz started throwing her giant athletic frame around and Houghton took exception. Just as the scuffle began to escalate, Arnell rushed in to pull them apart. Neither was about to take a backward step. The coach described the fiery wrestle as a positive moment because the players found a greater level to challenge each other within training. It sparked an eight-game winning streak that led the Power all the way to the 2024 preliminary final. Scholz’s mum Peta has also had some nervous moments watching her eldest daughter play. “She was so much taller than anyone else when she was younger, and all the coaches were

yelling out, ‘stop the big girl, stop the big girl’. Matilda had no idea how strong she was.



“I would often stand there with my hands to my eyes and not be able to watch, fearful that Matilda would accidentally hurt someone. I just hoped all the other players would walk off without an injury. It was definitely hard to watch.” Peta Scholz (nee Squire) played netball for Australia. As a hard-working, smart wing defence, she won a World Cup and Commonwealth Games gold medal alongside champions of the game, including Liz Ellis and Sharelle McMahon. Peta Squire (left) in 2003 playing netball for Australia. Steve Holland “I miss playing netball. I wanted to win, I wanted to beat my opponent and I wanted to be the best there was as well,” she says. Matilda has inherited her mother’s white-line fever.



Her dad, David, recalls a game when she was just 10 playing for the Mitcham Hawks under-14s. “It was a game against the Henley Sharks. She was going OK in the ruck, and they just got into her. It was pretty brutal. They literally were targeting her, jumping into her, running into her to stop her getting the ball. Anyway, she reacted in a way which I feel like we see a fair bit today – where it actually fires her up a bit. It was almost like a moment for me watching her and suddenly seeing a different kid. When she was pressed physically, she found another gear.” Scholz takes a mark. AFL Photos via Getty Images Scholz now bats away opposition players the way a cowboy swats flies. She has mastered the Dusty Martin “don’t argue”. In season 11, she’s on the cusp of becoming the game’s best player. She’ll need to dethrone Kangaroos champ Jasmine Garner to get there. The running ruck won her first All-Australian blazer last year. And at the halfway mark of the season, she’s on track to go back-to-back. On Saturday, she’ll be up against one of the AFLW’s most in-form talls, Swans ruck Ally Morphett.



But it’s not just Scholz’s footy attributes that stand out. It’s her marketability as well. Last month, the Power star graced the front cover of Women’s Health magazine. And she’s a social media darling, attracting the most followers on TikTok of all AFLW players. She’s in the top five on Instagram. Melbourne’s Tayla Harris is at No.1. She is outgoing, vivacious and self-assured. And a proud feminist. She’s gone from the reserved kid who bawled her eyes out before going on year 7 school camp to embracing life as a role model, visiting schools to educate kids about respectful relationships, domestic violence and gender equality. “Over the last few years, she’s developed a lot of clarity around what she wants to stand for. What’s important to her outside of football?” says David. Port star Matilda Scholz is unashamedly a feminist footballer. AFL Photos via Getty Images “We have these sorts of conversations about the Andrew Tates of the world and about the influence that him and others are having on Gen Z males. For example, our parents have a lot of antiquated ideas about females and what they should and shouldn’t do. But what we’re seeing now is being amplified in another generation. What I love about Matilda is she wants to be a role model to girls, but also to boys as well.”



And the Scholz family is quite the modern, blended family. David and Peta separated when Matilda was in year 5. Peta, a police officer, has been with her partner, Kate, for 10 years. They married in January. David has also re-partnered and has a three-year-old son, Ned. He’s the apple of Matilda’s eye. At Alberton home games, they sit together along with both sets of grandparents. And of course, there’s Poppy, Matilda’s younger sister, who was drafted to Carlton as a key defender but has made a name for herself kicking goals in the navy blue this year.



They are very different people and players but the best of friends. For now, their parents agree they’re better off playing at different clubs. Poppy Scholz plays for Carlton. Getty Images “I think, in time, definitely they’d love to play in the same team, and I’d like to see that too, maybe not now, but definitely in the future,” Peta says. This week Matilda signed a three-year extension that will see her remain at Alberton until the end of the 2030 season.

World.title: Thai suitcase murder suspect pleads not guilty to all charges
World.content:
Breaking WorldAsiaCourts Thai suitcase murder suspect pleads not guilty to all charges Zach Hope September 18, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content Pattaya: Australian Simon Peter Carman has pleaded not guilty to murdering a Thai teenager and hiding her body in a suitcase. Carman, 45, is accused of picking up 17-year-old Thanchanok Donhomla for sex at about 3am on June 25 and taking her back to his unit on the outskirts of coastal Pattaya, about 150 kilometres south of Bangkok, before killing her and stuffing her slender frame into one of his suitcases. Australian Simon Peter Carman, 45, after his arrest in Thailand. TPBS via AP He is charged with intentionally killing a person, concealing a body and two charges relating to taking a minor for indecent acts.



At his first court appearance, in Pattaya on Friday, Carman said he had been on a long walk near the beach and wanted to go home to sleep, but Thanchanok had followed him. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Australian murder suspect shopped, did laundry while girl’s body lay in suitcase, say police He insisted the pair never had sex and claimed Thanchanok asked for money and grabbed a knife from the kitchen when he didn’t have what she wanted, pointing it at his throat. He pleaded not guilty to all charges. The case will return to court on October 12. Carman has been detained since he was intercepted by immigration officials the night after the alleged murder, just minutes before boarding a flight to Australia at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi airport.



Much of his time in custody has been spent without legal representation. Related Article Thailand ‘She wanted to see the beach’: Family grieves for teen killed in alleged suitcase murder Outside court, appearing gaunt, Carman said he had been assaulted twice in prison by inmates, lost about 30 kilograms, and had barely slept for months. He said he was given a state-appointed lawyer only three weeks ago, despite, he claimed, having asked for one through the Australian embassy about two weeks after his arrest. In June, police released CCTV footage from Carman’s multi-tower complex in Jomtien that captured him doing laundry and picking up food before leaving with a suitcase later that night. More CCTV of him driving through the streets with the suitcase strapped to the back of his rented scooter, before returning without it. Police later found Thanchanok’s concealed body in long grass near railway tracks.



The Ballarat-born, long-term resident of Thailand initially told the arresting officials at the airport that scratches on his body were the result of a fight with a friend, Pattaya City Police Colonel Anek Srathongyoo previously told this masthead. But when he was confronted with the security footage, Srathongyoo said Carman admitted to unintentionally killing the 17-year-old in a struggle after she had come at him with a knife. Though never confirmed by investigators, local media reported the pair argued over the equivalent of just $20. Thanchanok, nicknamed Nong Cake, had travelled close to 600 kilometres from the north-east province of Kalasin only a week before her death on what her family insisted was a holiday to see friends.



The judge suppressed this masthead and the ABC, the only media inside the Pattaya courtroom, from reporting Carman’s emotional testimony in detail. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Gus says he’s ‘the next Cody Walker’. Is Trindall also the NRL’s best value playmaker?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Gus says he’s ‘the next Cody Walker’. Is Trindall also the NRL’s best value playmaker? Dan Walsh September 18, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the final minutes of a run-of-the-mill Sunday afternoon game at Shark Park in early June, Phil Gould, in commentary, saw something in a late try from Braydon Trindall that piqued his interest. “Braydon Trindall will be the next Cody Walker,” Gould opined after the Sharks five-eighth dummied his way over for a 77th-minute try in Cronulla’s comfortable 34-12 win over the Dragons. It’s tricky: Sharks star Braydon Trindall. Oscar Colman “His best football is way in front of him. Cody Walker didn’t debut until he was 26. Trindall is going to be a really dominant player when he gets to the back end of his 20s, and into his early 30s when most of the playmakers are excelling these days. “I won’t be around, but mark my words, he’s going to be a dominant playmaker in this competition for a long time. He’s only just getting started.”



Consider the words marked. But also consider Trindall – back from a dislocated shoulder, grimacing through every moment of contact and all 80 minutes against the Cowboys last week – a dominant playmaker. Ahead of Saturday’s sudden-death showdown with the Roosters, consider the prodigious No.6 Cronulla’s most influential figure. Tricks of the trade with Braydon Trindall. Edwina Pickles Across the remaining finals teams, the offensive linchpins and most important players are obvious. Nathan Cleary at Penrith. Newcastle, Kalyn Ponga. For the Roosters, while Sam Walker is injured, it’s James Tedesco. Isaiya Katoa is the Dolphins’ main man. The Warriors are a fascinating outlier because you could argue captain and spiritual leader James Fisher-Harris is their key, or even underrated attacking figures Wayde Egan and Erin Clark. But Trindall’s recent absence at the Sharks has only rammed home the unavoidable.



The 27-year-old is the single most indispensable player in their attack, and on a salary of about $700,000 a year, does so at excellent value. Of those key playmakers, the likes of Cleary, Ponga, Walker and Tedesco all earn $1 million and above, while at Cronulla, Nicho Hynes and Addin Fonua-Blake pull in seven-figure pay packets, too. Trindall leads the NRL with 31 try-assists this season despite his injury lay-off. But in his return against North Queensland, the rest of rugby league met the “Tricky” Cronulla teammates know all too well. “Oh, I never once doubted that he was playing,” co-captain Blayke Brailey said with a laugh.

World.title: Anaesthetics over aesthetics: welcome to rugby league’s painkiller knockouts
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Anaesthetics over aesthetics: welcome to rugby league’s painkiller knockouts Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist September 18, 2026 — 3:30pm

September 18, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A





Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios. Marijan Murat/Picture Alliance via Getty Images If we compared how many ex-athletes have harmful long-term addictions to painkillers to how many develop a cocaine habit, we might re-think what’s legal and what’s not. The World Anti-Doping Authority (WADA) makes an exemption for “therapeutic use” of drugs that might otherwise be illegal. These include drugs for conditions ranging from asthma to acne as well as potentially addictive painkillers. The rationale, according to WADA, is that “there are no reasonable, permitted, alternative treatments available” and “the substance does not enhance performance, it just brings the athlete back to normal health.” This is, for want of a better word, warped. Of course there are no alternative treatments: this is why injuries are injuries. They hurt. You can only play with injuries by numbing the pain. As for “not enhancing performance”, let me suggest that an athlete who can run and pass and kick with the help of painkillers is enjoying a more enhanced performance than if he was lying on his couch watching – which is what, for the sake of his “normal health”, he should be doing. And what is a drug addict doing if not taking a substance to feel “normal”? The therapeutic exemption for strong painkillers exposes the arbitrariness of deciding which drugs are banned and which are allowed. Cocaine enhances no-one’s performance unless they take it on the field – it acts quickly and then stops. Since Diego Maradona’s time, no top athletes have been spotted having a bump during play. This is not to say anything positive about cocaine, just that it’s not a performance-enhancing drug. Likewise, cannabinoids are on the banned list even though the only Olympian who performs better for having it in their system is Snoop Dogg. Interestingly, many ex-athletes are using cannabis, legally, for pain management after they have retired. Yet, it has no exemption while they are still playing.



Diego Maradona holds up his team’s trophy after Argentina’s 3-2 victory over West Germany at the World Cup final soccer match at Atzeca Stadium in Mexico City 1986. AP Painkiller abuse is sport’s biggest dirtiest secret, and it starts with prescribed, approved painkiller use. There is a distressingly long list of athletes who have begun using them while playing and then, unable to stop, have their lives wrecked by them in retirement. If harm were the true criterion by which drugs were made illegal, the list of “therapeutic exemptions” would look very different. And when it comes to “drug cheating”, painkillers are a lot closer to obtaining a pharmaceutical advantage than smoking a joint or snorting a line on holidays. Related Article NRL 2026 Gus says he’s ‘the next Cody Walker’. Is Trindall also the NRL’s best value playmaker? But … it’s the finals! We want to see Cleary, Yeo, Trindall, Walker and all those players who are being “brought back to normal health” with the help of pills and potions. If painkillers were illegal, we might not get the star power or the Cronkish legends of drug-fuelled heroics. If rugby league players were not allowed to get needled up to play, then the winners would have an asterisk over them because so many injured stars would be missing. Yet, we tolerate a different kind of asterisk. We encourage footballers to play like there’s no tomorrow. We allow rules that call this “bringing them back to normal health”, so they can legally take dangerous substances. Among all the offerings that athletes make and that we ask of them, the trading away of their long-term health is the one that comes with the biggest asterisk and the deepest regrets. There’s nothing heroic about getting shot up with chemicals to play with a broken body; it’s just a legalised form of human sacrifice that shows the inconsistencies in our rules about drugs in sport. World.title: Teen facing 30 extremist charges after FBI tip-off
World.content:
A Queensland teen allegedly operated several social media accounts to post extremist material that supported violence against migrants and people of both Islamic and Jewish faith. Federal investigators say they were tipped off by the FBI about an Australian who was posting extremist content on social media advocating for violence and referencing terrorist attacks, leading to the teen’s arrest. Police raided a home in Warner, north of Brisbane, in May and seized several devices they will allege were used to commit the crimes. The teenager was arrested in May. AFP The 18-year-old, was charged with 28 offences related to posting extremist material online, one count of using a carriage service to menace or harass, and one count of possessing child abuse material.



He has been remanded in custody since May 27. The matter was briefly heard in the Pine Rivers Magistrates Court, where the teenager did not appear. His lawyer said there would be no application for bail. Later, a neighbour, who cannot be named, said news of the arrest was shocking. “[It was] pretty shocking to see it on the community page and it’s really close to home,” she said.



She said it was worrying her son went to school with the accused teenager. “They go to school, they’re in the neighbourhood, and the FBI was the one that tipped the government off,” she said. When asked about the teenager’s charges, the woman said: “It’s terrible. Ever since Bondi – you wouldn’t think it would happen somewhere else but it’s in our suburbs.” Magistrate Michelle Howard ordered for a brief of evidence to be supplied by late October. The case was adjourned to November. Spokespeople from both the AFP and the FBI have lauded the arrest, which they said came from a memorandum of understanding signed by the agencies.



“As our adversaries become more agile across borders in the online space, so must we as law enforcement and intelligence agencies,” the FBI’s Ryan Maxwell said. Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington declined to comment on the specifics of the case before the courts, but said the state government had cracked down on violent extremism. “I have stood shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish community here in Queensland,” she told reporters on Friday morning. “Every community, including the Muslim community, are respected and loved by all other Queenslanders, and there is no place in Queensland for this type of extremism.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How Matilda Scholz became a football powerhouse, feminist and TikTok sensation
World.content:
SportAFLAFLW How Matilda Scholz became a football powerhouse, feminist and TikTok sensation Kelli Underwood September 18, 2026 — 3:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matilda Scholz is a towering presence. At 189 centimetres she’s the third-tallest player in the AFLW. Matilda Scholz is a formidable physical presence. AFL Photos via Getty Images Throw in a ruthless streak on the footy field – and she can spell trouble for opponents. Former Port Adelaide coach Lauren Arnell recalled having to step in at training to separate Scholz and her veteran teammate Gemma Houghton.



Arnell had encouraged the players to bring their physicality to the session. Scholz started throwing her giant athletic frame around and Houghton took exception. Just as the scuffle began to escalate, Arnell rushed in to pull them apart. Neither was about to take a backward step. The coach described the fiery wrestle as a positive moment because the players found a greater level to challenge each other within training. It sparked an eight-game winning streak that led the Power all the way to the 2024 preliminary final. Scholz’s mum Peta has also had some nervous moments watching her eldest daughter play. “She was so much taller than anyone else when she was younger, and all the coaches were

yelling out, ‘stop the big girl, stop the big girl’. Matilda had no idea how strong she was.



“I would often stand there with my hands to my eyes and not be able to watch, fearful that Matilda would accidentally hurt someone. I just hoped all the other players would walk off without an injury. It was definitely hard to watch.” Peta Scholz (nee Squire) played netball for Australia. As a hard-working, smart wing defence, she won a World Cup and Commonwealth Games gold medal alongside champions of the game, including Liz Ellis and Sharelle McMahon. Peta Squire (left) in 2003 playing netball for Australia. Steve Holland “I miss playing netball. I wanted to win, I wanted to beat my opponent and I wanted to be the best there was as well,” she says. Matilda has inherited her mother’s white-line fever.



Her dad, David, recalls a game when she was just 10 playing for the Mitcham Hawks under-14s. “It was a game against the Henley Sharks. She was going OK in the ruck, and they just got into her. It was pretty brutal. They literally were targeting her, jumping into her, running into her to stop her getting the ball. Anyway, she reacted in a way which I feel like we see a fair bit today – where it actually fires her up a bit. It was almost like a moment for me watching her and suddenly seeing a different kid. When she was pressed physically, she found another gear.” Scholz takes a mark. AFL Photos via Getty Images Scholz now bats away opposition players the way a cowboy swats flies. She has mastered the Dusty Martin “don’t argue”. In season 11, she’s on the cusp of becoming the game’s best player. She’ll need to dethrone Kangaroos champ Jasmine Garner to get there. The running ruck won her first All-Australian blazer last year. And at the halfway mark of the season, she’s on track to go back-to-back. On Saturday, she’ll be up against one of the AFLW’s most in-form talls, Swans ruck Ally Morphett.



But it’s not just Scholz’s footy attributes that stand out. It’s her marketability as well. Last month, the Power star graced the front cover of Women’s Health magazine. And she’s a social media darling, attracting the most followers on TikTok of all AFLW players. She’s in the top five on Instagram. Melbourne’s Tayla Harris is at No.1. She is outgoing, vivacious and self-assured. And a proud feminist. She’s gone from the reserved kid who bawled her eyes out before going on year 7 school camp to embracing life as a role model, visiting schools to educate kids about respectful relationships, domestic violence and gender equality. “Over the last few years, she’s developed a lot of clarity around what she wants to stand for. What’s important to her outside of football?” says David. Port star Matilda Scholz is unashamedly a feminist footballer. AFL Photos via Getty Images “We have these sorts of conversations about the Andrew Tates of the world and about the influence that him and others are having on Gen Z males. For example, our parents have a lot of antiquated ideas about females and what they should and shouldn’t do. But what we’re seeing now is being amplified in another generation. What I love about Matilda is she wants to be a role model to girls, but also to boys as well.”



And the Scholz family is quite the modern, blended family. David and Peta separated when Matilda was in year 5. Peta, a police officer, has been with her partner, Kate, for 10 years. They married in January. David has also re-partnered and has a three-year-old son, Ned. He’s the apple of Matilda’s eye. At Alberton home games, they sit together along with both sets of grandparents. And of course, there’s Poppy, Matilda’s younger sister, who was drafted to Carlton as a key defender but has made a name for herself kicking goals in the navy blue this year.



They are very different people and players but the best of friends. For now, their parents agree they’re better off playing at different clubs. Poppy Scholz plays for Carlton. Getty Images “I think, in time, definitely they’d love to play in the same team, and I’d like to see that too, maybe not now, but definitely in the future,” Peta says. This week Matilda signed a three-year extension that will see her remain at Alberton until the end of the 2030 season.

Warning: This story contains graphic content Pattaya: Australian Simon Peter Carman has pleaded not guilty to murdering a Thai teenager and hiding her body in a suitcase. Australian Simon Peter Carman, 45, after his arrest in Thailand. TPBS via AP He is charged with intentionally killing a person, concealing a body and two charges relating to taking a minor for indecent acts.



At his first court appearance, in Pattaya on Friday, Carman said he had been on a long walk near the beach and wanted to go home to sleep, but Thanchanok had followed him. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Australian murder suspect shopped, did laundry while girl’s body lay in suitcase, say police He insisted the pair never had sex and claimed Thanchanok asked for money and grabbed a knife from the kitchen when he didn’t have what she wanted, pointing it at his throat. He pleaded not guilty to all charges. The case will return to court on October 12. Carman has been detained since he was intercepted by immigration officials the night after the alleged murder, just minutes before boarding a flight to Australia at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi airport.



Much of his time in custody has been spent without legal representation. Related Article Thailand ‘She wanted to see the beach’: Family grieves for teen killed in alleged suitcase murder Outside court, appearing gaunt, Carman said he had been assaulted twice in prison by inmates, lost about 30 kilograms, and had barely slept for months. He said he was given a state-appointed lawyer only three weeks ago, despite, he claimed, having asked for one through the Australian embassy about two weeks after his arrest. In June, police released CCTV footage from Carman’s multi-tower complex in Jomtien that captured him doing laundry and picking up food before leaving with a suitcase later that night. More CCTV of him driving through the streets with the suitcase strapped to the back of his rented scooter, before returning without it. Police later found Thanchanok’s concealed body in long grass near railway tracks.



The Ballarat-born, long-term resident of Thailand initially told the arresting officials at the airport that scratches on his body were the result of a fight with a friend, Pattaya City Police Colonel Anek Srathongyoo previously told this masthead. But when he was confronted with the security footage, Srathongyoo said Carman admitted to unintentionally killing the 17-year-old in a struggle after she had come at him with a knife. Though never confirmed by investigators, local media reported the pair argued over the equivalent of just $20. Thanchanok, nicknamed Nong Cake, had travelled close to 600 kilometres from the north-east province of Kalasin only a week before her death on what her family insisted was a holiday to see friends.



The judge suppressed this masthead and the ABC, the only media inside the Pattaya courtroom, from reporting Carman’s emotional testimony in detail. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
