Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington declined to comment on the specifics of the case before the courts, but said the state government had cracked down on violent extremism. “I have stood shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish community here in Queensland,” she told reporters on Friday morning. “Every community, including the Muslim community, are respected and loved by all other Queenslanders, and there is no place in Queensland for this type of extremism.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: 'A real degree of nastiness' and the need for respect: Andrew Bayly on politics
World.content:
Outgoing National Party MP Andrew Bayly (Port Waikato) knows better than most the highs and lows of public office. In his valedictory speech on Wednesday he described his resignation from cabinet as one of the most brutal experiences of his life.

Parliament exit interview: Andrew Bayly The House Download MP3 6m

After his farewell speech, he joined us to reflect on the good, the bad, and the ugly of being an MP, and how social media has changed the dynamic, bringing with it a "real degree of nastiness".

He recalled an incident from early in his parliamentary career, when The Post published a story about an accident involving his brother when Bayly was just 15 or 16. The incident was decades old, but the story was published under the headline "MP Shoots Brother".

Bayly said members of the public questioned why the incident was being revisited, and the newspaper eventually took the story down, but believes the media environment has gotten worse since.

"Today, I'd be beset not only by the media here in Parliament, but also on social media. I would just be brutalised."

He thinks increasing personal attacks and even threats are a deterrent to attracting talented people into politics.

"If we want good people [to leave] nice, secure jobs and an easier life and come into this demanding life in politics, it's increasingly becoming a much harder sell, because why would you do it?"

Asked what pastoral support was available to MPs, his response was fairly blunt: "Very little."

Bayly said politicians had to find their own ways of dealing with the pressure, and that in those moments, support from colleagues was particularly important.

He said the cohort of National MPs who also entered Parliament in 2014 used to meet regularly and decompress together, providing a relaxed environment to share their experiences and laugh things off. Only five of the initial ten remain and two more retire this election (Bayly and Shane Reti).

Particularly difficult periods, like his resignation from Cabinet, were managed by keeping busy. Alongside other passion projects, he began writing a book, which he hopes to publish soon.

He says it pays to have hobbies as an MP. For some, this could be knitting or playing the piano. Bayly's own hobbies aren't exactly restful - he's known to be keen on mountaineering, tramping and endurance racing.

It is fitting, then, that one passion project bridges his political and intrepid foci. In 2019 he dedicated significant time to establishing the Antarctic Parliamentarians Assembly in London.

"I look back and think, …that's a piece of history that I've created. Those are the type of things you've just got to get on and do."

I asked Bayly what he'll miss most about being an MP. He tells me it's being in the midst of the action.

"This is where it happens," he muses. "I came from a business background [where] you do a big deal, and it's reported in the paper, but it's nothing like Parliament."

Beyond the buzz, Bayly will also miss the people. He has developed friendships across the House, mostly through time spent together on select committees.

"You get to see who's really good, who's diligent, who reads the papers, who's got intellectual heft and is actually across the select committee. You get very close relationships with people."

Given the belligerence of events like Question Time, especially close to an election, the perception is that Parliament is intrinsically antagonistic, but Bayly says that's not accurate.

He believes however that MPs need to be more tolerant of different perspectives.

"Every MP here is here for the right reason. They want to do good. It's just that people have different perspectives, and actually sometimes we should just respect their perspective. Not everyone's wrong and not everyone's right. Sometimes we just need to say - what you've said there, there's a kernel of something that's really helpful and useful, and as a country, it would be better if we actually started talking about that."

For Bayly, the ability to work across differences is an important part of a functioning Parliament.

"Outside of the election period [which] is confrontational, having that [respectful] approach, makes a good parliament, it makes good democracy, and that's how we're going to move New Zealand forward."

World.title: Hamilton arrest fuels critics' concerns over citizen's arrest
World.content:
Teen in court after citizens arrest goes too far Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

It's a scenario critics of citizen's arrests say they've feared all along with untrained members of the public detaining people.

Now, a 19-year-old has appeared in court after an alleged arrest in Hamilton went too far.

This comes just weeks after new laws came into effect allowing anyone to use reasonable force to hold someone they suspect has committed a crime.

Police were called to a business on Victoria Street around 5.15pm on Saturday following reports of shoplifting.

When officers arrived, Hamilton City Area Commander inspector Scott Miller said they found the suspected shoplifter detained.

Police alleged the person who detained the suspected shoplifter also assaulted them.

A 19-year-old had been charged with common assault and appeared in the Hamilton District Court today, while police said the suspected shoplifter would go through the youth justice process.

Retail NZ spokesperson Carolyn Young. Supplied

Retail NZ spokesperson Carolyn Young said her organisation had always been concerned about allowing anyone to use reasonable force when making a citizen's arrest.

"A citizen like you or I, I don't have any training. I have no capacity other than anything I see on TV and that's probably not very realistic, right?

"So being able to understand how you would react in the moment to a situation that is probably inflamed, at a heightened sense of anxiety. Understanding what would be the appropriate thing to do in that situation comes from training."

She said de-escalation was the most important thing, and that meant making sure you get enough information to report the crime, keeping yourself and others safe, and letting police deal with the matter.

"If you don't have the right level of training, you won't know necessarily if you've crossed the line and it looks like in this situation there's a question mark around whether that happened."

Human rights lawyer Michael Bott. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Human rights lawyer Michael Bott said staying within the law when making an arrest could be extremely nuanced for an untrained civilian.

"The police have particular training in terms of the use of force and proportionality, whereas the public don't. And so they've been given this carte blanche power and they haven't got the skills to do the job. It's dangerous."

Bott said the law allowing civilian arrests was appalling.

"The power itself is extremely loosely worded and it's fraught with difficulty and you can see that people will tragically get it wrong."

He wondered what will happen if the suspected shoplifter in the Hamilton incident was innocent, and there was a mistake.

"Does that mean that there's going to be some kind of kidnapping where the person was prevented unreasonably from exiting a building or exiting a street? Because some well-meaning shopkeeper or their staff, believe without reasonable evidence that they've committed the crime and they hadn't.

"Similarly, you can easily imagine a situation where unreasonable force is applied, and the person who is suspected of being a thief is in fact the victim of an assault, and they could be justified in using reasonable force and self-defence.

"So you have an escalation in terms of potential for violence due to the landscape that's being created by rushed legislation."

Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said he stood by the policy, which was an extension of previous citizens arrest powers - where they were allowed at night and when more serious offences were suspected.

"We passed a law and we expect people to follow that law. The clear directions in that is if the situation is appropriate, people can hang on to somebody and then call the police and follow the instructions of the police."

World.title: Tauranga teen urges government to give youth a greater say over social media ban
World.content:
A Tauranga teen is urging the government to set up a youth advisory committee to give the country's rangatahi more of a say in political decision-making.

Ōtūmoetai College student Liam Howard recently surveyed his peers about the proposed social media ban for under-sixteens, and got almost 600 responses.

The 15-year-old told Checkpoint that about two thirds of respondents opposed the ban.

"They mainly had concerns about losing contact with family and friends, but they were also worried about losing their community, because a lot of people belong to communities that they can't find - especially in rural areas - when they're not in particularly safe households, and they find that refuge online."

He personally spent about two hours a day on social media platforms like TikTok, and had himself been exposed to content he'd rather not have seen.

"Once this is introduced it's going to be very hard to change, and that's why we need to make sure that it actually will help youth rather than giving them an even worse situation where they can't talk to anyone about the problems they face when they do get on to social media," he said.

The current proposal "was just giving the companies leeway out of their responsibilities to manage their algorithms properly", he told Checkpoint.

Teen surveys hundreds of peers on the proposed social media ban Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Companies needed to ensure they were not showing predatory content, "whether that be this manosphere that's been happening online, or content that's giving them anxiety or hurting their self-confidence", he said.

Howard said a youth advisory committee could work by surveying students to discover their views.

"We need the actual data to make an informed response, we can't just base it on opinions."

Initially, he believed the committee should focus on the proposed social media ban. There was potential for expanding it to address other legislation if it went well though, he said.

It would be difficult to set up a committee with non-partisan members, so Howard suggested it be made up of people with views from across the political spectrum.

That would help the nation's youth feel like politicians were actually listening, he said.

"I don't think this government has been particularly responsive to students.

"[Education Minister] Erica Stanford says she talked to 13 students - that's not enough. I've talked to 600, they've told me the truth," he said.

At the end of July, Stanford posted on social media, saying she had "invited 13 students from across Auckland to sit down with me and share their experiences of social media and online harm".

Ōtūmoetai College student Liam Howard says most of the students he surveyed opposed the social media ban. Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via AFP

National and Labour back proposal

National has indicated it will move forward with its proposed ban on social media for under-sixteens.

Current coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill, while Labour had said it will support it.

In August, Stanford said the bill would bring New Zealand into line with other countries that were placing greater responsibility on tech companies to protect children online.

"The bill places legal obligations on platforms. No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.

"It doesn't just introduce a minimum age requirement. It creates an enduring framework that can evolve alongside technology and holds platforms responsible for understanding and reducing the risks they create for children."

World.title: Major property developer doubts Auckland CBD height removal will prompt short-term building
World.content:
Removing Auckland CBD height limits won't work - Residential CEO Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A major Auckland property developer says a government proposal to remove building height restrictions in the CBD is just politics and he doesn't believe there will be a single new apartment built in the short term because of the change.

Under current rules, parts of the Auckland CBD have building height limits of 72.5 metres - in other areas the limit is 35 metres.

The proposal would remove these caps for the majority of the central city and scrap other rules about how big and far apart buildings have to be.

RMA Minister Chris Bishop said that current CBD planning rules are holding back growth.

"The modelling suggests that these changes are potentially very significant. At full uptake, annual GDP is expected to increase by $1.87 billion.

"Tens of thousands of new homes in the city centre, tens of thousands of new jobs in the city centre."

Bishop commissioned a report on the planning rules, which was released today.

Its recommendations include removing height and dimension limits on high-rise buildings, and removing the heritage status of what the report refers to as "non-contributing sites" within the historic Karangahape Rd precinct.

The report estimated the changes will provide about 17,000 more dwellings in the city, and 20.3 million square metres more floor space.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the changes will help to capitalise on the newly opened $5.5 billion City Rail Link.

"I think now is the opportunity to ensure that Auckland is shaped by that investment, prioritising more growth in our city where our new CRL stations are just a stone's throw away."

Developer Mark Todd, of Ockham Residential, said getting rid of height restrictions and pesky regulations downtown is all well and good, but it's not what's holding back vertical housing in the city.

"There is just this myth that if I just tweak the regulations, Auckland CBD will just suddenly start sprouting apartments," he said.

"It's not going to go vertical until there's some incentives. Enablement is good, but it's not enough. That's the key issue here.

"These are political announcements. Auckland's got enough vertically-zoned land for the rest of the century - easily."

The problem, Todd said, is the lack of people living there.

"Auckland has got less than half the residents than it should have in its CBD if you benchmark it with comparable international cities. This won't result in a single new apartment being built down there."

Todd said there won't be large-scale mixed-used developments around the CRL without local and national government support.

"You've just had 20 years proving the private sector isn't going to build you apartments in the CBD to leverage the billions of dollars we've invested.

"It's one of the most beautiful CBDs in the world - The Victoria St green belt has just been completed, amazing. CRL, amazing. Quay St, amazing, beautiful. Wynyard Quarter, Britomart, amazing.

"We've been waiting for 20 years for the people to come. It's not happening and why is that? Because policy settings are wrong."

Todd said he's never constructed a building in the CBD and is just speaking as an Aucklander.

The government's proposal is being welcomed by others in the sector.

Property Council chief executive Leonie Freeman said it's a positive step for the city, and timely given the opening of the CRL.

"So this isn't something that's going to change the Auckland skyline in the next five years, but in the next 30 to 50 years we will see greater growth, and I think that's a positive thing."

Thom Gill, from Cohausing Projects Limited, doubts there will be anything like the building activity that the policy says will be enabled, but he welcomes the government proposal.

"I think the ability to maximise the good opportunities of a particular site without having to worry about the building height [and] all the more subjective things, in principle I think that is a good idea in a modern city."

However, Gill opposed allowing high rises around Karangahape Rd, which he said is already a coherent urban environment.

World.title: South African police find a ninth woman's body near Johannesburg, serial killer fears grow
World.content:
Warning: This story contains details that may disturb some readers.

South African police said they found a ninth woman's body near Johannesburg on Thursday (local time) as they investigated a series of killings in the same area over the last two months.

Officers said the young woman appeared to be in the same age range as the other bodies, but stopped short of saying there was a definite link.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed "no stone will be left unturned" in the investigation into the deaths, which have caused widespread alarm.

The victims are mostly aged in their 20s or 30s, and some have been found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual violence.

Violence against women is one of the country's most entrenched social problems, despite years of government pledges to tackle it. The deaths have reignited anger over gender-based violence and poor public safety.

"I am feeling a lot of fear and paranoia, especially for us with daughters," said Nomgqibelo Tshabalala, a resident of the Ekurhuleni area east of Johannesburg where the bodies had been found.

"My daughter caught an Uber yesterday and I did not sleep worried and when I heard about this incident on the radio this morning I got even more scared."

The woman's body found on Thursday appeared to have been dumped there and the crime could have happened somewhere else, police said.

"We were called here this morning after the discovery of yet another body of a young woman," Deputy National Commissioner for Policing Tebello Mosikili said.

World.title: Nearly 1000 stalking warnings, 140 charges, but 0 convictions
World.content:
Nearly 1000 notices warning potential stalkers about their behaviour have been issued since new stalking and harassment laws came into effect earlier this year, along with 140 charges, but no convictions.

The Ministry of justice said 19 of the 140 charges had been finalised in court

The remaining 121 are progressing through the courts.

"All of the finalised charges were withdrawn; none have been convicted and sentenced," Sector Insights general manager Rebecca Parish said.

"Cases can take time to progress through the courts, and some charges may be withdrawn before reaching a final outcome," she said.

"The absence of convictions at this stage is not necessarily unexpected."

The new law came into effect in May and criminalises making unwanted, persistent, and repetitive intrusions into another person's life, causing serious psychological, social, and economic harm.

Police's Acting Director of Prevention, Inspector Natasha Allan, said those who engage in stalking and harassment should expect police action.

"We want people affected by stalking and harassment to know that they will be listened to, taken seriously, and supported. We encourage anyone experiencing this behaviour to report it to Police," she said.

"This behaviour is unacceptable and can have serious consequences for victims and their families."

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the government was sending a clear message to stalkers.

"For too long this insidious behaviour went unpunished, yet victims were left with often long-term side effects," he said.

"Our government is committed to fixing the basics in law and order, and this is a prime example of a gap in the law which made no sense."

The new law carried a maximum penalty of five years' in prison.

'Heartbreaking' for victims

Victim advocate Claire Buckley said she wasn't surprised by the lack of convictions.

Victim advocate Claire Buckley. (File photo) Supplied

"The stalking legislation was an excellent, excellent piece of legislation that needed to come in, but the police have been relatively reluctant initially to follow it through because, precedent setting, it's unusual, they don't quite know what form the stalking is required to meet the legislative bar, or to meet the bar for conviction," she said.

"It's gone through this whole process, and they're arresting, and they're putting people out for charges, but they haven't actually met the bar for criminal conviction, which means that then the charges get withdrawn."

Buckley said charges needed to be followed through.

"To me, that says that the police investigators on the front line are saying 'these guys people are terrifying their victims, they need to be stopped," she said.

"So the police are doing what they supposed to be doing, but then it falls down at the prosecution level."

She wanted to know why police prosecutors were not taking the next step.

"It's heartbreaking for the victim of those crimes to have their perpetrator arrested and then for that perpetrator to end up with absolutely no consequences."

Aotearoa Free From Stalking project lead Leonie Morris said the lack of convictions is "bizarre" and "disappointing".

"Obviously, between today and when the law was passed in May, there will be people who have broken the law and they need to be convicted," Morris said.

"This is all about keeping people safe from stalking, and it doesn't sound like that's happening at the moment."

She said more needed to be done to support the law.

"We need the online platforms to be regulated," she said.

"There's so much misogyny and racist messaging now on the online platforms that embolden stalkers, so that's a really important measure the government could take to help keep people safe."

One of the problems with the unregulated platforms was the use algorithms to determine what you see, Morris said.

She said tech companies should be required to clearly show how their algorithms work, what content they recommend, what they remove, and how complaints were handled.

Independent oversight was also needed and the companies should be required to actively make sure their products and services were safe by design, Morris said.

She was keen to see anti-stalking attitude campaigns.

"There's people that don't understand what stalking is, and they need to know what it is and how harmful it can be."

Morris said 50 percent of those who are stalked are in a family violence situation, and they could seek help from their local women's refuge.

"But if you its not somebody that you were or are in a family violence relationship with, then there isn't a fabulous, specialist stalking service that you can go to," she said.

"We need these other things to support the law, we don't want to live in a society where all we rely on is laws and possibly laws that people don't understand."

"We need to support people to understand how harmful stalking is, and if they're contemplating stalking, to get help," Morris said.

World.title: How the NRL's most underrated player explains the Knights
World.content:
In the modern rugby league landscape it's hard for any NRL player to be truly underrated.

Coverage of the game is more granular and intense than ever before and the rise of fantasy sports means every statistical contribution comes into focus, which makes it difficult for anyone to slide under the radar.

But Mat Croker, the man who explains how Newcastle have managed to find themselves in a sudden-death final against the Warriors on Sunday, has managed it after putting together a season of low-key excellence that makes him worthy of the title.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

The lock forward is the only Knight to have played every game this year and his ball-playing in the middle of the field is the straw that stirs the drink for their dynamic attack.

"I'm the link man to our halves and making sure our weapons out wide, guys like KP [Kalyn Ponga] and Braddy [Bradman Best] and Gags [Dane Gagai] get the ball if the cues are there in the defender," Croker said.

"If they're not, just go through the middle."

The 27-year-old makes his job sound simple, and maybe it is, but that's not the same as easy. If it was, someone else would be doing it.

Croker is a microcosm of Newcastle's turnaround from wooden spooners to the brink of the club's first preliminary final since 2013 because, like his team, he knows his strengths and has been empowered to play to them.

There are more explosive and dazzling players at the Knights but Croker's passing, communication and structure helps give them the opportunity to explode and dazzle. He is the rock on which you can build a church that worships attacking football.

Mat Croker has been a fixture at the back of the scrum for Newcastle. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

Newcastle lead the league in tries from their own half with 31. More than a quarter of those begin with Croker at first receiver, setting shape and creating time for the men outside him.

Like the other things Croker does well — chasing kicks, leading line speed in defence, slowing down the ruck — his impact in attack is a hard thing to quantify with numbers. But if you know what you're looking for, it becomes impossible to miss.

Sidelined halfback Dylan Brown believes it's invaluable and that Croker is part of the reason the Knights have been able to stay on their feet and make it to the second week of the finals despite a heavy injury toll.

Mat Croker has enjoyed the best season of his NRL career. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"He understands the game really well. His footy smarts, when to play it out the back and when to run — he knows he's not the biggest player on the field but he knows how to find a gap and he knows when the spine needs the ball," said Brown.

"We've had all these new players come in but we still have the core. We still have Mat Croker and Phoenix Crossland, they haven't changed all year, and the more the ball goes through their hands the easier it's going to be for the rest of the team.

"You need that. Every team needs those guys."

It's been a season of great improvement for Croker, who notched his 100th NRL game earlier this year.

Since his debut in 2021 he has been a solid contributor for the Knights and a good clubman who mainly came off the bench, starting just 13 of his 82 appearances prior to this year.

Mat Croker spent much of his early years coming off the bench. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

But after working closely with new coach Justin Holbrook and attack coach Steven Hales over the summer, Croker was given a chance to start in the club's trip to Las Vegas in Round 1.

He has since transformed from honest toiler to a genuine ball-playing lock, a coalfields remix of the sophisticated passing middle that every decent team needs.

"Ever since day one they've put a lot of responsibility on my shoulders and I'm really grateful they've done that because I think it's brought out the best football of my career," Croker said.

"Back in Vegas they backed a hunch and took a bit of a punt of me to start and I've had the luxury of starting every game since. That's a lot of faith and I try to repay it."

The greatest compliment you can pay a middle forward is to say "he's got a bit of footy in him" and Croker has proven he's got more than most.

Newcastle can progress to their first preliminary final since 2013 with a win on Sunday. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

The skills were always there, he just needed the chance to unlock them.

"Without being arrogant, I always felt like I had some skills with passing and I'm not a barnstorming forward, so I had to work around that and find other ways to improve," said Croker.

"The ability to pass and show and go was part of that — the cues, I've worked really hard with Halesy and Justo to see those.

"He's said the same thing to me for 28 games — if they're tight, move it, and if they're not go through it."

In sticking to that mantra, Croker has become to Newcastle what his opposite number on Sunday, reigning Dally M Lock of the Year Erin Clark, is to the Warriors or what Cameron Murray is to last week's vanquished foes, South Sydney.

Croker had a strong game in that one, leading the way for Newcastle's depleted pack by holding the middle together and making 42 tackles without a miss, and says he was inspired by the prospect of taking on Murray.

"I was coming up against a good 13 in Cameron Murray, who's one of the best players in the whole competition," Croker said.

How Knights finals rookie shut down Souths Newcastle was not short of heroes in its sudden-death finals win over South Sydney, but no player stood taller than 21-year-old backrower and play-off debutant Jermaine McEwen.

"I'm not saying I played over him but I knew I had a big challenge because we play similar roles and I tried to embrace that challenge without the two front-rowers I've beside me all year.

"I had to use my leadership a bit more and I'm proud of how I did it."

Repeating the dose against Clark and the Warriors in front of 50,000 fans at Eden Park is a tall order but few dare write the Knights off.

They're dangerous because they've had a whole season of learning how to play to their strengths, like they did against South Sydney and like Croker has all year to become the NRL's hidden gem.

If they pull off the upset, look for Croker at the heart of it and if he is he sure won't stay underrated for long.

World.title: Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Ryan is the most eyebrow-raising omission from Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players, for games against Brazil in Brisbane on September 25 and Townsville on September 28.

The 34-year-old lost his starting spot to young goalkeeper Patrick Beach at the World Cup, then was bizarrely substituted on for the round-of-32 penalty shootout against Egypt.

The Socceroos skipper, capped 105 times, said after that loss he was only told he might replace Beach as extra time kicked off, though Popovic has since insisted Ryan knew that was a possibility pre-match.

Tony Popovic's Socceroos are set to face Brazil in Brisbane and Townsville. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Levante goalkeeper Ryan has been omitted despite a strong start to the La Liga season.

"We know what Maty Ryan is to Australian football," Popovic said.

"A player that has a distinguished career, continues to have one, over 100 caps.

"But we'd like to have a look at another keeper."

Pressed on how Ryan, who the Socceroos boss also dropped in his first games in charge in 2024, had taken the omission, Popovic said: "He's good.

"He's the ultimate professional that he is, and that's why he's had such a distinguished career.

"He's still available for us, and he's certainly not out of the picture moving forward."

Uncapped St Mirren goalkeeper Jacob Chapman replaces Ryan, joining Beach and Paul Izzo in the squad.

Untried left-back Kasey Bos, younger brother of injured star Jordan Bos, has been called up along with fellow untested defender Dylan Leonard, 19.

Former A-League sensations Marcus Younis (Brondby IF) and Eli Adams (Gamba Osaka) earn maiden call-ups alongside Kealey Adamson (QPR), Chapman and Yaya Dukuly (NK Celje) after impressive stints overseas.

"They've been rewarded for the hard work they've put in to get an opportunity overseas," Popovic said.

"They've had to go through the struggles when you go outside of your comfort zone.

"You go through the ups and downs; not playing, playing, injuries, and that helps you grow.

"And these players get mentally tougher; they know how to handle the difficult situations in games, and I believe they all deserve an opportunity."

Sixteen players from the 26-man World Cup squad return.

Star left-back Jordan Bos (knee) and central defender Cam Burgess (Achilles) are unavailable.

Court battle looms for Socceroos star Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle as the Socceroos star's lawyer confirms he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

Cristian Volpato (hamstring) is sidelined with injury.

The Sassuolo attacker was last week fined $722 for driving with cocaine in his system in July. Volpato has maintained his innocence and will challenge the charges in court.

Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek return after missing the World Cup through injury while Alex Robertson has been recalled.

Cameron Devlin, Nishan Velupillay, Mathew Leckie, Ajdin Hrustic, Kai Trewin and Awer Mabil have been omitted.

Aziz Behich is the only A-League Men player in the squad.

The Socceroos could have played up to four games this window but have settled for two, which Popovic said allowed players to get back to their clubs.

"We feel that with the games in November, we'll be ready for the Asian Cup," he said.

World.title: A-League season start under threat with referees on strike
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It is seemingly a rare occurrence indeed that Australian football does not find itself in some degree of turmoil.

So it is perhaps of little surprise that as the A-League Men's and Women's seasons fast approach, the code is once again lurching towards another crisis.

The nations top referees have been on strike since September 4, citing "significant changes to the elite refereeing structure" proposed by Football Australia (FA).

The change would see the referees contracted directly by the league, instead of FA.

The Professional Football Referees Association (PFRA) says those changes would be "detrimental to individual referees and represent a drastic step backwards for the professional refereeing program".

The A-League seasons begin in four weeks. And the parties are, as things stand, at something of a stalemate.

The APL and FA have all told ABC Sport they are continuing to work together with the aim of reaching a resolution.

The referee's body said in a statement earlier this month that it would "continue to engage with Football Australia with the aim of resolving the outstanding matters and returning its members to the field as soon as an acceptable outcome can be reached".

As players and supporters at all levels know, without referees there can be no game, so how have we got here?

Who runs the A-Leagues?

The A-League Men and A-League Women seasons get underway in mid-October. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

To get into the weeds of this dispute, we can go back to the 2020 decision to decouple the A-League from Football Australia.

FA relinquished full control to a newly formed body, the Australian Professional Leagues, after a long period of agitation from both the clubs and world body FIFA about governance issues within the game.

In practice, this meant handing over the commercial reins of the A-Leagues to the clubs, in line with many other professional football leagues around the world, such as the Premier League, Bundesliga and J-League, among others.

The clubs believed the separation from the national governing body would help the competition's long-term viability.

The reality has been somewhat different.

In 2024, half of A-League Men players said they were "dissatisfied" with how the competition had been managed by the APL, and close to half said they had "low trust" in whether it could improve the league.

That same year, APL slashed the annual distribution to the clubs from close to $2 million to just $530,000 on account of an increasingly worrying financial outlook.

That followed a frankly disastrous plan to sell off grand finals to Sydney and rapidly declining interest and attendances.

Since then, the stalled expansion drive and the removal of failed club Western United and last month's breakdown of talks between the league and the players over the collective bargaining agreement have added to an environment of intense distrust.

Why are the referees on strike?

The referees are not striking about on-field behaviour. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Since the league unbundled from Football Australia, the sport's governing body has still provided the referees to the league, with the APL reimbursing FA for those costs.

Now, Football Australia has proposed that it will only pay for matches that come under their jurisdiction: the Australia Cup and Australian Championship.

That means the APL has to pay the referees to officiate its competitions directly, which FA says is the APL's responsibility under the contract it has signed with the league.

However, this is one of the issues that the PFRA has railed against, arguing in essence it would be a conflict of interest to officiate the clubs, who are in effect their employers.

"Such an arrangement would place referees in an unacceptable position of potential conflict and raise serious concerns regarding the integrity and impartiality of the refereeing program," the PFRA said in a statement.

The referees would prefer the formation of an independent referees body, as is the case in England with Pro Ref, formerly known as PGMOL.

The PFRA added that the proposed structure was "untenable" and that referees "cannot grow without trust [or] succeed without independence".

Football Australia said there were no issues around the integrity with their proposal, and that it was consistent with FIFA regulations.

The PFRA also said match officials who officiated in trial matches involving A-League clubs had not been paid their outstanding match fees by FA, which was refuted by FA, which said there were no outstanding debts owed.

Have games been affected?

Referee Rowan Fisher took charge of the Australia Cup semifinal. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Football Australia was forced to fly in four Singaporean referees for the Australia Cup semifinal clash between Sydney FC and Melbourne Victory on September 9.

Young Australian referee Rowan Fisher, who does not have any A-League experience, took charge of the second semifinal between South Melbourne and Lions FC earlier this week.

It is understood that there is no risk of the Australia Cup final between South Melbourne and Melbourne Victory on October 10 not being played.

This is due to a group of referees that have signed a contract with FA despite the stand-off.

The second season of the second-tier Australian Championship, which kicks off on Thursday October 15, is also not expected to be at risk.

Both those competitions are administered by FA.

However, no assurances have been given about the A-Leagues, Men and Women, which both start that same weekend.

'Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services'

One could understand the A-League referees not wanting to rush back… (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

The nation's referees are clear they want to get back to the business of refereeing.

But they feel their voices need to be heard.

"Our members have delivered an overwhelmingly clear message. They are seeking certainty around their employment, payment of outstanding amounts, and a clear and sustainable structure for professional refereeing in Australia," PFRA president Evgeny Vizelman said in a statement.

"We do not take the decision to stop officiating matches lightly. Our members want to officiate football, prepare for the upcoming season and positively contribute to the success of football in Australia.

"Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services.

"Taking ourselves off the field hurts. There comes a point where people have to stand together and say the way they are being treated is not good enough."

World.title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.

Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.

In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.

At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.

Netball Australia was not idly watching.

As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.

This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.

This is the third year the First Nations Tournament has run. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.

Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.

Embraced in Alice Springs

Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.

Gabby Coffey says it means a lot to bring Indigenous netballers together for the tournament. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.

She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.

Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.

"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.

While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.

The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.

Coffey (left) played for Birmingham in England's top competition. (Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.

Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.

"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.

"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."

Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.

"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."

Visible Indigenous role models key

Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.

"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.

Coffey says it is important to have visible role models. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.

"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.

"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."

She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.

A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.

Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.

Scarlet Jauncey is representing Western Australia, and has captained the Black Swans. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.

"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.

Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.

"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.

In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.

"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.

"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."

Jauncey in action during this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".

"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.

Cultural safety means listening to community

Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.

It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.

Ali Tucker-Munro is Netball Australia's general manager for First Nations. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.

"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."

Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.

"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.

"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."

Players have enjoyed coming together in Melbourne for this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.

The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes

Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.

"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.

"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.

"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.

"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

World.title: From African shepherd to Australia's marathon record holder
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia's men's marathon record holder, Haftu Strintzos, thrives on hard work but still finds it hard to believe where life has taken him.

Born in eastern Tigray in northern Ethiopia, he grew up standing barefoot in fields for hours, helping provide for his family from dawn to dusk.

"I feel as though I have lived a double life in a way," he said after celebrating his 27th birthday in Melbourne.

"I consider myself very privileged to live this life.

" I spent my early days as a shepherd, herding goats and sheep through the mountains of my local village. I grew up without a TV or running water. "

In his remote community, 2,300 metres above sea level, the only source of information he had until age 10 was a mobile phone.

Haftu lost both biological parents by the time he was six, and was taken in by his maternal grandmother, living with his aunt and cousins.

A Greek Australian aid worker by the name of Maria Strintzos came calling, meeting Haftu in 2007 at the age of eight.

Aid worker Maria Strintzos adopted Haftu Strintzos in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

After decades working across Ethiopia, she asked him if he'd like to be her son, adopted him and helped him migrate to Melbourne in 2011 — more than 12,000 kilometres from the mountains of Tigray.

Today, Haftu speaks five languages (Tigrinya, Amharic, Greek, Japanese and English), holds a Master of Electrical Engineering from Villanova University in the USA and recently broke the national marathon record.

Feeling the 'weight of the world'

Maria always felt compelled to help others. Growing up in South Melbourne in the 1960s, she found strength in the local Greek community, even while migrant families faced racism.

"We had absolutely everybody there. As much as I loved growing up there, it built a strength in me," she said.

Haftu Strintzos would walk barefoot from the mountains of eastern Tigray to the village with his blind grandmother, Shifta, to meet his future mother, Maria. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"I grew up knowing what social injustice and inequality looked like."

Her aid work took her through Indonesia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, supporting famine relief, water schemes, food security, women's empowerment and communities affected by conflict, spending 35 years around wars and disease, but also hope, in the Horn of Africa.

But something different about young Haftu stood out.

He would walk barefoot through dry riverbeds, guiding his almost blind grandmother, Shifta, through the mountains to meet Maria.

"He was very respectful," she said.

"And he would sit there really quietly … didn't muck around like the other kids.

"He always had this sort of sad and serious look about him. It's like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.

Haftu Strintzos took every opportunity and excelled at school, with his mother Maria Strintzos helping him go on to the US college system and graduate with a Masters of Electrical Engineering. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"But the way he looked after his grandmother and the way the grandmother would talk about him was very moving at the time too."

With the pull of family ties in Australia, Maria found herself at a crossroads.

"I was challenged at that time because I didn't particularly want to leave Ethiopia," she said.

"I loved my life. I loved what I did … I felt like I was achieving something."

Embracing the challenge of two different worlds

Excelling at school and winning education awards, Haftu embraced every opportunity.

When he migrated to Australia in 2011, he took nothing for granted in his new environment.

Can a marathon help you beat addiction? The science says yes From addiction recovery to mental health, science is revealing why running a marathon can feel so good.

Growing up without electricity, he became fascinated by anything electrical.

Maria bought Haftu toy cars that he would unpack and dismantle.

"He literally pulled them apart with the motors, everything, and reassembled them," she said.

Having never seen a TV, he would sit on the couch for hours waiting for people to appear outside the screen.

"Sometimes I'd catch him sort of looking behind the TV because he thought there was people in there," she said.

"I still can't believe it. It was quite incredible that given his background, that he had this innate gift, something about electricity."

A reward for excelling at school, Haftu Strintzos would relish the chance to earn new stationery and school supplies in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

Maria said she's most proud of how Haftu had risen above adversity in his life.

"Where he's come from it was a rock hut, and they would sleep on the floor and the animals were next to them," she said.

" The uniqueness of Haftu is that he's managed to retain the positive qualities of his experience. I'm in awe of him. "

But the culture shock wasn't easy; different foods, subtle racism and grappling with Western values were also some of Haftu's greatest tests.

Warming climate forcing marathon changes to keep runners cool Marathon organisers across the United States are rethinking when they hold events due to warmer temperatures.

"My biggest challenges in assimilating to Australian culture were learning the English language and motion sickness while riding in cars," he said.

"I remember a time in my early days where the only way I would not throw up while Mum drove the car was if I sat in the front passenger seat and kept my eyes on the road in front."

From a school oval to an athlete with no fear

It wasn't until he moved to Australia that Haftu realised his potential in athletics, having grown up in Tigray not knowing it was even a sport or profession.

"My PE teacher at school encouraged me to pursue it when he saw me run a cross-country race at the school oval," he said.

Adding more strings to his bow, Haftu Strintzos won the 2026 Australian Athletics Cross Country Championships in Ballarat, Victoria. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

In that school race, he just kept running and didn't stop after the finish line, such was his determination for long-distance.

"I have grown up through this sport and learned my most valuable life lessons through it," he said.

"Running helped me connect with my local community, just getting out and about and meeting like-minded people."

His talent soon attracted attention, including from Cathy Freeman, who became like a mentor and even attended his birthday party during his teens.

Training up to 190 kilometres a week under coach Adam Didyk, Haftu broke the Australian men's marathon record in two hours, six minutes and 20 seconds at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

He became the first Australian winner in 20 years, smashed the course record and set a new Oceania record — all on his fourth attempt at the distance.

Haftu Strintzos regularly trains in Melbourne around Albert Park Lake as he prepares for global events. (ABC Sport: Damien Peck)

Didyk, who also coaches Australian women's marathon record holder Jessica Stenson, has guided Haftu remotely from Adelaide for two years.

"He's a fairly no-fuss kind of individual. He'll just take the work and get it done," Didyk said.

"He's obviously very capable when it comes to longer distances and feels confident running at the pace he needs to for the marathon; quite extraordinarily, mind you."

Didyk said Haftu's college experience and early development give him a strong understanding of racing, matched by mental strength.

"He backs himself. He has a lot of confidence in his ability, and he believes in what he can do.

"He's one of those no-fear athletes who sets a goal that looks pretty daunting, but it excites him more and more the scarier he makes it."

Having broken the Australian marathon record in July, Haftu Strintzos (third from left) is aiming for a podium at the Olympics in future years. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

Australian records are just the beginning

Haftu's talent comes as a package. Didyk said the physical ability, mental strength and calmness on race day were all put together to make good decisions, ultimately which led to the record-breaking performance at the Gold Coast Marathon.

"He's just a sensible, quite an intelligent young guy, and that all comes together to match what he can physically do as well," he said.

Haftu's calmness and patience on the Gold Coast reinforced Didyk's belief that he had world-class potential.

"There's so many positives about Haftu that he can go and achieve what no Australian has before in the marathon," Didyk said.

"He's very determined to be successful in international level … it was a phenomenally strong close.

"I think what's probably most important to us now with seeing that is if he's going to be competitive at an Olympic or World Championships level, he's going to need that ability to be able to close really fast over those last 10 kilometres.

Robert de Castella (right) held the national marathon record for 36 years until 2022. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

"He's shown he's got the foundations to do something like that."

"Off the back of that, it started to give us the knowledge of him to go, 'that's the game he can play when he goes to a major championship, he can put himself in there and he can put himself in a competitive situation late in the race'.

"And that's ideally what we're aiming to do with him over the coming years."

From his humble beginnings in Ethiopia, Haftu's dreams of standing on an Olympic podium remain his driving force for motivation for the 2027 World Championships in China, and Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Australia hasn't had an Olympic marathon medallist since Lisa Ondieki won silver in 1988.

"I am very fortunate to have the support systems I need to help me to achieve my goals — something that not every athlete gets to have," he said.

"I want to continue to break records. After all, records are there to be broken."

World.title: How Swans rebuilt their midfield to challenge for premiership
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Rome wasn't built in a day, and neither is an AFL midfield.

But instant construction seemed to be the task for the Sydney Swans after suspending five key players following last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

While the suspensions were the catalyst for major change, smaller moves had been afoot in the weeks and months beforehand.

No midfield has been hotter than the Swans over the past five games. Sydney has gone from a league-average side across the middle to perhaps being the best.

This is despite losing three-time All-Australian Isaac Heeney, fellow superstar Chad Warner and premiership player James Jordon.

Two weeks ago, Sydney surprised the AFL by comprehensively beating reigning premiers Brisbane.

That victory was largely driven by this makeshift force in the middle dynamically (and aggressively) moving the ball while protecting their defence.

Instead of star power, the Swans are relying on structure and balance to drive them deeper into the finals.

System against talent

There's long been a debate in the footy world about system against talent. The Swans have placed themselves firmly in the camp of the former.

In their first game after the suspensions, Sydney tried new combinations, testing them in real footy.

It indicated coach Dean Cox was exploring how the available talent would fit the much-vaunted system, a message he had been preaching all year.

"One thing we want to make sure is that we are a system-based team and role-focused team," Cox said of covering injuries to Heeney and Gulden in March.

The changes to the frontline are the most visible. Sydney relied heavily on Heeney, Warner and Jordon to drive their midfield engine.

Those three accounted for about half of their midfield centre-bounce contributions, let alone their impact around the ground.

But that role focus may have made it easier to replace the suspended stars and, along the way, find a better balance.

Pieces of the puzzle

Midfield balance is often a delicate beast.

If a team is too aggressive, it can be beaten back the other way in transition.

Too passive or defensive, and you can struggle for territory and scoreboard pressure.

As a result, replacing Heeney, Warner and Jordon required some lateral thinking.

Excluding ruck Brodie Grundy, arguably the most important player is James Rowbottom.

Shuffled in and out of different roles, Rowbottom's flexibility within and between games has become a strength.

"I just do what the team needs," Rowbottom told reporters ahead of the qualifying final against the Lions.

"I sort of have done that for the last eight years or so. My role's been ever-changing this year.

"I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing."

However, Rowbottom does his best work hunting the ball and his opponent at the bottom of packs and contests.

Rowbottom sits sixth all-time for tackles per game.

In the past fortnight, he has applied the clamps with 56 pressure acts over the two games, which is a league-leading rate.

He's unafraid to do the dirty work to make his teammates look better.

The reignited star

Two years ago, there were few more valuable young players in the league than Errol Gulden.

However, two injury-struck years dulled his star. It took just a month and a half for that supernova to reignite.

Since their round-20 win over cross-town rivals GWS, Gulden has quickly re-emerged as Sydney's attacking focal point.

Few see angles and hit potential kicks on the field better than Gulden.

As a result, the Swans look to get the ball into Gulden's hands more often than any other player in the league.

Gulden doesn't just blaze away. He's second among midfielders and sixth overall for retained metres gained, normally the specialty of defenders landing safer kicks.

In every way, Gulden finds ways to advance the ball with threat.

Without Heeney and Warner, Gulden is getting even more opportunity with ball in hand. This has improved their overall ball use and added more danger to their impressive attack.

Like all players, Gulden does have flaws.

While his attacking side is nearly unmatched, he is far from a defensive powerhouse.

At just 175 centimetres tall, he can be muscled out and pushed off balance when unable to use his speed.

It means his impact is best realised next to bigger bodies willing to do the hard yards.

The converted defender

While Jai Serong made last year's VFL Team of the Year at Hawthorn, he was unable to crack the stellar Hawks defence or in a wing role.

Given this, few expected Serong to be thrown into the heart of the contest.

But, needing a defensive boost around contest and given his aerobic ability, the Swans decided to explore using Serong as an inside midfielder.

His arrival at stoppage in round 22 accompanied a heavier dose of Gulden at the middle, with Serong further protecting the elite ball-user.

With Serong in the heat of battle, the Swans have become a dominant stoppage force.

He not only provides a safety blanket but has done damage off his own boot, much like Rowbottom.

Young gun

Like many young players in good teams, former first-round pick Angus Sheldrick had to bide his time with short stints on the edges of the midfield rotation.

Sheldrick has firmly established himself as an impact player, both as a regular sub last year and on limited time this season.

But he has made that time count, focusing those minutes on high-impact, stoppage play.

He is able to cover the gaps of the other three with minimal drop-off so far.

The second layer

Often the pinch isn't felt in the front line when changes are made. Instead, it's beyond the main group where depth is really tested.

The Swans are suddenly fielding a slew of names only briefly seen at the top level. Billy Cootee, Tom Hanily, Jesse Dattoli and Caiden Cleary have made leaps in relatively unsung roles around the outside midfield and high half-forward.

Pressure, holding position and supporting structures have been the order of the day. These players, hungry and well-educated, are tasked with forming the outside layer and impacting post clearance.

Alongside more senior figures such as Tom Papley, Jake Lloyd, Braeden Campbell and the potentially returning Justin McInerney, they have helped control the middle of the ground.

Formidable Dockers

In the Swans' path to the grand final stands self-proclaimed minor premier "underdogs" Fremantle.

The Dockers, with a midfield led by Serong's brother Caleb, can pile on points and defend with aplomb.

Winning territory through the middle is critical for the Swans' chances of staying alive one more week. But it's an area that the Dockers have been susceptible to in the past.

The Swans may have had an advantage in the element of surprise against Brisbane. Few knew exactly how Sydney would set up.

But Fremantle may have more of an idea now, unless Cox and the Swans have yet another surprise up their sleeves.

World.title: HYROX athlete apologises and withdraws for defecating mid-race
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has learned "there is more to life than racing" and apologised for continuing to compete in a HYROX competition after soiling herself.

In a contest last weekend in Beijing, Wietrzyk soiled herself and went on to win the event, but has now withdrawn from the race and forfeited all points earned.

Videos of her continuing the race with faecal matter running down her legs were shared widely on social media.

Amid scrutiny over why she continued, Wietrzyk has issued an apology in a statement posted on Instagram.

Joanna Wietrzyk shared an apology online on Thursday, withdrawing and handing back points from the race she won. (Instagram: @joannawietrzyk)

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organisers for what happened during the race in Beijing," the post said.

"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness.

" Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. "

The athlete said she had learned from the experience "that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away".

"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

Loading...

In the statement, Wietrzyk said she had chosen to retroactively withdraw from the race and hand back the points she earned from competing.

Within the HYROX elite framework, athletes accumulate ranking points based on their placement and finishing time. The points contribute to national and global ranking systems.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) has issued an apology. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

HYROX, a popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

The athletics brand, which came under fire over health and safety standards, has since apologised for "not reacting immediately" to the incident.

Rules changed after backlash

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste had earlier taken to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

Social media posts about the incident during the HYROX race in Beijing. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," he added in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

HYROX apologises after athlete soiling The apology comes after different arms of the organisation tried to explain how the situation was managed after the competition went viral online.

He said new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

World.title: Court battle looms for Socceroos star after drug test
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle with the Socceroos star's lawyer confirming he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.

He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

He later underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

However, Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

He copped a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test, but on Thursday his lawyer Paul McGirr confirmed to AAP that he had elected to take the matter to court.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy, which was negative, his club side Sassuolo said.

The Sydney-born player was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

In a statement provided to AAP, a Football Australia spokesperson confirmed the organisation was aware of reports concerning Volpato and a "traffic matter currently subject to a police process".

"As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for Football Australia to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Regardless, the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have previously told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The 22-year-old is currently playing in Serie A with Sassuolo but is sidelined with a right leg injury sustained against Bologna this month.

AAP

Tech.title: Waymo says Singapore will be its next international robotaxi city
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Waymo says it will launch a robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028, as the Alphabet-owned company continues to eye overseas markets for expansion.

Waymo’s vehicles will begin arriving in Singapore in “the coming months,” the company says, in preparation of mapping and autonomous testing with human safety drivers behind the wheel in 2027. Waymo says it is “working toward offering fully autonomous ride-hailing to the public” by 2028.

Waymo will need approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority (LTA) before it can begin accepting passengers. The city-state requires all autonomous vehicles to undergo a safety assessment conducted at the Centre of Excellence for Testing and Research (CETRAN) before they can be deployed on public roads. The tests have been developed by LTA and CETRAN, with input from the Traffic Police. But Waymo isn’t totally unknown in Singapore. The company established a corporate entity there earlier this year and participates in Singapore’s Steering Committee on Autonomous Vehicles.

Singapore has become a hotbed for autonomous vehicle testing. The local authorities have green-lit autonomous freight delivery and road-sweepers, as well as self-driving buses for airport workers. Motional, a US-based company majority owned by Hyundai, conducted a robotaxi pilot in Singapore in 2016.

In addition to Singapore, Waymo has said it plans on launching a robotaxi service in London by the end of 2026, and Tokyo in 2027. The company has also said it will bring its robotaxis to Munich, Germany, in late 2027, marking its first expansion in the European Union.

“Singapore has built one of the safest, most efficient, and most forward-thinking transportation ecosystems in the world,” Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said in a statement. “Their focus on reliability, sustainability, and human-centric progress directly mirrors how we have built Waymo’s technology and service.”

This year, Waymo has announced several new domestic markets, including Nashville, Denver, San Diego, and Las Vegas. The company has around 4,000 vehicles operating in about 15 US cities.

But regulatory hurdles and political opposition have kept it out of some of the US’ most important cities, including New York City, Chicago, and Washington, DC. As the robotaxi debate continues to rage on in America, Waymo has signaled that it intends to keep growing overseas — with no signs of slowing down.

Tech.title: The AI Superintelligence Slowdown
Tech.content:
Remember when tech leaders would tell their employees to “move fast and break things”? It seemed that would be the way of AI too. But after a summer where rogue AI agents became reality, and researchers warned that AI could kill us all, a number of leading US AI companies are publicly suggesting it’s time to pump the brakes and “pace the frontier” of bleeding-edge AI development.

Their motivations are suspect, but leaders at major AI companies — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and X — are at least paying lip service to the idea of a superintelligence slowdown.

Will these AI companies actually slow down? Will anyone step in to regulate these companies like they claim to have wanted for years? Will they manage to convince world leaders that the US must “beat China” to superintelligence and go even faster?

The coordinator keeps work organized, but if any threads work on the same code, the overlap is resolved as a merge conflict just like any other PR. Each thread can further split its delegated work into pieces using subagents, loops, and workflows when needed so large assignments finish faster.
